# Codex desktop context
- You are running inside the Codex (desktop) app, which allows some additional features not available in the CLI alone:

### Images/Visuals/Files
- In the app, the model can display images, videos, and audio using standard Markdown image syntax: ![alt](url)
- When an app or connector generates or edits media, prefer native media already displayed inline or a local output file already returned by the tool. For remote images, prefer Markdown image embeds when permitted by the app's URL-safety policy.
- For media that cannot be displayed directly, including remote video and audio, use the app's preview or display tool when available. Provide a Markdown link to a usable result URL only as a last resort if no preview or display tool can show the result.
- Do not download remote media to work around display restrictions.
- When sending or referencing a local image, video, or audio file, always use an absolute filesystem path in the Markdown image tag (e.g., ![alt](/absolute/path.png)); relative paths and plain text will not render the media.
- When a user asks to play an audio file, render it using Markdown image syntax with an absolute path (e.g., ![audio](/absolute/path.mp3)).
- When referencing code or workspace files in responses, always use full absolute file paths instead of relative paths.
- If a user asks about an image, or asks you to create an image, it is often a good idea to show the image to them in your response.
- Return web URLs as Markdown links (e.g., [label](https://example.com)).

### Pull request diff links
When referencing code from a GitHub PR, you can link directly to its diff in the app using:
[label](codex://review?pr=PR_URL&path=FILE_PATH&line=LINE&side=right)
URL-encode PR_URL and the repository-relative FILE_PATH. Use a verified one-based LINE from the current PR diff. Use side=left for the original code or side=right for the updated code. Enterprise links must use the hostname of this task's configured Git remote. Use ordinary file links for workspace code.

### Workspace Dependencies
- For sheets, slides, and documents, use the MCP server's `load_workspace_dependencies` tool (`mcp__codex_app__load_workspace_dependencies`) to find the bundled runtime and libraries.

### Automations
- This app supports recurring automations, reminders, monitors, follow-ups, and thread wakeups. When the user asks to create, view, update, delete, or ask about automations, search for the `automation_update` tool first, then follow its schema instead of writing raw automation directives by hand.
- For heartbeat monitors, preserve the user's notification intent in the saved prompt. Unless the user explicitly asks for periodic status updates, instruct the heartbeat to stay quiet while the monitored state is unchanged or non-actionable and to notify only on a meaningful change, completion, failure, or required user action. Do not add instructions such as "leave a brief status update" on every run.
- When an automation should archive a Codex thread on completion, use `set_thread_archived` instead of emitting raw archive directives.

### Thread Coordination
- Treat the terms "task", "thread", "chat", and "conversation" as synonyms when they clearly refer to conversations in Codex. Use "chat" when referring to conversations in the product. In technical discussions, preserve the terminology used by the code, APIs, logs, and documentation.
- When the user asks to create, fork, inspect, continue, hand off, pin, archive, unarchive, rename, or otherwise manage Codex threads, search for the relevant thread tool first: `create_thread`, `fork_thread`, `list_threads`, `list_archived_threads`, `read_thread`, `wait_threads`, `send_message_to_thread`, `handoff_thread`, `set_thread_archived`, or `set_thread_title`.
- When following another task's progress, prefer compact `wait_threads` snapshots over repeated `read_thread` calls. Use one target for single-task coordination and `timeoutMs: 0` for a compact immediate snapshot. `create_thread` dispatches asynchronously, so explicitly wait for progress. Use one bounded call for 1-8 targets with each target's `hostId` and cursor as `afterCursor`; it wakes on the first target that completes or needs attention, and timeout includes the latest commentary for all targets without waking on every commentary update. An up-to-date cursor suppresses already-delivered final text. Separate waits from one task may run serially. Do not narrate unchanged snapshots, and leave approval or user-input requests for the user.
- Only use `create_thread` when the user explicitly asks to create a new thread. Threads created this way are user-owned: they appear in the sidebar, and the user is expected to follow up with them directly. For subtasks of the current request, use multi-agent tools instead, including when the user explicitly asks for a subagent.
- After a successful `create_thread` call, emit `::created-thread{threadId="..."}` for a created thread or `::created-thread{clientThreadId="..."}` for queued worktree setup on its own line in your final response.

### Worktrees
- Prefer reusing a suitable active worktree. Create another when no existing checkout is available or work needs separate isolation. When creating one, choose a short name describing the work, such as `worktree-lifecycle` or `composer-input`. An existing name does not need to match every subsequent task; do not rename or replace a worktree just because the work changes.
- Use `archive_worktree` when a worktree is no longer needed, rather than after every PR. Use `restore_worktree` only when the user requests it or to recover specific work archived prematurely.
- A worktree is free for new work when no ongoing task or process relies on it and any existing changes have been accounted for. Prepare the appropriate branch and base before starting new work. Preserve work still in progress; completed or abandoned work can be archived with local changes or unpushed commits because archive saves a recoverable Git snapshot of tracked files and non-ignored untracked files. Ignored files are not saved; preserve any needed ignored files before archival. Do not delete files just to make a worktree eligible for archival. Preserve pinned, shared, or in-use worktrees when cleaning up. Keep the chat open when retiring an individual worktree, and never close an open PR merely to clean up attachments. Use the worktree tools for cleanup and recovery instead of shell deletion. Check at these lifecycle transitions, not every turn.
- When a new isolated checkout is needed, discover and use `create_worktree` before shell worktree creation. It attaches a managed worktree on the chat's host without moving the chat. Wait for completed paths, then use the returned workspace directory explicitly and request filesystem permissions if needed. Use manual Git worktree creation only when the tool is unavailable or the user explicitly requests it.

### Sidebar Organization
- Use `list_threads` to inspect pinned, custom, project, and task sidebar sections, and `list_projects` for project details. Use `create_sidebar_section`, `rename_sidebar_section`, `delete_sidebar_section`, `move_thread_to_sidebar_section`, `move_project_to_sidebar_section`, `reorder_sidebar_projects`, or `reorder_sidebar_sections` to organize tasks and projects. Moving an item into the pinned section pins it.

### Inline Code Comments
- Use the ::code-comment{...} directive when you need to attach feedback directly to specific code lines.
- Emit one directive per inline comment; emit none when there are no actionable inline comments.
- Required attributes: title (short label), body (one-paragraph explanation), file (path to the file).
- Optional attributes: start, end (1-based line numbers), priority (0-3).
- file should be an absolute path or include the workspace folder segment so it can be resolved relative to the workspace.
- Keep line ranges tight; end defaults to start.
- Example: ::code-comment{title="[P2] Off-by-one" body="Loop iterates past the end when length is 0." file="/path/to/foo.ts" start=10 end=11 priority=2}

### Inline Artifact Follow-Ups
- Format each artifact follow-up as an unescaped Markdown list item, `- :codex-followup[visible phrase]{prompt="Complete user request"}`; avoid closing brackets in the visible phrase and escape double quotes in the prompt.

### Git
- Branch prefix: `codex/`. Use this prefix by default when creating branches, but follow the user's request if they want a different prefix.

# AGENTS.md instructions for C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os

<INSTRUCTIONS>
# Global rules — Joshua

These apply on **every** project on this machine, in every session. Project-level
`AGENTS.md` files add to this; they do not replace it.

Keep this file short. It reloads on every message.

---

## Who

Joshua Fisseha — `contact@aspiringattorneys.com`. Builds **LSAT U** (lsatprep.study) and
the Aspiring Attorneys brand. Teaches the LSAT: ~25 one-to-one sessions a week plus
consultations. Windows 11; a MacBook Pro runs some sessions too, so paths differ between
them — never assume `/Users/joshuaf/...` resolves here.

## Where things live

- **AI OS / second brain:** `C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os` — the Obsidian vault. `context/`,
  `wiki/`, `students/`, `corpus/`, `decisions/`, `brainstorms/`, `skills/`, `projects/`.
  Open this folder rather than starting with no folder, or memory cannot accumulate.
- **Skill catalog:** `dev/ai-os/skills/Codex` (179) and `skills/codex` (154), with
  `PARITY.md` declaring deliberate single-runtime skills and `INDEX.md` cataloging them.
- **LSAT U app:** repo `vnjkoxpl-42905/lsatu-684d89db` — React + Vite + TS + Tailwind +
  shadcn, Supabase backend, hosted on Lovable.
- **GitHub:** account `vnjkoxpl-42905` (auto-generated name, correct account).

## How to work with him

- **Do the whole task.** Deliver the finished thing, then say plainly what you skipped
  and why. Don't hand back a plan when the work was asked for.
- **Look before asking.** If the answer is on disk or reachable through a connected tool,
  go get it. He has Firecrawl, Google Workspace (`gws`), and `gh` — use them.
- **Say what's actually true.** Distinguish verified from assumed, every time. If a step
  failed or was skipped, lead with that. A confident wrong answer costs more than "I
  don't know yet."
- **Surface your own mistakes immediately**, including scope errors you notice mid-task.
- Absolute dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`), never "yesterday" or "last week".
- Don't re-ask what he already answered. Don't pad with options he didn't request.

- **Dictation fixes.** A message shaped like `word --> word` (any arrow, any spacing), or
  "save X in my vocabulary", is a Superwhisper correction. Invoke the `superwhisper` skill
  and apply it in that turn, whatever else is in progress.

## Writing as Joshua

Anything published under his name — course copy, lessons, emails, posts.

Plain, direct, confident. Short sentences. Teach the reasoning rather than asserting the
conclusion; this is a teaching brand and the reasoning *is* the product. Concrete beats
abstract. Never condescend to the reader.

**Never use:** "delve into", "dive deep", "unlock", "unleash", "harness the power of",
"in today's fast-paced world", "ever-evolving landscape", "it's not just X, it's Y",
"navigate the complexities", "at the end of the day", "elevate", "supercharge",
"game-changer", "seamless", "robust", "I hope this helps!", "Great question!",
"Certainly!". No em-dash pile-ups. No paragraph opening with "Moreover," /
"Furthermore," / "Additionally,". No emoji in professional writing unless asked.

Headers should say something, not label a category — "Why students miss this", not
"Analysis".

## Safety

- **Draft by default; send only when he says "send".** Email, messages, posts are drafted
  and shown to him. When he says "send it" (or equivalent) in chat, send it, then log it in
  `wiki/send-ledger.md`. Never send on your own initiative, and never treat a request to
  draft as a request to send.
- **Never delete** files, emails, or records without explicit confirmation.
- The Google Workspace grant is broad (it includes deleting all Drive files), so the
  restraint has to live in tool permissions, not in wording. A prompt is not a permission
  layer.
- Secrets stay in `.env` and the OS keyring. Never paste a key into a note, a commit, or
  a chat.

## Tools already connected

- **Firecrawl** — CLI + 28 skills. Prefer it over MCP; the hosted MCP server was removed
  on purpose (the key would sit in plaintext in `~/.Codex.json`).
- **Google Workspace** — `gws` CLI, GCP project `ai-os-joshua`. Gmail, Calendar, Drive,
  Docs, Sheets, Slides, Tasks, People.
- **GitHub** — `gh` CLI, authenticated.

## Cost discipline

`AGENTS.md` reloads on every message, so keep this file lean. Prefer CLIs to MCP servers
(an MCP server can cost ~18k tokens per message in tool definitions). `/clear` between
unrelated tasks. Run the `handoff` skill past ~25% context rather than waiting for
auto-compact.

# Jay 2 — operating instructions for Codex (ai-os)

The canonical root is the repository directory containing this file (`C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os` on this Windows machine). Resolve paths from the repository root instead of assuming a saved Mac or Windows absolute path. This is the router: it holds pointers, not knowledge. Read it, then follow the routing map to the right file instead of searching blind. Twin for Claude Code: `CLAUDE.md`.

## Identity and mission

You are **Jay 2**, Joshua's executive assistant. This root is his EA workspace and command center. Joshua is the founder of Aspiring Attorneys and builder of LSAT U (lsatprep.study), a premium LSAT prep platform; he is the product, voice, and content authority. Your job: take operations, admin, drafting, and research off his plate so his time goes to teaching and building. Frame work as decisions and tradeoffs, not basics.

Standing duties, run from here without re-briefing: student operations (transcripts, assignments, follow-ups via `students/`), prospect and consultation correspondence (drafted in his voice, **never auto-sent unless a pre-approved template**), platform actions on lsatprep.study, session-note ingestion from Gmail/Drive, and keeping the wiki ledgers (`tasks`/`hot`/`log`) current so the next session starts oriented.

## Routing map

Paths are relative to the repository root.

| Need | Path |
|---|---|
| **Who Joshua is** (identity, preferences, contact) | `context/about-me.md` |
| **The business** (offers, money, channels, gaps) | `context/work.md` |
| **Current priorities** (the 90-day slate) | `context/priorities.md` |
| **What we decided and why** (locked decisions) | `decisions/log.md` |
| Freshest session state (hot cache) | `wiki/hot.md` |
| Master index · work ledger · dated history | `wiki/index.md` · `wiki/tasks.md` · `wiki/log.md` |
| Product ground truth (pointers to live backends) | `wiki/dashboard.md` |
| LSAT teaching knowledge | `corpus/index.md` |
| A student — profile, transcripts, work, correspondence | `students/<name>/` — start at `students/README.md` |
| Voice for anything a student or prospect reads | `wiki/teaching-voice.md` |
| Was it sent? (every outbound draft/send) | `wiki/send-ledger.md` — append-only; Gmail is authority |
| Who the students are (name, email, sessions, links) | `students/roster.generated.md` — regenerate, never hand-edit |
| Learned facts and preferences (automemory) | native store `~/.claude/projects/C--Users-Joshu-dev-ai-os/memory/` + `MEMORY.md` index |
| Skill / agent catalog | `skills/INDEX.md`, `agents/` |
| Systems Jay 2 can reach (registry) | `connections.md` — 7 data domains, mechanism/auth/freshness; read by `/audit` |
| Operator brain (how to think about automation) | `references/3ms-framework.md` — the Three Ms; walked weekly by `/level-up` |
| Automation build backlog (what to build next, ranked) | `references/automation-backlog.md` — corpus-derived gaps + tiers; feeds `/level-up` |
| How-it-works reference notes (methods, not state) | `references/` — also `references/claude-plus-codex.md`, `references/obsidian-command-center.md`, `references/second-brain-levels.md` |
| Web research and Firecrawl agents | `references/firecrawl.md` (guidelines in `references/firecrawl/`) |
| Immutable source evidence · intake queue | `raw/sources/` · `raw/inbox/` — one inbox, one archive |
| Archived web clips, with provenance + hashes | `raw/sources/clips/<slug>/` — clip + `PROVENANCE.md` + `SHA256SUMS` |
| Raw personal-data exports (Google Takeout, Gemini session transcripts) | `raw/data-about-me/` — unprocessed PII, git-ignored; never read wholesale |
| Design/plan thinking, dated (grill-me + interview outputs) | `brainstorms/` — supersedes the retired `aios/` reform folder |
| Session handoffs · chat exports | `handoffs/` — operational records, deliberately OUTSIDE `raw/`; `session-handoff` writes here |
| External teardowns and research, dated | `research/` |
| Web-clipped articles (Obsidian Web Clipper) | `raw/inbox/` — unprocessed only; `ingest` moves them to `raw/sources/clips/` when done |
| Application code | `projects/lsatu/` — own repo, own instructions, own remote |
| Other projects (life-path, …) | `projects/<name>/` — each with its own `CLAUDE.md` + `.claude/` |

## Retrieval order

1. `wiki/hot.md` — current-session narrative and open threads.
2. `wiki/index.md` → the page (teaching knowledge: `corpus/index.md`; a student: their folder). Follow links; there is no semantic search and none is needed at this size.
3. The live system — the final freshness escalation.

**Live systems are authority for operational state; the brain mirrors them:** Cal.com + Google Calendar own sessions scheduled/used, LSAT U Supabase owns homework status/dossier/publish state, Stripe owns payment events, Gmail owns correspondence. On any disagreement, the backend wins. The brain is primary — nothing upstream holds them — for transcripts, teaching notes, judgments, prep briefs, curriculum, product specs, and decisions.

**Do not read the wiki unless the task needs it.** Retrieval costs context every turn. Skip it for: code edits in `projects/lsatu/`; shell/Git/file ops; questions the injected memories already answer; a skill run that names its own inputs; anything mechanical and self-contained. Route to it for: what is X · what did we decide and why · who a student is and where they stand · anything drafted in Joshua's voice for someone else · any decision touching roadmap, pedagogy, or UX.

**Wiki operations (LLM-wiki pattern):** the LLM writes/maintains `wiki/` and `corpus/`; Joshua sources, explores, asks. Raw sources are immutable — read, never modify. *Ingest:* read the source from `raw/`, discuss takeaways, write/update the pages it touches, update `wiki/index.md`, append to `wiki/log.md` (`## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | Title`); one source at a time, supervised, unless Joshua says batch. *Query:* index first, then pages; file valuable answers back as pages so explorations compound. *Lint:* `second-brain-lint` for contradictions, stale claims, orphans, missing pages.

## Voice

- **No em-dashes, ever.** Joshua never types them; a stray em-dash reads as AI and costs trust.
- **No AI-slop vocabulary** — never "delve," "tapestry," "testament," "demystify," "boasts," "in the realm of," and their kin.
- **Anything a student or prospect will read** routes through `wiki/teaching-voice.md` and is drafted, never sent, unless it is a pre-approved template.
- **When an outbound message is authorized**, preserve the draft's paragraph breaks, list lines, and intentional spacing. After sending, compare the recipient-facing rendering with the draft and confirm exactly one copy landed. Report any mismatch; never resend automatically.
- **Lead with your recommendation, not a menu.** Be decisive; don't over-hedge.
- **Any prompt Joshua will paste elsewhere** goes inside a fenced code block, never inline prose.

## Tools, keys, and secrets

- **The entire secret model is `.env` + `.gitignore`.** The root `.env` (git-ignored — verify with `git check-ignore .env`) is Joshua's single central store for **everything**: API keys, passwords, and bank/account info (decided 2026-07-17). OAuth client secrets live in `~/.config/gws/`, outside the repo. There is no vault, no Keychain, no encrypted store (`records.sparsebundle` is dead) and none is wanted. Never paste a credential into chat — add it to `.env` directly in the editor.
- **Safety is the tool layer, not prompts:** allow/deny tool lists + scoped API keys. Jay 2 acts under its own credentials and never impersonates Joshua.
- **Connected live systems:** Cal.com, Google Calendar, LSAT U Supabase, Stripe, Gmail. Full registry in `connections.md`.
- **Google access is `gws` CLI only** (`gws gmail|drive|calendar|docs …`, keyring-auth; see `skills/codex/gws-shared/`). Never the Google connector MCPs — the CLI is faster, batchable, and exports Docs to markdown.
- **Government IDs stay outside this OS.** Everything else (student names, emails, schedules, transcripts, notes, payment *links*) is ordinary local working material — classify by content, never by filename.
- **No Git remote**, ever, without first completing the scrub checklist in `wiki/HANDLING.md`. The outer repo never tracks `.env`, `projects/lsatu/` (own repo), runtime logs, or locks. Do not create gitlinks.

## Skills

Everything is a skill — **there are no slash commands** (decided 2026-07-17: one kind, one home, one activation path). The catalog at `skills/` and `agents/` is inert storage; nothing auto-loads. An item runs only once **activated by copy** (not symlink) into `.agents/skills/` (Claude: `.claude/skills/`). Creating one writes to **both** the project and the catalog (`skills/{claude,codex}/`), project-scoped — never auto-global. `claude/` and `codex/` subtrees are never merged; a vendor item is a live symlink + a frozen `_snapshots/` copy. `system/scripts/check-skills.sh` validates the model; `skills/INDEX.md` indexes it.

Active in this root. Run `pickup` only when Joshua explicitly asks for it. Do not run it automatically at session start. Use `wrapup` at the end of substantive sessions:

| Skill | Use it when |
|---|---|
| `pickup` / `wrapup` | `pickup` only on Joshua's explicit request / `wrapup` at session end (wrapup persists to the wiki ledgers) |
| `session-handoff` | mid-work context reset near ~250k, or passing work Codex↔Claude — chat-only, writes nothing |
| `audit` | scoring the OS against the Four Cs (structural health, /100) |
| `level-up` | weekly 3Ms interview to find + ship one automation |
| `consultation-inquiry-drafts`, `-followup-drafts`, `inbound-tutoring-replies` | drafting to prospects/students — always via the teaching voice |
| `guided-drill-assignment` | assigning a student a drill |
| `lsat-u-platform-actions` | doing anything ON lsatprep.study from here (assign, post, message, ingest) |
| `tutorocean-profile-fill` | TutorOcean profile work |
| `prompt-architect-refiner` | refining a prompt before it ships |
| `accommodations-email` | "accommodations email to X" (dictation: "accommodations scale"); pre-approved send, QP form attached, self-logging |

When a skill run exposes a gap, improve the skill before moving on. Runtime-specific catalog differences must be justified in `skills/PARITY.md`; undeclared differences are defects.

## Guardrails

- **95% rule.** Make no changes until you are 95% confident what Joshua wants. Ask until you are.
- **Lovable credits require confirmation.** Never take an action that spends or may spend Lovable credits without Joshua's explicit confirmation immediately before the action. Do not infer approval from a broader request to fix, build, deploy, or continue. Free Lovable controls and direct deployment paths may be used without this credit-spend confirmation.
- **Lovable Cloud deploys through Lovable.** LSAT U currently uses a Lovable Cloud-managed backend. Deploy its Edge Functions through the Lovable agent, not the Supabase CLI, unless the backend has first been migrated to a separately managed Supabase project. Confirm this route with Joshua before starting a Lovable deployment.
- **Root stays thin.** Don't accumulate files at the root; work products go to their homes (wiki, students, corpus, projects). Anything left at root gets filed before the session ends.
- **Delegate bulk work.** Exploration or analysis spanning 3+ files goes to a sub-agent that returns summaries, not file dumps.
- **Shell ergonomics.** Run one command per call — chained `cmd; cmd` and `rm -rf X && clone Y` forms trip permission denials that the split commands would not. Never poll with `sleep`. Use backgrounded execution for anything slow, and raise the timeout explicitly for known-slow ops (large moves, typecheck-gated pushes, full verify runs) rather than eating the default.
- **Search before creating.** One authoritative page per subject — update it, don't grow a parallel truth. `wiki/index.md` catalogs every page and updates on every ingest.
- **Preserve provenance and source hashes.** Never move, delete, or modify a migration source root — copy and hash-verify. Never follow a source symlink outside its registered root.
- **Conflicts stay explicit until adjudicated** — never silently overwrite one source generation with another.
- **Automation writes only generated files or fenced generated sections,** through compare-and-swap.
- **Obey nested instruction files** — they win over broader ones for their subtree. LSATU's recovered `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` are inviolate: never regenerate them without Joshua's explicit approval.
- **Memory = native automemory.** "Remember that…" writes one fact per file to the native store; `MEMORY.md` indexes it. This file is the rules; memory is learned facts — never mix them. Transcripts and raw captures never auto-promote.
- **Append meaningful system changes** to `wiki/log.md`; log locked decisions to `decisions/log.md`.

## Dual-runtime (Codex + Claude)

- Begin at the Git-root `AGENTS.md` and follow directory-scoped instruction files toward the working path; the nearest file wins for its subtree.
- Keep root instructions inside the runtime byte budget. Move narrow rules to the narrowest owning directory rather than growing this file.
- Activated skills are **copies** in `.agents/skills/` (from `skills/codex/`); agent definitions convert to `.codex/agents/*.toml` with the instructions in `developer_instructions`.
- Claude reads `CLAUDE.md` and never this file. Anything that must hold for both runtimes goes in BOTH files — when you change it here, mirror it there; keep the routing map and guardrails byte-identical between them.
- Activation is unequal by design: Codex reads copies in `.agents/skills/`, Claude reads copies in `.claude/skills/`. Codex runs the catalog minus the wiki/Obsidian and `graphify` skills, so the two skill tables legitimately differ.
- Never have Claude and Codex editing the same file at once; pass work between them by session handoff (summarize → clear → paste). At ~250k tokens, hand off rather than riding autocompact.

and\r\n- keeps private teaching judgments below the `Notes for me (not posted)` divider.\r\n\r\n## Reference structure\r\n\r\nThe Sofia note uses this content-shaped progression:\r\n\r\n1. **Concept title.** `Conditional Must Be True: Facts, Rules, and Bridges`\r\n2. **Direct orientation.** The two moves are stated immediately: connect rules or use a\r\n   fact to activate a rule.\r\n3. **Method at a glance.** A small table distinguishes chaining from triggering.\r\n4. **Foundational distinction.** Facts and rules are defined before either is applied.\r\n5. **First method.** Chaining is taught through a definition, positional test, diagram,\r\n   valid example, invalid example, hidden case, and longer-chain consequence.\r\n6. **Second method.** Triggering is taught through its two legal moves and the two facts\r\n   that produce no inference.\r\n7. **Decision aid.** A four-row table makes valid and invalid directions visible.\r\n8. **Execution advice.** The student learns when to contrapose, when to diagram, and how\r\n   to test a conditional answer from its trigger.\r\n9. **Repeatable process.** A numbered procedure turns the lesson into something usable\r\n   on the next question.\r\n10. **Practice.** Checkboxes state the work actually assigned.\r\n11. **Private continuation.** Weak spots, Joshua's follow-ups, and teaching judgments are\r\n    separated from the student-facing note.\r\n\r\n## What to copy and what to vary\r\n\r\nCopy the depth, hierarchy, and independence from remembered question context. This is a glossary, not a\r\nspec. Implementation lives in the skills and scripts; decisions live in\r\n`decisions/log.md`.\r\n\r\n## Language\r\n\r\n### Paying and scheduling\r\n\r\n**Package**:\r\nFive or ten hours of tutoring bought upfront through Stripe, with\r\nbetween-session coaching included.\r\n_Avoid_: Bundle, plan, subscription, credits (credits are the pass's units, not the product)\r\n\r\n**Booking pass**:\r\nThe prepaid entitlement a student holds when sessions are **owed** to them,\r\ncarrying the count owed and the count used. Reachable at `/book/<slug>`.\r\n_Avoid_: Booking link (that is the pass's URL, not the thing), booking access, pass token\r\n\r\n**Owed sessions**:\r\nSessions a student has paid for and not yet taken. The booking pass is the\r\n**only** record of these; if no pass exists, nothing is owed.\r\n_Avoid_: Balance, remaining sessions, package balance (there is no separate balance model)\r\n\r\n**Arrangement**:\r\nWhat a student actually bought, and when. A ten-hour package on a given date,\r\nor pay-per-session at a given rate. Authored on the student's page, durable,\r\nand never rewritten: it is history, not state.\r\n_Avoid_: Plan, deal, terms\r\n\r\n**Live status**:\r\nThe regenerated mirror of a student's current backend state, including how many\r\nowed sessions remain. Lives in `live-status.generated.md`, is rebuilt from the\r\nbackend, and is never hand-edited or hand-corrected.\r\n_Avoid_: Balance sheet, status page\r\n\r\n**Single session**:\r\nOne tutoring session paid for individually through a Stripe-linked Cal.com\r\nlink, rather than out of a package. Needs no booking pass.\r\n_Avoid_: One-off, ad hoc session, hourly\r\n\r\n**Three-tier offer**:\r\nThe standard offer presented after a consultation: a single session at $45 per\r\nhour, a five-hour package at $40 per hour, and a ten-hour package at $35 per\r\nhour. Each offer carries its own verified action link. A prospect-specific\r\narrangement agreed during the consultation replaces the standard offer\r\nentirely.\r\n_Avoid_: Pricing menu, universal rate, package discount table\r\n\r\n**Consultation**:\r\nA free introductory call, booked through the Cal.com complimentary link. Does\r\nnot make the person a student.\r\n_Avoid_: Intro call, discovery call, free session\r\n\r\n**Consultation follow-up**:\r\nA message to a prospect who completed a consultation and has not paid. Payment\r\nends the consultation follow-up stage and moves the person into onboarding. The\r\nmessage presents the three tutoring offers so the prospect can choose how to\r\nbegin.\r\n_Avoid_: Onboarding email, post-payment email, student follow-up, application form email\r\n\r\n**Onboarding**:\r\nThe stage triggered by confirmed payment when a new student receives LSAT U\r\naccess and completes intake inside the platform. It does not require the person\r\nto reply to the consultation follow-up.\r\n_Avoid_: Consultation follow-up, application form, sales follow-up\r\n\r\n**LSAT U account creation**:\r\nCreating an account at `lsatprep.study`. A prospect may do this before payment,\r\nbut account creation alone does not grant student permissions or begin\r\nonboarding.\r\n_Avoid_: Onboarding, student access, enrollment\r\n\r\n### Relationship\r\n\r\nOne path, and everyone is on it. There is no separate category for a\r\nconsultation that never converted; that is a prospect who went quiet.\r\n\r\n**Prospect**:\r\nSomeone who has had a consultation but has never been taught a session.\r\n_Avoid_: Lead, inquiry, non-student\r\n\r\n**Active**:\r\nSomeone who is owed sessions, or who has been taught recently.\r\n_Avoid_: Current, enrolled, ongoing\r\n\r\n**Lapsed**:\r\nSomeone owed nothing who has gone quiet. Applies to a prospect who never\r\nconverted as much as to a student who stopped.\r\n_Avoid_: Churned, inactive, dormant, lost\r\n\r\n**Student record**:\r\nThe folder under `students/` holding everything authored about a person. A\r\nperson earns one by being **taught a session**, because teaching is what\r\nproduces notes, transcripts, and judgments the brain alone holds. A\r\nconsultation alone does not earn a record.\r\n_Avoid_: Profile, student file\r\n\r\n### Identity\r\n\r\n**Contact address**:\r\nThe address a student actually replies from, as evidenced in Gmail. Its canonical\r\nshape is `https://7sage.com/u/usr_<id>/review`.\r\n_Avoid_: 7Sage login-token URL, drill link, settings link, generic 7Sage URL\r\n\r\n### Notes on the model\r\n\r\n- **A student with no booking pass is the normal case, not a gap.** It means\r\n  nothing is owed to them; they book single sessions through their Cal.com\r\n  link. Only a student who is owed sessions should hold a pass.\r\n- The two paths are not exclusive. Someone can hold a pass from a package and\r\n  also have a Cal.com single-session link.\r\n- A **revoked** pass is a dead link and must never be treated as a way to book.\r\n  An **exhausted** pass is live but has no owed sessions left.\r\n- Status is authored, not computed: it is a judgment about the relationship.\r\n  But hard evidence that contradicts it gets surfaced rather than silently\r\n  tolerated, the same way a contact address that disagrees with the backend\r\n  does.\r\n- A prospect who never converts has no record, but is still tracked by name so\r\n  follow-up remains possible. Losing sight of them is the failure this guards\r\n  against.\r\n- **Arrangement and live status are different things and live apart.** What was\r\n  bought is authored and permanent; what remains is mirrored and regenerated. The group after “of” is your starting group. Keep it fixed as you reason. Most mistakes come from silently switching to the other group or treating a possible amount as a proven amount.\r\n\r\n## The three quantities\r\n\r\n| Statement | What it guarantees | What it leaves open |\r\n|---|---|---|\r\n| Some A are B | At least one A is B | It could be a small minority, a majority, or all A. |\r\n| Most A are B | More than half of A are B | It could be all A. Nothing establishes how much of B is A. |\r\n| All A are B | Every A is B | B may include many things outside A. |\r\n\r\n“Most” means **more than 50%**, not necessarily exactly 51%. The minimum whole-number count depends on the size of the group. Among five apples, three is most. Among one hundred apples, fifty-one is most.\r\n\r\nIf a group exists, `all A are B` establishes `most A are B`, and `most A are B` establishes `some A are B`. The reverse steps do not work. “Some” permits “all” as a possibility; it does not prove it.\r\n\r\n## Keep the direction when you switch groups\r\n\r\n`Some apples are green` also means `some green things are apples`. The same apple witnesses both statements. “Some” is reversible.\r\n\r\n`Most apples are green` establishes `some green things are apples`, but it does **not** establish `most green things are apples`. Green things may include a vast number of objects that are not apples. Likewise, “most apples are green” gives you no basis to claim that any apples are *not* green. All apples could be green.\r\n\r\nWhen you read “most A are B,” ask: **Most of which group?** The answer is A. The proportion is measured against A, not B.\r\n\r\n## Two majorities of one group must meet\r\n\r\nSuppose most of a class takes history, and most of the same class takes biology. At least one student must take both. If the groups did not overlap, two separate groups each containing more than half the class would not fit inside the class.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nMost A are B.\r\nMost A are C.\r\nTherefore, some B are C.\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe repeated starting group matters. Two “most” statements about different starting groups do not automatically create this overlap.\r\n\r\n## Carry a quantity through a universal rule\r\n\r\n```text\r\nSome apples are green.\r\nAll green apples are edible.\r\nTherefore, some apples are edible.\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe second rule applies to the green apples identified by the first statement. You can carry that same group forward. If **most** apples are green, then most apples are edible under that universal rule.\r\n\r\nCheck the middle idea before chaining. The rule must apply to the things already identified. “Some apples are green” plus “most green things are edible” is insufficient: the green apples might all be among the green things that are not edible.\r\n\r\n## Compare total group sizes without reversing “most”\r\n\r\nConsider two groups, banjo players and guitar players. Suppose **most banjo players also play guitar**, while **most guitar players do not play banjo**.\r\n\r\nLet the overlap be the people who play both. The overlap is more than half of the banjo group. Yet it is less than half of the guitar group, because the majority of guitar players are outside the overlap. The same overlap cannot be more than half of a larger group and less than half of a smaller group. The guitar group must therefore be larger.\r\n\r\nYou did not reverse either “most” statement. You compared how the shared overlap sits inside each total group.\r\n\r\n## A check for each quantity question\r\n\r\n1. Name the starting group in each statement.\r\n2. Mark what is guaranteed: at least one, more than half, or every member.\r\n3. If the groups overlap, ask whether the same people are being counted on both sides.\r\n4. Reject a backward “most” inference unless the premises independently establish it.\r\n5. Test a tempting answer against a possible arrangement of the groups. If the premises can be true while the answer is false, the answer is not guaranteed.\r\n\r\n## Before next session\r\n\r\n- [ ] Finish the remaining conditional drills, including the medium drill.\r\n- [ ] Text me about a Friday time for the remaining session. We know that at least one is chocolate, but we do not know how many. The words *some*, *most*, and *all* tell us how many cookies a sentence commits us to.\n+\n+![A range chart showing that some of 10 means 1 through 10, most means 6 through 10, and all means exactly 10.](./assets/quantity-ranges.svg)\n+\n+The colored ranges show **possibilities**, not additional facts. If a sentence says “some cookies are chocolate,” all 10 *could* be chocolate. You cannot conclude that all 10 *are* chocolate.\n+\n+## Some: at least one\n+\n+> **Some cookies are chocolate.**\n+\n+At least one cookie is chocolate. It might be **1 of 10, 6 of 10, or 10 of 10**. The sentence rules out zero and leaves every other count open.\n+\n+In ordinary conversation, “some” often suggests “some, but not all.” On the LSAT, that suggestion is not part of the claim. **Some can include most or all.**\n+\n+The sentence also works in reverse: if some cookies are chocolate, then some chocolate things are cookies. The same cookie proves both claims.\n+\n+## Most: more than half\n+\n+> **Most cookies are chocolate.**\n+\n+More than half the cookies are chocolate. On a plate of 10, that means **6 through 10**. On a plate of 5, it means **3 through 5**. The threshold depends on the size of the group; “most” is not always 51%.\n+\n+All 10 could be chocolate. So “most” does **not** tell you that any non-chocolate cookies exist.\n+\n+It also does not tell you that most *chocolate things* are cookies. The sentence counts cookies, while that reversed claim would count every chocolate thing in the world. What you can say in reverse is **some chocolate things are cookies**.\n+\n+## All: every one\n+\n+> **All cookies are chocolate.**\n+\n+Every cookie on the plate is chocolate: **10 of 10**. There is no room for a non-chocolate cookie. The sentence still does not say that every chocolate thing is a cookie.\n+\n+Because all 10 are chocolate, more than half are chocolate, and at least one is chocolate. That is why the guaranteed claims run this way, assuming the group has at least one member:\n+\n+![A one-way implication diagram: all implies most, and most implies some. The reverse arrows are crossed out.](./assets/quantity-implications.svg)\n+\n+**Read the arrows as guarantees.** “All” guarantees “most,” and “most” guarantees “some.” “Some” merely *allows* “all”; it does not guarantee it.\n+\n+## The question to ask when the groups switch\n+\n+Ask **“What are we counting?”** in each sentence.\n+\n+| Claim | We are counting | Safe conclusion about the other group |\n+|---|---|---|\n+| Most cookies are chocolate. | Cookies | Some chocolate things are cookies. |\n+| Most chocolate things are cookies. | Chocolate things | Some cookies are chocolate. |\n+\n+Neither row follows from the other. Both claims count the same class. If they count different groups, there is no guaranteed overlap.\n+\n+## When a rule lets you carry a group forward\n+\n+Suppose some apples are green, and **all green apples are edible**. At least one apple is green, and every green apple is edible. So some apples are edible. If most apples are green, then most apples are edible under that same rule.\n+\n+Change the second sentence to “most green things are edible,” and the conclusion fails. The green apples could all be among the green things that are not edible. A *most* claim cannot do the work of an *all* rule here.\n+\n+## The banjo and guitar example\n+\n+Most banjo players also play guitar. Most guitar players do **not** play banjo. Think only about the people who play both instruments:\n+\n+| Same overlap | Compared with banjo players | Compared with guitar players |\n+|---|---|---|\n+| People who play both | More than half | Less than half |\n+\n+The shared overlap fills a larger fraction of the banjo group than of the guitar group. Therefore, the guitar group is larger. We did not reverse a “most” claim; we compared the same people against two different totals.\n+\n+## A reminder from the conditional drills\n+\n+“No A are B” translates to **A → not B**. First learn the amount each word guarantees. Then learn which conclusions you can carry forward, reverse, or combine.\n+\n+## First, learn the ranges\n+\n+Imagine **10 cookies**. We are asking how many of them are chocolate.\n+\n+![A chart showing the possible number of chocolate cookies out of ten: some allows one through ten, most allows six through ten, and all requires ten.](./assets/quantity-ranges.svg)\n+\n+| Sentence | What it guarantees | What it still allows |\n+|---|---|---|\n+| **Some cookies are chocolate.** | At least 1 of 10 is chocolate. | Anywhere from 1 to 10 could be chocolate. |\n+| **Most cookies are chocolate.** | More than half are chocolate: at least 6 of 10. | Anywhere from 6 to 10 could be chocolate. |\n+| **All cookies are chocolate.** | Exactly 10 of 10 are chocolate. | No non-chocolate cookie is possible. |\n+\n+“Some” often suggests “some, but not all” in ordinary conversation. That suggestion is not part of the LSAT claim. **Some can include most or all.** “Most” can include all too.\n+\n+These are ranges of *possible* counts. They are not all counts you have *proved*. If you are told “some,” you have proved at least one. You have **not** proved most or all.\n+\n+![Three rows of cookies illustrating one valid example each: one chocolate cookie for some, six for most, and ten for all.](./assets/cookie-examples.svg)\n+\n+The cookie rows are examples. The range chart shows every count each word permits.\n+\n+## Which statement is strong enough to prove another?\n+\n+![A one-way diagram in which all guarantees most, and most guarantees some.](./assets/quantity-implications.svg)\n+\n+If a group has at least one member, **all → most → some**. Every stronger statement proves the weaker ones. The reverse does not follow:\n+\n+- “Some cookies are chocolate” could describe all 10, but it does not prove all 10 are chocolate.\n+- “Most cookies are chocolate” could describe all 10, but it does not prove all 10 are chocolate.\n+- “Some cookies are chocolate” does not prove that most are chocolate. One chocolate cookie would make “some” true and “most” false.\n+\n+**Possible is not guaranteed.** That is the distinction to keep in mind whenever you move between these words.\n+\n+## The arrows work differently\n+\n+Let **A** be one group and **B** another. An arrow describes what the sentence lets you say about their relationship. These are quantity arrows, except for the ordinary conditional arrow under “all.”\n+\n+![The three quantity arrow patterns: some works in both directions as some; most gives some in reverse; all gives a one-way conditional arrow and its contrapositive.](./assets/quantity-arrows.svg)\n+\n+### Some: the overlap works in both directions\n+\n+If **some A are B**, at least one thing belongs to both groups. That same thing proves **some B are A**. You can turn the sentence around without changing “some.”\n+\n+```text\n+Some A are B  ⇔  Some B are A\n+```\n+\n+This is a two-way **some** relationship. It does **not** mean every A is B or every B is A.\n+\n+### Most: keep the majority in its original direction\n+\n+If **most A are B**, more than half of A are B. Because at least one A is B, **some B are A**. That is the safe conclusion when you look back from B.\n+\n+```text\n+Most A are B  →  Some B are A\n+```\n+\n+You cannot reverse it as **most B are A**. The sentence measured a majority of A; it did not tell you what fraction of B is A. You also cannot assume that some A are *not* B, because all A could be B.\n+\n+### All: use the conditional arrow\n+\n+If **all A are B**, every A is B:\n+\n+```text\n+A → B\n+not B → not A    (contrapositive)\n+```\n+\n+The contrapositive is valid because something outside B cannot be inside A if every A is inside B. The reverse, **B → A**, is not valid. B may contain things that are not A.\n+\n+If at least one A exists, “all A are B” also gives you **some A are B** and **some B are A**. Without that existence, an all-rule alone does not establish that any A exists.\n+\n+## When arrows can be joined\n+\n+The middle group has to connect the claims in a way that covers the members you are carrying forward.\n+\n+| Given | What follows | Why |\n+|---|---|---|\n+| All A are B. All B are C. | **All A are C.** | Every A enters B, and every B enters C. |\n+| Some A are B. All B are C. | **Some A are C.** | The A that are B are covered by the all-rule. |\n+| Most A are B. All B are C. | **Most A are C.** | The majority of A inside B are all covered by the rule. |\n+| Most A are B. Most A are C. | **Some B are C.** | Two majorities of the same A group must overlap. |\n+\n+For the last row, picture 10 members of A. More than 5 are B, and more than 5 are C. Those two sets cannot be separate within only 10 members. At least one member is both B and C.\n+\n+![Two majorities measured against the same ten members of A must overlap.](./assets/shared-majority.svg)\n+\n+## When the arrows do not join\n+\n+**Some A are B + most B are C** does not guarantee that any A are C. The A inside B could all be among the B that are not C.\n+\n+**Most A are B + most B are C** does not guarantee that any A are C. The two “most” claims count different groups, and the A inside B could sit outside C.\n+\n+**All A are B + some B are C** does not guarantee that any A are C. The B that are C could be B that are not A.\n+\n+When a connection feels tempting, ask: **Can the members identified by the first sentence all be outside the part described by the second?** If yes, the conclusion is not guaranteed.\n+\n+## Check yourself\n+\n+**1.** Some A are B. Could all A be B? Does the premise prove that all A are B?\n+\n+**Answer:** Yes, all A *could* be B. No, the premise does not prove it.\n+\n+**2.** Most A are B. What can you safely say about B that are A?\n+\n+**Answer:** Some B are A. You cannot say most B are A without another premise.\n+\n+**3.** Most A are B, and most A are C. The key distinction is: **“some” can include “most” or “all,” but “some” does not prove either.** For a group with members, the guarantees run **all → most → some**. “Some A are B” reverses as “some B are A.” “Most A are B” reverses only as “some B are A.” “All A are B” gives **A → B** and its contrapositive.

I also added a diagram showing why two majorities of the *same* group must overlap. Nothing has been posted.

How many are chocolate?\r\n\r\n- **Some** means at least one. It could be all 10.\r\n- **Most** means more than half. With 10 cookies, that means at least 6. It could be all 10.\r\n- **All** means every cookie. With 10 cookies, that means exactly 10.\r\n\r\n## The range each word leaves open\r\n\r\n![A chart showing the possible number of chocolate cookies out of ten: some allows one through ten, most allows six through ten, and all requires ten.](./assets/quantity-ranges.svg)\r\n\r\nIn ordinary conversation, “some” often sounds like “some, but not all.” On the LSAT, it just means **at least one**. The chart shows what each word *allows*. The sentence proves only what the word *guarantees*.\r\n\r\n![Three rows of cookies illustrating one valid example each: one chocolate cookie for some, six for most, and ten for all.](./assets/cookie-examples.svg)\r\n\r\nThe cookie rows are examples. The range chart shows every count each word permits.\r\n\r\n## What follows from what?\r\n\r\n![A one-way diagram in which all guarantees most, and most guarantees some.](./assets/quantity-implications.svg)\r\n\r\nIf there are cookies on the plate, **all → most → some**. Each step to the right makes a weaker claim. You cannot move left without more information:\r\n\r\n- “Some cookies are chocolate” could describe all 10, but it does not prove all 10 are chocolate.\r\n- “Most cookies are chocolate” could describe all 10, but it does not prove all 10 are chocolate.\r\n- “Some cookies are chocolate” does not prove that most are chocolate. One chocolate cookie would make “some” true and “most” false.\r\n\r\n**Could be true** is different from **must be true**. Keep that distinction in view whenever you move between these words.\r\n\r\n## The arrows work differently\r\n\r\nNow use **A** and **B** to stand for any two groups. The arrows show exactly what you can say when you turn a statement around.\r\n\r\n![The three quantity arrow patterns: some works in both directions as some; most gives some in reverse; all gives a one-way conditional arrow and its contrapositive.](./assets/quantity-arrows.svg)\r\n\r\n### Some: the overlap works in both directions\r\n\r\nIf **some A are B**, at least one thing is both A and B. That same thing proves **some B are A**. You can turn the sentence around and keep “some.”\r\n\r\n```text\r\nSome A are B  ⇔  Some B are A\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe **some** statement works both ways. This does **not** mean every A is B or every B is A.\r\n\r\n### Most does not reverse as most\r\n\r\nIf **most A are B**, more than half of A are B. At least one thing is therefore both A and B, so **some B are A**.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nMost A are B  →  Some B are A\r\n```\r\n\r\nYou cannot turn that into **most B are A**. The sentence tells you about the A group, not how many of all the B things are A. You also cannot claim that some A are *not* B. All A could be B.\r\n\r\n### All: use the conditional arrow\r\n\r\nIf **all A are B**, every A is B:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nA → B\r\nnot B → not A    (contrapositive)\r\n```\r\n\r\nIf every A is B, something that is **not B** cannot be A. That is why the contrapositive works. The reverse, **B → A**, does not: B may include things outside A.\r\n\r\nIf at least one A exists, “all A are B” also tells you **some A are B** and **some B are A**. The rule by itself does not tell you whether any A exists.\r\n\r\n## When two statements connect\r\n\r\nYou can carry A through B when the second statement covers the B members you already know about.\r\n\r\n| Given | What follows | Why |\r\n|---|---|---|\r\n| All A are B. All B are C. | **All A are C.** | Every A enters B, and every B enters C. |\r\n| Some A are B. All B are C. | **Some A are C.** | The A that are B are covered by the all-rule. |\r\n| Most A are B. All B are C. | **Most A are C.** | The majority of A inside B are all covered by the rule. |\r\n| Most A are B. Most A are C. | **Some B are C.** | Two majorities of the same A group must overlap. |\r\n\r\nFor the last row, picture 10 things in group A. More than 5 are B, and more than 5 are C. Those groups cannot stay separate inside a group of only 10. At least one A must be both B and C.\r\n\r\n![Two majorities measured against the same ten members of A must overlap.](./assets/shared-majority.svg)\r\n\r\n## When two statements do not connect\r\n\r\n**Some A are B + most B are C** does not guarantee that any A are C. The A inside B could all be among the B that are not C.\r\n\r\n**Most A are B + most B are C** does not guarantee that any A are C. The two “most” claims count different groups, and the A inside B could sit outside C.\r\n\r\n**All A are B + some B are C** does not guarantee that any A are C. The B that are C could be B that are not A.\r\n\r\nThe test is simple: **Could the A's from the first statement all be outside the part of B named by the second?** If they could, you do not have a guaranteed conclusion.\r\n\r\n## Try these before reading the answers\r\n\r\n**1.** Some A are B. Could all A be B? Does the premise prove that all A are B?\r\n\r\n**Answer:** Yes, all A *could* be B. No, the premise does not prove it.\r\n\r\n**2.** Most A are B. What can you safely say about B that are A?\r\n\r\n**Answer:** Some B are A. You cannot say most B are A without another premise.\r\n\r\n**3.** Most A are B, and most A are C. Why must some B be C?\r\n\r\n**Answer:** Both majorities are taken from the same A group. Each occupies more than half of it, so they must overlap.\r\n"}]

Check what a word\r\nalready means on the page before reusing it.\r\n\r\n### "say it back" → "tell it back", "The Read" → "The Recall"\r\nThe library door still carried both retired names. The clock is at the foot\r\nand in the long version. The stimulus count measured the work in a unit she has\r\nno feel for.\r\n**Lesson:** delete a line that repeats what is above it. Do not reword it.\r\n\r\n## Booking emails: hand over the link, not the pass settings (2026-09-08)\r\n\r\n**Cut:** "70 minutes each, and no expiration date, so there\'s no rush to use them."\r\n**Keep:** "You\'re set up on LSAT U with 10 sessions."\r\n\r\nSession length and expiry are admin fields. Everything else about the pass stays in the backend.\r\n\r\n**Lesson:** in a booking email, say who it\'s for, how many sessions, and the link.\r\nStop there.\r\n\r\n## Drill hub: say what the button does, not what the feature is called (2026-09-09)\r\n\r\nSix changes on `/classroom/drill`, from the run-3 pass. ## assistant

The references support a useful teaching order. The diagrams separate what a statement says about one group from what can be inferred about another, and they show that a chain works when an **all** rule covers the group you have reached. I’ll use one cookie example across the definitions and inference section so the reader does not have to learn a new scenario at every step.

const patch="*** Begin Patch\n*** Add File: brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/06-some-most-all-note.md\n+# Some, Most, and All: What Each Statement Proves\n+\n+Start with a tray of **10 cookies**. The sentence tells us how many cookies have a certain feature. Our job is to keep separate what it **proves** from what it merely **allows**.\n+\n+## Some means at least one\n+\n+> **Some of the cookies contain chocolate.**\n+\n+At least **one** cookie contains chocolate. That is the entire guarantee. It could be one cookie, six cookies, or all ten. The only count ruled out is zero.\n+\n+![One chocolate cookie and ten chocolate cookies both satisfy some of the cookies contain chocolate.](./assets/some-cookie-cases.svg)\n+\n+In everyday speech, “some” can sound like “some, but not all.” That is not how we read it here. **Some can include most. Some can include all.** Neither one follows *just* because we heard “some.”\n+\n+“Some” also works in both directions. If some cookies contain chocolate, then some things that contain chocolate are cookies. We are talking about the **same cookie** each time.\n+\n+```text\n+Some A are B  ⇔  Some B are A\n+```\n+\n+The double arrow connects two **some statements**. It does not mean that every A is B or every B is A.\n+\n+## Most means more than half\n+\n+> **Most of the cookies contain chocolate.**\n+\n+With ten cookies, **six or more** contain chocolate. With five cookies, **three or more** do. “Most” means more than half, so the minimum count changes with the size of the group.\n+\n+![Six chocolate cookies and ten chocolate cookies both satisfy most of the cookies contain chocolate.](./assets/most-cookie-cases.svg)\n+\n+All ten could contain chocolate. “Most” does not tell us that any plain cookies exist.\n+\n+Now watch what happens if we turn the sentence around. We know **some things that contain chocolate are cookies**. We do **not** know that *most* things that contain chocolate are cookies. The first sentence counted cookies. The reversed sentence would count every chocolate-containing thing.\n+\n+```text\n+Most A are B  →  Some B are A\n+Most A are B  ↛  Most B are A\n+```\n+\n+The majority stays attached to **A**. Looking back from B, we have only **some**.\n+\n+## All means every one\n+\n+> **All of the cookies contain chocolate.**\n+\n+Now all **ten out of ten** contain chocolate. One plain cookie would make the statement false.\n+\n+![Ten chocolate cookies are required for all of the cookies contain chocolate.](./assets/all-cookie-case.svg)\n+\n+“All” gives us a regular conditional rule. If something is a cookie on this tray, it contains chocolate. If it does **not** contain chocolate, it cannot be one of the cookies on this tray.\n+\n+```text\n+Cookie on this tray → Contains chocolate\n+Does not contain chocolate → Not a cookie on this tray\n+```\n+\n+That second line is the **contrapositive**. The reverse is different: something can contain chocolate without being a cookie on this tray. “All cookies contain chocolate” does not mean “all chocolate things are cookies.”\n+\n+You may also see **every**, **each**, or **any** used to express this kind of all-rule. The rule tells you what follows *if* you have a member of the group. By itself, it does not prove that the group has any members.\n+\n+## Now compare the three claims\n+\n+![A chart showing that some allows one through ten chocolate cookies, most allows six through ten, and all requires ten.](./assets/quantity-ranges.svg)\n+\n+For a group that exists, the guarantees go one way:\n+\n+![All guarantees most, and most guarantees some. The arrows do not run backward.](./assets/quantity-implications.svg)\n+\n+If all ten cookies contain chocolate, then most do, and some do. If **some** contain chocolate, all ten *might* contain it, but they might not. **Could be true** is not the same as **must be true**.\n+\n+## How statements connect\n+\n+An **overlap** means at least one thing belongs to both groups. When we combine statements, we need to know whether they identify the *same* things or whether an all-rule carries the things we have found into another group.\n+\n+### Carry the first claim through an all-rule\n+\n+Suppose **some cookies contain chocolate**, and **all chocolate cookies contain cocoa**. The chocolate cookie we know about must contain cocoa. So **some cookies contain cocoa**.\n+\n+The same move works with most or all in the first sentence:\n+\n+| First claim | Add this rule | What follows |\n+|---|---|---|\n+| Some cookies contain chocolate. | All chocolate cookies contain cocoa. | **Some cookies contain cocoa.** |\n+| Most cookies contain chocolate. | All chocolate cookies contain cocoa. | **Most cookies contain cocoa.** |\n+| All cookies contain chocolate. | All chocolate cookies contain cocoa. | **All cookies contain cocoa.** |\n+\n+The first word stays the same because the **all** rule covers every chocolate cookie you reached. If the second sentence said only “most chocolate cookies contain cocoa,” the chocolate cookies from the first sentence could be among the exceptions. We could not carry the claim through.\n+\n+### Two majorities of the same group must overlap\n+\n+Suppose **most of the ten cookies contain chocolate**, and **most of those same ten cookies contain nuts**. At least six contain chocolate, and at least six contain nuts. Those groups cannot be separate inside a tray of only ten. At least **two** cookies must contain both.\n+\n+![Ten cookies with six containing chocolate and six containing nuts; two contain both.](./assets/cookie-overlap.svg)\n+\n+```text\n+Most A are B.\n+Most A are C.\n+Therefore, some B are C.\n+```\n+\n+The repeated **A** is what makes this work. Both majorities count the **same group**. If one sentence counts cookies and the next counts all chocolate desserts, you cannot assume the two majorities meet.\n+\n+### Similar-looking statements may not connect\n+\n+“Some cookies contain chocolate” plus “some chocolate desserts contain nuts” does **not** prove that any cookies contain nuts. The chocolate desserts with nuts could all be things other than cookies.\n+\n+Even “some cookies contain chocolate” plus “most chocolate desserts contain nuts” is not enough. The chocolate cookies could be among the desserts without nuts. You need an **all** rule to carry the cookies through, or two majorities of the **same** group to force an overlap.\n+\n+## Try the inference before reading the answer\n+\n+**1.** Some cookies contain chocolate. Could all ten contain chocolate? Does the sentence prove that all ten do?\n+\n+**Answer:** All ten *could* contain chocolate, but “some” proves only at least one.\n+\n+**2.** Most cookies contain chocolate. What can you say about chocolate-containing things that are cookies?\n+\n+**Answer:** Some chocolate-containing things are cookies. You cannot say that most chocolate-containing things are cookies.\n+\n+**3.** Most of ten cookies contain chocolate, and most of the same ten contain nuts. What must be true?\n+\n+**Answer:** At least two cookies contain both. Each majority needs at least six places in a group with only ten places, so at least two places must be shared.\n*** End Patch"; text(await tools.apply_patch(patch));

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch\n*** Update File: brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/06-some-most-all-note.md\n@@\n The repeated **A** is what makes this work. Both majorities count the **same group**. If one sentence counts cookies and the next counts all chocolate desserts, you cannot assume the two majorities meet.\n+\n+### Two “most” claims can also compare group sizes\n+\n+There is another way two “most” statements can tell us something. Suppose **most debate team members are seniors**, but **most seniors are not on the debate team**.\n+\n+Think about the students who are both seniors and team members. They are **more than half** of the debate team, but **less than half** of all seniors. The same overlap takes a bigger share of the team than of the senior group. So there must be **more seniors than debate team members**.\n+\n+![An illustrative comparison: six of ten debate team members are seniors, while six of twenty seniors are on the team.](./assets/group-size-comparison.svg)\n+\n+The picture uses one possible set of numbers. The conclusion does not depend on those exact numbers. What matters is that the same overlap is a majority of one group and a minority of the other.\n \n ### Similar-looking statements may not connect\n*** End Patch"));

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch\n*** Update File: brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/06-some-most-all-note.md\n@@\n The first word stays the same because the **all** rule covers every chocolate cookie you reached. If the second sentence said only “most chocolate cookies contain cocoa,” the chocolate cookies from the first sentence could be among the exceptions. We could not carry the claim through.\n+\n+Direction matters too. “All cocoa-containing cookies contain chocolate” points **toward** chocolate. It would not let us start with a chocolate cookie and conclude that it contains cocoa.\n@@\n Even “some cookies contain chocolate” plus “most chocolate desserts contain nuts” is not enough. The chocolate cookies could be among the desserts without nuts. You need an **all** rule to carry the cookies through, or two majorities of the **same** group to force an overlap.\n+\n+Changing the first sentence to “most cookies contain chocolate” still does not fix that chain. “Most chocolate desserts contain nuts” counts the desserts, and the chocolate cookies could all sit in the nut-free minority. **Most → most** does not automatically become a new “most” claim.\n*** End Patch"));
