Do not bypass paywalls or browser/web safety interstitials.\n- When confirmation is needed, describe the exact action, destination site/account, and data involved. Do not ask vague proceed-or-continue questions.\n\n### Local Environment\nThe agent is operating on the user\'s computer. Hence, the agent\'s actions on the local environment would directly affect the user\'s computer.\n\n\n# Browser Visibility Guidance\n- Keep browser work in the background by default.\n- Show the browser when the user\'s request is primarily to put a page in front of them or let them watch the interaction, such as opening a URL for them, showing the current tab, or keeping the browser visible while testing.\n- Do not show the browser when navigation is only a means to answer a question or verify behavior. Localhost targets and ordinary page navigation do not by themselves require visibility.\n- When the browser should be visible, call `await (await browser.capabilities.get("visibility")).set(true)`.\n\n\n# Tab Cleanup\n- Agent-created tabs are temporary by default and close when the turn ends. Tabs opened by the user remain open unless explicitly closed.\n- Call `tab.markDeliverable()` on a tab that should remain open as a user-facing output.\n- Call `tab.markHandoff()` only when work should continue in a later turn.\n- Marks are turn-scoped and the latest mark for a tab wins. Marked tabs survive the turn and are available in later turns. Mark tabs again in a later turn if it must survive that turn too.\n\n\n# Browser Control Interruption\n- If browser use is interrupted because the extension or user took control, do not quote the raw runtime error. Summarize it naturally for the user, for example: "Browser use was stopped in the extension." Avoid internal terms like `turn_id`, runtime, retry, or plugin error text unless the user asks for details.\n\n\n# API Use\n## How to use the API\n* REPL state persists: use `const` for stable handles and `let` for changing values; reassign instead of redeclaring. Never use `globalThis` or reacquire handles unless they become stale.\n* Always make sure you understand what is on the screen before proceeding to your next action. After clicking, scrolling, typing, or other interactions, collect the cheapest state check that answers the next question. Prefer a fresh DOM snapshot when you need locator ground truth, prefer a screenshot when visual confirmation matters, and avoid requesting both by default.\n* If an interaction has no effect, do not blindly repeat it or immediately switch to lower-level coordinate actions. Inspect the visible state for a blocker or changed state, resolve it when appropriate, then retry the most direct semantic action or retarget the interaction.\n* Browser interactions may add a response content item with notifications about changes in browser state or page content. Read and act on non-empty notifications.\n\n## General guidance\n* Minimize interruptions as much as possible. Only ask clarifying questions if you really need to. If a user has an under-specified prompt, try to fulfill it first before asking for more information.\n* Base interactions on visible page state from the DOM and screenshots rather than source order. The "first link" on the page is not necessarily the first `a href` in the DOM.\n* Try not to over-complicate things. It is okay to click based on node ID if it is not clear how to determine the UI element in Playwright.\n* If a tab is already on a given URL, do not call `goto` with the same URL. This will reload the page and may lose any in-progress information the user has provided. When you intentionally need to reload, call `tab.reload()`.\n* Browsing history may prompt user approval. Call `browser.history()` only when necessary for the request, never speculatively; when needed, make one focused call with date bounds, using a small known set of `queries` instead of repeated exploratory calls.\n* **Proof of work:** After completing an action that changes something on a website, or when asking the user to approve an action, save a screenshot and embed it directly in your reply; showing it only in the tool output doesn’t count. Choose the view where the user can verify the result or see exactly what they’re approving. Prefer showing the page with its surrounding context; crop only if it makes the result clearer without losing that context.\n\n## Lookup and discovery tasks\n* For read-only lookup tasks, it is acceptable to make one focused direct navigation to an obvious result/detail URL or a parameterized search URL derived from the requested filters, then verify the result on the visible page. Prefer this when it avoids a long sequence of filter interactions.\n* Do not iterate through guessed URL variants, query grids, or candidate URL arrays. If that one focused direct attempt fails or cannot be verified, switch to visible page navigation, the site\'s own search UI, or give the best current answer with uncertainty.\n* If you use a search engine fallback, run one focused query, inspect the strongest results, and open the best candidate. Do not keep rewriting the query in loops.\n* Once you have one strong candidate page, verify it directly instead of collecting more candidates.\n* When the page exposes one authoritative signal for the fact you need, such as a selected option, checked state, success modal or toast, basket line item, selected sort option, or current URL parameter, treat that as the answer unless another signal directly contradicts it.\n* Do not keep re-verifying the same fact through header badges, alternate surfaces, or repeated full-page snapshots once an authoritative signal is already present.\n\n\n# WebMCP\nBrowser notifications may list page-defined tools. Prefer WebMCP when one\ncovers the requested action:\n\n```js\nconst webmcp = await tab.capabilities.get("webmcp");\nconst tools = await webmcp.fetchTools();\nawait tools.call("tool_name", input);\n```\n\nIf no current notification lists the tools, print `tools.description()`. Call\nonly listed tools. Reuse the same tool handle while on the same page. Fetch again\nonly if a call reports a stale or invalid handle, or a notification says the\npage’s available tools changed.\n\n\n# Additional Documentation\nUse `await agent.documentation.get("<name>")` when you need one of these topics:\n- `browser-troubleshooting`: read when a selected browser fails while interacting with a page\n- `local-web-development`: read when building or testing a local web app\n- `file-uploads`: read before uploading files through a webpage\n- `screenshots`: read when the user asks for screenshots\n\n# Additional Capabilities\n## Browser Capabilities\n- `visibility`: Use to show or hide the browser to the user, and to determine the browser\'s current visibility. Keep browser work in the background unless the user asks to see it or live viewing is useful. When the browser should be visible, call set(true).\n  Read with `await (await browser.capabilities.get("visibility")).documentation()`.\n- `viewport`: Controls an explicit browser viewport override for responsive or device-size testing. Use it when a task calls for specific dimensions or breakpoint validation; otherwise leave it unset so the browser uses its normal viewport. Reset temporary overrides before finishing unless the user asked to keep them.\n  Read with `await (await browser.capabilities.get("viewport")).documentation()`.\n## Tab Capabilities\n- `pageAssets`: List assets already observed in the current page state and bundle selected assets into a temporary local artifact.\n  Read with `await (await tab.capabilities.get("pageAssets")).documentation()`.\n- `webmcp`: Fetch page-defined WebMCP tools bound to the current document, then call them through the returned object.\n  Read with `await (await tab.capabilities.get("webmcp")).documentation()`.\n- `cdp`: Send raw Chrome DevTools Protocol commands and read debugger events through a supported tab for developer use cases.\n  Read with `await (await tab.capabilities.get("cdp")).documentation()`.\n\n# API Reference\n\nUse this as the supported `agent.browsers.*` surface.\n\n```ts\n// Returned by setupBrowserRuntime().\n// browser was selected during bootstrap.\ninterface Agent {\n  browsers: Browsers; // API for finding and selecting browsers.\n  documentation: Documentation; // API for reading packaged browser-use documentation by name.\n}\n\ninterface Browsers {\n  get(id: string): Promise<Browser>; // Get a browser by id or client type.\n  list(): Promise<Array<{ family?: string; id: string; metadata?: { codexSessionId?: string; extensionInstanceId?: string }; name: string; profileName?: string; type: "iab" | "extension" | "cdp" }>>; // List available browsers.\n}\n\ninterface Browser {\n  browserId: string; // Browser id selected by `agent.browsers.get()`.\n  capabilities: BrowserCapabilityCollection; // Browser-scoped optional capabilities advertised by the connected backend; discover IDs with `await browser.capabilities.list()`, then call `await (await browser.capabilities.get(id)).documentation()` for method details.\n  tabs: Tabs; // API for interacting with browser tabs.\n  documentation(): Promise<string>; // Read browser guidance and the core API reference.\n  history(options: BrowserHistoryOptions): Promise<Array<BrowserHistoryEntry>>; // List recent browsing history ordered by `dateVisited` descending.\n  nameSession(name: string): Promise<void>; // Name the current browser automation session.\n}\n\ninterface Tabs {\n  get(id: string): Promise<Tab>; // Get a tab by id.\n  list(): Promise<Array<TabInfo>>; // List open tabs in the browser.\n  new(): Promise<Tab>; // Create and return a new tab in the browser.\n  selected(): Promise<undefined | Tab>; // Return the currently selected tab, if any.\n}\n\ninterface Tab {\n  capabilities: TabCapabilityCollection; // Tab-scoped optional capabilities advertised by the connected backend; discover IDs with `await tab.capabilities.list()`, then call `await (await tab.capabilities.get(id)).documentation()` for method details.\n  clipboard: TabClipboardAPI; // API for interacting with the browser session\'s clipboard.\n  content: ContentAPI; // API for exporting tab content.\n  dev: TabDevAPI; // API for developer-oriented tab inspection.\n  id: string; // A tab\'s unique identifier\n  playwright: PlaywrightAPI; // API for interacting with the tab via the playwright api\n  back(): Promise<void>; // Navigate this tab back in history.\n  close(): Promise<void>; // Close this tab.\n  forward(): Promise<void>; // Navigate this tab forward in history.\n  getJsDialog(): Promise<undefined | Dialog>; // Get the active JavaScript dialog for this tab, if one is currently open.\n  goto(url: string): Promise<void>; // Open a URL in this tab.\n  markDeliverable(): Promise<void>; // Keep this tab as a deliverable after the turn completes.\n  markHandoff(): Promise<void>; // Keep this tab available for a later turn after the current turn completes.\n  reload(): Promise<void>; // Reload this tab.\n  screenshot(options: ScreenshotOptions): Promise<Uint8Array>; // Capture a screenshot of this tab.\n  title(): Promise<undefined | string>; // Get the current title for this tab.\n  url(): Promise<undefined | string>; // Get the current URL for this tab.\n}\n\ninterface ContentAPI {\n  exportGsuite(type: "pdf" | "md" | "xlsx" | "csv" | "docx" | "pptx"): Promise<string>; // Export a Google Workspace tab using an explicit GSuite export type.\n  exportYouTubeTranscript(): Promise<string>; // Export an HTTPS youtube.com or www.youtube.com /watch transcript to a UTF-8 .txt file.\n}\n\ninterface PlaywrightAPI {\n  domSnapshot(): Promise<string>; // Return a snapshot of the current DOM as a string, including expanded iframe body content when available.\n  evaluate<TResult, TArg>(pageFunction: PlaywrightEvaluateFunction<TArg, TResult>, arg?: TArg, options?: PlaywrightEvaluateOptions): Promise<TResult>; // Evaluate JavaScript in a read-only page scope.\n  expectNavigation<T>(action: () => Promise<T>, options: { timeoutMs?: number; url?: string; waitUntil?: LoadState }): Promise<T>; // Expect a navigation triggered by an action.\n  frameLocator(frameSelector: string): PlaywrightFrameLocator; // Create a frame-scoped locator builder.\n  getByLabel(text: TextMatcher, options: { exact?: boolean }): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by label text within the page.\n  getByPlaceholder(text: TextMatcher, options: { exact?: boolean }): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by placeholder text within the page.\n  getByRole(role: string, options: { exact?: boolean; name?: TextMatcher }): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by ARIA role within the page.\n  getByTestId(testId: string): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by test id within the page.\n  getByText(text: TextMatcher, options: { exact?: boolean }): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by text within the page.\n  locator(selector: string): PlaywrightLocator; // Create a locator scoped to this tab.\n  waitForEvent(event: "download", options?: WaitForEventOptions): Promise<PlaywrightDownload>; // Wait for the next download to complete; call before clicking its download control.\n  waitForEvent(event: "filechooser", options?: WaitForEventOptions): Promise<PlaywrightFileChooser>; // Wait for a file chooser.\n  waitForLoadState(options: PageWaitForLoadStateOptions): Promise<void>; // Wait for the page to reach a specific load state.\n  waitForTimeout(timeoutMs: number): Promise<void>; // Wait for a fixed duration.\n  waitForURL(url: string, options: PageWaitForURLOptions): Promise<void>; // Wait for the page URL to match the provided value.\n}\n\ninterface PlaywrightFrameLocator {\n  frameLocator(frameSelector: string): PlaywrightFrameLocator; // Create a locator scoped to a nested frame.\n  getByLabel(text: TextMatcher, options: { exact?: boolean }): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by label within this frame.\n  getByPlaceholder(text: TextMatcher, options: { exact?: boolean }): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by placeholder within this frame.\n  getByRole(role: string, options: { exact?: boolean; name?: TextMatcher }): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by ARIA role within this frame.\n  getByTestId(testId: string): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by test id within this frame.\n  getByText(text: TextMatcher, options: { exact?: boolean }): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by text within this frame.\n  locator(selector: string): PlaywrightLocator; // Create a locator scoped to this frame.\n}\n\ninterface PlaywrightLocator {\n  all(): Promise<Array<PlaywrightLocator>>; // Resolve to a list of locators for each matched element.\n  allTextContents(options: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<Array<string>>; // Return `textContent` for *all* elements matched by this locator.\n  and(locator: PlaywrightLocator): PlaywrightLocator; // Return a locator matching elements that satisfy both this locator and `locator`.\n  check(options: LocatorCheckOptions): Promise<void>; // Check a checkbox or switch-like control.\n  click(options: LocatorClickOptions): Promise<void>; // Click the element matched by this locator.\n  count(): Promise<number>; // Number of elements matching this locator.\n  dblclick(options: LocatorClickOptions): Promise<void>; // Double-click the element matched by this locator.\n  downloadMedia(options: LocatorDownloadMediaOptions): Promise<string>; // Download the matched media or file link and return its saved file path.\n  evaluate<TResult, TArg>(pageFunction: LocatorEvaluateFunction<TArg, TResult>, arg?: TArg, options?: PlaywrightEvaluateOptions): Promise<TResult>; // Evaluate JavaScript in a read-only scope; the locator must resolve unambiguously to one element.\n  evaluateAll<TResult, TArg>(pageFunction: LocatorEvaluateAllFunction<TArg, TResult>, arg?: TArg, options?: PlaywrightEvaluateOptions): Promise<TResult>; // Evaluate read-only JavaScript against all elements matched by this locator.\n  fill(value: string, options: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<void>; // Replace the element\'s value with the provided text.\n  filter(options: LocatorFilterOptions): PlaywrightLocator; // Narrow this locator by additional constraints.\n  first(): PlaywrightLocator; // Return a locator pointing at the first matched element.\n  getAttribute(name: string, options: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<null | string>; // Return an attribute value from the first matched element.\n  getByLabel(text: TextMatcher, options: { exact?: boolean }): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by label text, scoped to this locator.\n  getByPlaceholder(text: TextMatcher, options: { exact?: boolean }): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by placeholder text, scoped to this locator.\n  getByRole(role: string, options: { exact?: boolean; name?: TextMatcher }): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by ARIA role, scoped to this locator.\n  getByTestId(testId: string): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by test id, scoped to this locator.\n  getByText(text: TextMatcher, options: { exact?: boolean }): PlaywrightLocator; // Find elements by text content, scoped to this locator.\n  innerText(options: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<string>; // Return the rendered (visible) text of the first matched element.\n  isEnabled(): Promise<boolean>; // Whether the first matched element is currently enabled.\n  isVisible(): Promise<boolean>; // Whether the first matched element is currently visible.\n  last(): PlaywrightLocator; // Return a locator pointing at the last matched element.\n  locator(selector: string, options: LocatorLocatorOptions): PlaywrightLocator; // Create a descendant locator scoped to this locator.\n  nth(index: number): PlaywrightLocator; // Return a locator pointing at the Nth matched element.\n  or(locator: PlaywrightLocator): PlaywrightLocator; // Return a locator matching elements that satisfy either this locator or `locator`.\n  press(value: string, options: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<void>; // Press a keyboard key while this locator is focused.\n  pressSequentially(value: string, options: LocatorPressSequentiallyOptions): Promise<void>; // Focus the element and press each character in the text sequentially without clearing its existing value.\n  selectOption(value: SelectOptionInput | Array<SelectOptionInput>, options: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<void>; // Select one or more options on a native `<select>` element.\n  setChecked(checked: boolean, options: LocatorCheckOptions): Promise<void>; // Set a checkbox or switch-like control to a checked/unchecked state.\n  textContent(options: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<null | string>; // Return the raw textContent of the first matched element (or null if missing).\n  type(value: string, options: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<void>; // Type text into the element without clearing existing content.\n  uncheck(options: LocatorCheckOptions): Promise<void>; // Uncheck a checkbox or switch-like control.\n  waitFor(options: LocatorWaitForOptions): Promise<void>; // Wait for the element to reach a specific state.\n}\n\ninterface PlaywrightDownload {\n  path(options: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<null | string>; // Return the local path to the downloaded file, if available.\n}\n\ninterface PlaywrightFileChooser {\n  isMultiple(): boolean; // Whether the input allows selecting multiple files.\n  setFiles(files: FileChooserFiles, options: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<void>; // Set the files for this chooser using absolute paths visible to the browser.\n}\n\ninterface TabClipboardAPI {\n  read(): Promise<Array<TabClipboardItem>>; // Read clipboard items, including text and binary payloads.\n  readText(): Promise<string>; // Read plain text from the browser clipboard.\n  write(items: Array<TabClipboardItem>): Promise<void>; // Write clipboard items.\n  writeText(text: string): Promise<void>; // Write plain text to the browser clipboard.\n}\n\ninterface TabDevAPI {\n  logs(options: TabDevLogsOptions): Promise<Array<TabDevLogEntry>>; // Read console log messages captured for this tab.\n}\n\ninterface AlertDialog {\n  type: "alert";\n  dismiss(): Promise<void>;\n}\n\ninterface BeforeUnloadDialog {\n  type: "beforeunload";\n  dismiss(): Promise<void>;\n}\n\ninterface ConfirmDialog {\n  type: "confirm";\n  accept(): Promise<void>;\n  dismiss(): Promise<void>;\n}\n\ninterface Documentation {\n  get(name: string): Promise<string>; // Read packaged documentation by its extensionless relative path.\n}\n\ninterface PromptDialog {\n  type: "prompt";\n  accept(text: string): Promise<void>;\n  dismiss(): Promise<void>;\n}\n\ntype BrowserCapabilityCollection = {\n  get(id: string): Promise<unknown>;\n  list(): Promise<Array<{ id: string; description: string }>>;\n};\n\ninterface BrowserHistoryOptions {\n  from?: string | Date; // Lower bound for visit timestamps.\n  limit?: number; // Maximum number of history entries to return.\n  queries?: Array<string>; // Optional terms to filter browser history with.\n  to?: string | Date; // Upper bound for visit timestamps.\n}\n\ninterface BrowserHistoryEntry {\n  dateVisited: string; // ISO 8601 timestamp for the visit.\n  title?: string; // Page title captured for the visit.\n  url: string; // Visited URL.\n}\n\ninterface TabInfo {\n  id: string; // Metadata describing an open tab.\n  providerTabId?: string; // Provider-owned identifier for matching an explicitly mentioned tab.\n  title?: string;\n  url?: string;\n}\n\ntype TabCapabilityCollection = {\n  get(id: string): Promise<unknown>;\n  list(): Promise<Array<{ id: string; description: string }>>;\n};\n\ntype Dialog = AlertDialog | BeforeUnloadDialog | ConfirmDialog | PromptDialog;\n\ntype ScreenshotOptions = {\n  clip?: ClipRect; // Crop to a specific rectangle instead of the full viewport.\n  fullPage?: boolean; // Capture the full page instead of the viewport.\n};\n\ntype PlaywrightEvaluateFunction<TArg, TResult> = string | (arg: TArg) => TResult | Promise<TResult>;\n\ntype PlaywrightEvaluateOptions = {\n  timeoutMs?: number; // Maximum time to spend setting up the read-only DOM scope and running the script.\n};\n\ntype LoadState = "load" | "domcontentloaded" | "networkidle";\n\ntype TextMatcher = string | RegExp;\n\ntype WaitForEventOptions = {\n  timeoutMs?: number;\n};\n\ntype PageWaitForLoadStateOptions = {\n  state?: LoadState;\n  timeoutMs?: number;\n};\n\ntype PageWaitForURLOptions = {\n  timeoutMs?: number;\n  waitUntil?: WaitUntil;\n};\n\ntype LocatorCheckOptions = {\n  force?: boolean;\n  timeoutMs?: number;\n};\n\ntype LocatorClickOptions = {\n  button?: MouseButton;\n  force?: boolean;\n  modifiers?: Array<KeyboardModifier>;\n  timeoutMs?: number;\n};\n\ntype LocatorDownloadMediaOptions = {\n  timeoutMs?: number; // Download timeout in milliseconds; defaults to 120000, excluding permission prompts.\n};\n\ntype LocatorEvaluateFunction<TArg, TResult> = string | (element: Element, arg: TArg) => TResult | Promise<TResult>;\n\ntype LocatorEvaluateAllFunction<TArg, TResult> = string | (elements: Array<Element>, arg: TArg) => TResult | Promise<TResult>;\n\ntype LocatorFilterOptions = {\n  has?: PlaywrightLocator;\n  hasNot?: PlaywrightLocator;\n  hasNotText?: TextMatcher;\n  hasText?: TextMatcher;\n  visible?: boolean;\n};\n\ntype LocatorLocatorOptions = {\n  has?: PlaywrightLocator;\n  hasNot?: PlaywrightLocator;\n  hasNotText?: TextMatcher;\n  hasText?: TextMatcher;\n};\n\ntype LocatorPressSequentiallyOptions = {\n  timeoutMs?: number;\n};\n\ntype SelectOptionInput = string | SelectOptionDescriptor;\n\ntype LocatorWaitForOptions = {\n  state: WaitForState;\n  timeoutMs?: number;\n};\n\ntype FileChooserFiles = string | Array<string>;\n\ntype TabClipboardItem = {\n  entries: Array<TabClipboardEntry>;\n  presentationStyle?: "unspecified" | "inline" | "attachment";\n};\n\ninterface TabDevLogsOptions {\n  filter?: string; // Optional substring filter applied to the rendered log message.\n  levels?: Array<"debug" | "info" | "log" | "warn" | "error" | "warning">; // Optional levels to include.\n  limit?: number; // Maximum number of logs to return.\n}\n\ninterface TabDevLogEntry {\n  level: "debug" | "info" | "log" | "warn" | "error"; // Console log level.\n  message: string; // Rendered log message text.\n  timestamp: string; // ISO 8601 timestamp for when the runtime captured the log.\n  url?: string; // Source URL reported by the browser runtime, when available.\n}\n\ntype ClipRect = {\n  height: number;\n  width: number;\n  x: number;\n  y: number;\n};\n\ntype WaitUntil = LoadState | "commit";\n\ntype MouseButton = "left" | "right" | "middle";\n\ntype KeyboardModifier = "Alt" | "Control" | "ControlOrMeta" | "Meta" | "Shift";\n\ntype SelectOptionDescriptor = {\n  index?: number;\n  label?: string;\n  value?: string;\n};\n\ntype WaitForState = "attached" | "detached" | "visible" | "hidden";\n\ntype TabClipboardEntry = {\n  base64?: string;\n  mimeType: string;\n  text?: string;\n};\n```\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Browser tab: 4, Title: "Some, Most, and All | LSAT U draft preview", URL: "http://127.0.0.1:8765/brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/07-quantity-statements-preview.html".\n0 AXWebArea Some, Most, and All | LSAT U draft preview, URL: 127.0.0.1:8765/brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/07-quantity-statements-preview.html\n\t1 text LOCAL DRAFT PREVIEW\n\t2 container\n\t\t3 text U LSAT U CLASSROOM Home Notes and recaps Assigned work Flagged Wrong answers PREVIEW This shows the draft in the Classroom reading layout. Nothing has been posted to a student.\n\t4 container\n\t\t5 text September 29, 2026\n\t\t6 text | Note\n\t\t7 heading Some, Most, and All, Value: 1\n\t\t\t8 text Some, Most, and All\n\t\t9 text Draft visual preview. The answer panels below can be opened.\n\t\t10 text Quantity statements tell us whether a claim applies to some members of a group, most of them, or all of them. Suppose a class has been assigned a case to read. “Some students read it,” “most students read it,” and “all students read it” are three different claims about that same class. We do not need an exact headcount to understand the difference.\n\t\t11 container\n\t\t\t12 text For each sentence, ask:  What must be true? What could still be true?  The answer changes with the word we use.\n\t\t13 heading Some guarantees at least one, Value: 2\n\t\t\t14 text Some guarantees at least one\n\t\t15 container\n\t\t\t16 text Imagine a shelf with eight books. I tell you that  some of the books are hardcover . How many hardcover books must there be?\n\t\t17 container\n\t\t\t18 text At least  one . There could be one, four, or all eight. “Some” rules out zero. It does not rule out “most” or “all.”\n\t\t19 image Eight books showing that one hardcover book and eight hardcover books both satisfy some.\n\t\t20 text This is easy to miss because in ordinary conversation “some” often suggests “some, but not all.” On the LSAT, that extra phrase is not part of the statement. If all eight books are hardcover, it is still true that some are hardcover.\n\t\t21 container\n\t\t\t22 text Try it:  “Some applicants received an interview.” Could every applicant have received one? Does the sentence tell us that anyone was denied an interview?\n\t\t23 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t24 text Check your answer\n\t\t25 container\n\t\t\t26 text Whenever you read  some , replace it with  at least one  in your head. That tells you exactly what the sentence guarantees:\n\t\t27 container\n\t\t\t28 text Some of the books are hardcover.\n\t\t\t29 text At least one of the books is hardcover.\n\t\t30 text Now focus on that one book. It belongs to both groups: it is a book, and it is hardcover. If we describe the same object from the hardcover side, we can say:\n\t\t31 container\n\t\t\t32 text Some hardcover items are books.\n\t\t\t33 text At least one hardcover item is a book.\n\t\t34 container\n\t\t\t35 text We have not found a new object. We have described the same overlap in the other direction. That is why a  some  statement works both ways:\n\t\t36 text Books  ←some→  Hardcover\n\n\t\t37 text The double arrow tells us that at least one thing belongs to both groups. It does not tell us that every book is hardcover or that every hardcover item is a book.\n\t\t38 heading Most guarantees more than half, Value: 2\n\t\t\t39 text Most guarantees more than half\n\t\t40 container\n\t\t\t41 text Now I tell you that  most of the eight books are hardcover . We need at least  five  hardcover books. Four would be exactly half, and half is not most. Five, six, seven, or eight could satisfy the sentence.\n\t\t42 image Eight books showing that five hardcover books and eight hardcover books both satisfy most.\n\t\t43 text Notice that all eight could still be hardcover. “Most” does not tell us that an exception exists.\n\t\t44 container\n\t\t\t45 text Try it:  If most of the eight books are hardcover, must some of them be hardcover? Must any be paperback?\n\t\t46 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t47 text Check your answer\n\t\t48 container\n\t\t\t49 text Here is where the direction of the statement matters. From “most books are hardcover,” we know that  some hardcover things are books . We cannot say that  most hardcover things are books . The original sentence counts the books on this shelf. The reversed sentence would count every hardcover thing, including things outside that group.\n\t\t50 text Books  ─most→  Hardcover\nHardcover  ←some→  Books\n\n\t\t51 container\n\t\t\t52 text The first arrow gives the majority claim. The second line is the overlap that the majority guarantees. When we read a most statement backward, the word becomes  some .\n\t\t53 heading All leaves no exception, Value: 2\n\t\t\t54 text All leaves no exception\n\t\t55 container\n\t\t\t56 text If  all eight books are hardcover , every book on the shelf is hardcover. One paperback on that shelf would make the statement false.\n\t\t57 image Eight books showing that all eight must be hardcover to satisfy all.\n\t\t58 container\n\t\t\t59 text An all statement gives us a rule:  if it is a book on this shelf, then it is hardcover .\n\t\t60 text Book on this shelf  →  Hardcover\nNot hardcover       →  Not a book on this shelf\n\n\t\t61 text The second line is the contrapositive. Both lines go with the same rule. We cannot turn the first line around and conclude that every hardcover thing is a book on this shelf.\n\t\t62 container\n\t\t\t63 text Try it:  You pick up a paperback. What does the rule tell you? What if you pick up a hardcover notebook?\n\t\t64 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t65 text Check your answer\n\t\t66 text There is a small qualification. “All A are B” gives a rule about A. By itself, it does not tell us that any A exist. When we already know the group exists, all also guarantees most and some.\n\t\t67 heading Put the three statements side by side, Value: 2\n\t\t\t68 text Put the three statements side by side\n\t\t69 text The same shelf can help us see the whole range.\n\t\t70 image For eight existing books: some permits one through eight hardcover, most permits five through eight, and all requires eight.\n\t\t71 text Read the implications in one direction:\n\t\t72 text ALL  →  MOST  →  SOME       (when the group exists)\n\n\t\t73 container\n\t\t\t74 text If all eight books are hardcover, then most are, and some are. If only “some” is given, all eight  could  be hardcover, but we cannot conclude that they  are . Keep the distinction between a possible situation and a required one.\n\t\t75 heading Carry a claim through an all rule, Value: 2\n\t\t\t76 text Carry a claim through an all rule\n\t\t77 container\n\t\t\t78 text Now we can combine statements. Suppose  some library books are mysteries  and  all mysteries are fiction . We have at least one book that is a mystery. The all rule applies to every mystery, including that one. So  some library books are fiction .\n\t\t79 text Library books  ←some→  Mysteries  →  Fiction\nLibrary books  ←some→  Fiction\n\n\t\t80 container\n\t\t\t81 text The all arrow points  away from  the mystery group we reached. That is why the chain works. If the second sentence said only “most mysteries are fiction,” the mystery books we found could be among the exceptions.\n\t\t82 text The same reasoning preserves the first quantity word:\n\t\t83 table\n\t\t\t84 row\n\t\t\t\t85 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t86 text First statement\n\t\t\t\t87 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t88 text Rule\n\t\t\t\t89 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t90 text What follows\n\t\t\t91 row\n\t\t\t\t92 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t93 text Some library books are mysteries.\n\t\t\t\t94 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t95 text All mysteries are fiction.\n\t\t\t\t96 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t97 text Some library books are fiction.\n\t\t\t98 row\n\t\t\t\t99 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t100 text Most library books are mysteries.\n\t\t\t\t101 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t102 text All mysteries are fiction.\n\t\t\t\t103 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t104 text Most library books are fiction.\n\t\t\t105 row\n\t\t\t\t106 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t107 text All library books are mysteries.\n\t\t\t\t108 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t109 text All mysteries are fiction.\n\t\t\t\t110 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t111 text All library books are fiction.\n\t\t112 container\n\t\t\t113 text Try it:  “Most library books are mysteries. All fiction is mystery.” Can we conclude that most library books are fiction?\n\t\t114 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t115 text Check your answer\n\t\t116 heading Two majorities of the same group must meet, Value: 2\n\t\t\t117 text Two majorities of the same group must meet\n\t\t118 container\n\t\t\t119 text Suppose a club has ten members.  Most members study law , and  most members work part time . Each “most” needs at least six of the ten members. Those two sets cannot fit inside the club without sharing at least two people.\n\t\t120 image Ten club members. Six study law, six work part time, and at least two do both.\n\t\t121 container\n\t\t\t122 text So  some law students work part time . We can also say  some part-time workers study law . These are the same people, described from opposite sides of a some statement.\n\t\t123 text Club members  ─most→  Law students\nClub members  ─most→  Part-time workers\nLaw students  ←some→  Part-time workers\n\n\t\t124 container\n\t\t\t125 text The two most arrows begin with the  same group . That shared starting point is what forces the overlap. The conclusion is  some , not most. We know the two groups meet; we do not know what fraction of either group lies in the overlap.\n\t\t126 container\n\t\t\t127 text Try it:  If most club members study law and most club members work part time, could the two groups of members be completely separate?\n\t\t128 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t129 text Check your answer\n\t\t130 heading A second way two most statements can work, Value: 2\n\t\t\t131 text A second way two most statements can work\n\t\t132 container\n\t\t\t133 text Here is a different comparison.  Most debate team members are seniors , but  most seniors are not on the debate team . The seniors on the team are more than half of the team and less than half of the seniors. The same overlap takes up a larger share of the team than of the senior class. Therefore,  there are more seniors than debate team members .\n\t\t134 image An example in which six of ten debate team members are seniors, while six of twenty seniors are on the team.\n\t\t135 text The numbers in the picture are one possible case. The conclusion follows from the two majority claims, not from those particular numbers.\n\t\t136 heading Similar chains can leave a gap, Value: 2\n\t\t\t137 text Similar chains can leave a gap\n\t\t138 text Two some statements need not describe the same person or thing:\n\t\t139 text Some volunteers speak Spanish.\nSome Spanish speakers are trained.\n\n\t\t140 text The trained Spanish speakers could all be people who do not volunteer. We cannot conclude that any volunteers are trained.\n\t\t141 text Replacing the second “some” with “most” does not fix the gap. The Spanish-speaking volunteers could sit in the untrained minority. Even two most statements chained through different starting groups do not automatically produce a new majority claim.\n\t\t142 container\n\t\t\t143 text Before drawing a conclusion, ask:  Am I carrying a known group through an all rule? Or do two majorities count the same group?  If neither is true, check whether the groups could miss each other.\n\t\t144 heading The moves to keep, Value: 2\n\t\t\t145 text The moves to keep\n\t\t146 table\n\t\t\t147 row\n\t\t\t\t148 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t149 text What you have\n\t\t\t\t150 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t151 text What you may conclude\n\t\t\t152 row\n\t\t\t\t153 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t154 text Some A are B\n\t\t\t\t155 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t156 text Some B are A\n\t\t\t157 row\n\t\t\t\t158 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t159 text Most A are B\n\t\t\t\t160 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t161 text Some A are B, and some B are A\n\t\t\t162 row\n\t\t\t\t163 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t164 text All A are B\n\t\t\t\t165 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t166 text A → B, and not B → not A\n\t\t\t167 row\n\t\t\t\t168 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t169 text Some/most/all A are B; all B are C\n\t\t\t\t170 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t171 text The same first quantity of A are C\n\t\t\t172 row\n\t\t\t\t173 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t174 text Most A are B; most A are C\n\t\t\t\t175 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t176 text Some B are C\n\t\t177 text These are the useful moves. The arrows show exactly where each one is allowed to go.\n\t\t178 heading Short drill: diagram, combine, decide, Value: 2\n\t\t\t179 text Short drill: diagram, combine, decide\n\t\t180 container\n\t\t\t181 text Here are five statements about one volunteer program.  Volunteer ,  Spanish speaker ,  trained person ,  weekend worker , and  student  name groups of people. Treat each sentence as true.\n\t\t182 content list\n\t\t\t183 container\n\t\t\t\t184 AXListMarker 1. \n\t\t\t\t185 text Some volunteers speak Spanish.\n\t\t\t186 container\n\t\t\t\t187 AXListMarker 2. \n\t\t\t\t188 text All Spanish speakers are trained.\n\t\t\t189 container\n\t\t\t\t190 AXListMarker 3. \n\t\t\t\t191 text Most volunteers work weekends.\n\t\t\t192 container\n\t\t\t\t193 AXListMarker 4. \n\t\t\t\t194 text Most volunteers are students.\n\t\t\t195 container\n\t\t\t\t196 AXListMarker 5. \n\t\t\t\t197 text Most weekend workers are trained.\n\t\t198 text First, diagram each statement. Then answer these without looking below:\n\t\t199 content list\n\t\t\t200 container\n\t\t\t\t201 AXListMarker 1. \n\t\t\t\t202 text Which two statements prove that  some volunteers are trained ?\n\t\t\t203 container\n\t\t\t\t204 AXListMarker 2. \n\t\t\t\t205 text Which two statements prove that  some students work weekends ?\n\t\t\t206 container\n\t\t\t\t207 AXListMarker 3. \n\t\t\t\t208 text Do statements 3 and 5 prove that  most volunteers are trained ? Explain the gap or draw a counterexample.\n\t\t\t209 container\n\t\t\t\t210 AXListMarker 4. \n\t\t\t\t211 text Can you write either valid  some  conclusion in the reverse order?\n\t\t212 button (collapsed) Show the diagrams and worked answers, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t213 text Show the diagrams and worked answers\n\t\t214 button (disabled) Ask\n\t\t215 button (disabled) Back to notes\n\nThe focused UI element is 0 AXWebArea Some, Most, and All | LSAT U draft preview, URL: 127.0.0.1:8765/brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/07-quantity-statements-preview.html'}]

The answer panels below can be opened.</p>\\r\\n    <article class=\\"classroom-prose quantity-note\\"><style>${noteCss}</style>${contentHtml}</article>\\r\\n    <div class=\\"classroom-detail-actions\\"><button class=\\"classroom-button classroom-button-primary\\" type=\\"button\\" disabled>Ask</button><button class=\\"classroom-button\\" type=\\"button\\" disabled>Back to notes</button></div>\\r\\n  </div></main>\\r\\n</div>\\r\\n<script>if(new URLSearchParams(location.search).get(\'theme\')===\'dark\')document.documentElement.classList.add(\'dark\')</script>\\r\\n</body></html>`;\\r\\n\\r\\nconst out = path.join(here, \\"07-quantity-statements-preview.html\\");\\r\\nfs.writeFileSync(out, page, \\"utf8\\");\\r\\nconsole.log(out);\\r\\n"}}}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"i":2,"result":{"status":"fulfilled","value":{"chunk_id":"67a506","wall_time_seconds":7.8473888,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":3025,"output":"# Some, Most, and All\\r\\n\\r\\nQuantity statements tell us whether a claim applies to some members of a group, most of them, or all of them. Suppose a class has been assigned a case to read. “Some students read it,” “most students read it,” and “all students read it” are three different claims about that same class. We do not need an exact headcount to understand the difference.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor each sentence, ask: **What must be true? What could still be true?** The answer changes with the word we use.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Some guarantees at least one\\r\\n\\r\\nImagine a shelf with eight books. I tell you that **some of the books are hardcover**. How many hardcover books must there be?\\r\\n\\r\\nAt least **one**. There could be one, four, or all eight. “Some” rules out zero. It does not rule out “most” or “all.”\\r\\n\\r\\n![Eight books showing that one hardcover book and eight hardcover books both satisfy some.](./assets/some-books.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is easy to miss because in ordinary conversation “some” often suggests “some, but not all.” On the LSAT, that extra phrase is not part of the statement. If all eight books are hardcover, it is still true that some are hardcover.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Try it:** “Some applicants received an interview.” Could every applicant have received one? Does the sentence tell us that anyone was denied an interview?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery applicant could have received an interview. The sentence does not tell us that anyone was denied one. “Some” guarantees at least one applicant received an interview, but it leaves open how many others did.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\nWhenever you read **some**, replace it with **at least one** in your head. That tells you exactly what the sentence guarantees:\\r\\n\\r\\n> **Some of the books are hardcover.**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> **At least one of the books is hardcover.**\\r\\n\\r\\nNow focus on that one book. It belongs to both groups: it is a book, and it is hardcover. If we describe the same object from the hardcover side, we can say:\\r\\n\\r\\n> **Some hardcover items are books.**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> **At least one hardcover item is a book.**\\r\\n\\r\\nWe have not found a new object. We have described the same overlap in the other direction. That is why a **some** statement works both ways:\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nBooks  ←some→  Hardcover\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe double arrow tells us that at least one thing belongs to both groups. It does not tell us that every book is hardcover or that every hardcover item is a book.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Most guarantees more than half\\r\\n\\r\\nNow I tell you that **most of the eight books are hardcover**. We need at least **five** hardcover books. Four would be exactly half, and half is not most. Five, six, seven, or eight could satisfy the sentence.\\r\\n\\r\\n![Eight books showing that five hardcover books and eight hardcover books both satisfy most.](./assets/most-books.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\nNotice that all eight could still be hardcover. “Most” does not tell us that an exception exists.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Try it:** If most of the eight books are hardcover, must some of them be hardcover? Must any be paperback?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nAt least five are hardcover, so **some are hardcover**. No paperback book is required. All eight could be hardcover.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\nHere is where the direction of the statement matters. From “most books are hardcover,” we know that **some hardcover things are books**. We cannot say that **most hardcover things are books**. The original sentence counts the books on this shelf. The reversed sentence would count every hardcover thing, including things outside that group.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nBooks  ─most→  Hardcover\\r\\nHardcover  ←some→  Books\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe first arrow gives the majority claim. The second line is the overlap that the majority guarantees. When we read a most statement backward, the word becomes **some**.\\r\\n\\r\\n## All leaves no exception\\r\\n\\r\\nIf **all eight books are hardcover**, every book on the shelf is hardcover. One paperback on that shelf would make the statement false.\\r\\n\\r\\n![Eight books showing that all eight must be hardcover to satisfy all.](./assets/all-books.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\nAn all statement gives us a rule: **if it is a book on this shelf, then it is hardcover**.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nBook on this shelf  →  Hardcover\\r\\nNot hardcover       →  Not a book on this shelf\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe second line is the contrapositive. Both lines go with the same rule. We cannot turn the first line around and conclude that every hardcover thing is a book on this shelf.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Try it:** You pick up a paperback. What does the rule tell you? What if you pick up a hardcover notebook?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nThe paperback cannot be one of these books. The hardcover notebook tells us nothing about whether it is one of these books. Being hardcover is required of the books, but it is not enough to identify one.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\nThere is a small qualification. “All A are B” gives a rule about A. By itself, it does not tell us that any A exist. When we already know the group exists, all also guarantees most and some.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Put the three statements side by side\\r\\n\\r\\nThe same shelf can help us see the whole range.\\r\\n\\r\\n![For eight existing books: some permits one through eight hardcover, most permits five through eight, and all requires eight.](./assets/book-quantity-ranges.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\nRead the implications in one direction:\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nALL  →  MOST  →  SOME       (when the group exists)\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nIf all eight books are hardcover, then most are, and some are. If only “some” is given, all eight **could** be hardcover, but we cannot conclude that they **are**. Keep the distinction between a possible situation and a required one.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Carry a claim through an all rule\\r\\n\\r\\nNow we can combine statements. Suppose **some library books are mysteries** and **all mysteries are fiction**. We have at least one book that is a mystery. The all rule applies to every mystery, including that one. So **some library books are fiction**.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nLibrary books  ←some→  Mysteries  →  Fiction\\r\\nLibrary books  ←some→  Fiction\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe all arrow points **away from** the mystery group we reached. That is why the chain works. If the second sentence said only “most mysteries are fiction,” the mystery books we found could be among the exceptions.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe same reasoning preserves the first quantity word:\\r\\n\\r\\n| First statement | Rule | What follows |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| Some library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Some library books are fiction. |\\r\\n| Most library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Most library books are fiction. |\\r\\n| All library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | All library books are fiction. |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Try it:** “Most library books are mysteries. All fiction is mystery.” Can we conclude that most library books are fiction?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nNo. The all arrow goes from fiction to mystery. We cannot start at mystery and travel backward to fiction.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n## Two majorities of the same group must meet\\r\\n\\r\\nSuppose a club has ten members. **Most members study law**, and **most members work part time**. Each “most” needs at least six of the ten members. Those two sets cannot fit inside the club without sharing at least two people.\\r\\n\\r\\n![Ten club members. Six study law, six work part time, and at least two do both.](./assets/club-majority-overlap.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\nSo **some law students work part time**. We can also say **some part-time workers study law**. These are the same people, described from opposite sides of a some statement.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nClub members  ─most→  Law students\\r\\nClub members  ─most→  Part-time workers\\r\\nLaw students  ←some→  Part-time workers\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe two most arrows begin with the **same group**. That shared starting point is what forces the overlap. The conclusion is **some**, not most. We know the two groups meet; we do not know what fraction of either group lies in the overlap.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Try it:** If most club members study law and most club members work part time, could the two groups of members be completely separate?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nNo. Two separate majorities would require more members than the club has. At least one member must have both traits.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n## A second way two most statements can work\\r\\n\\r\\nHere is a different comparison. **Most debate team members are seniors**, but **most seniors are not on the debate team**. The seniors on the team are more than half of the team and less than half of the seniors. The same overlap takes up a larger share of the team than of the senior class. Therefore, **there are more seniors than debate team members**.\\r\\n\\r\\n![An example in which six of ten debate team members are seniors, while six of twenty seniors are on the team.](./assets/group-size-comparison.svg)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe numbers in the picture are one possible case. The conclusion follows from the two majority claims, not from those particular numbers.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Similar chains can leave a gap\\r\\n\\r\\nTwo some statements need not describe the same person or thing:\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nSome volunteers speak Spanish.\\r\\nSome Spanish speakers are trained.\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe trained Spanish speakers could all be people who do not volunteer. We cannot conclude that any volunteers are trained.\\r\\n\\r\\nReplacing the second “some” with “most” does not fix the gap. The Spanish-speaking volunteers could sit in the untrained minority. Even two most statements chained through different starting groups do not automatically produce a new majority claim.\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore drawing a conclusion, ask: **Am I carrying a known group through an all rule? Or do two majorities count the same group?** If neither is true, check whether the groups could miss each other.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The moves to keep\\r\\n\\r\\n| What you have | What you may conclude |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| Some A are B | Some B are A |\\r\\n| Most A are B | Some A are B, and some B are A |\\r\\n| All A are B | A → B, and not B → not A |\\r\\n| Some/most/all A are B; all B are C | The same first quantity of A are C |\\r\\n| Most A are B; most A are C | Some B are C |\\r\\n\\r\\nThese are the useful moves. The arrows show exactly where each one is allowed to go.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Short drill: diagram, combine, decide\\r\\n\\r\\nHere are five statements about one volunteer program. **Volunteer**, **Spanish speaker**, **trained person**, **weekend worker**, and **student** name groups of people. Treat each sentence as true.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Some volunteers speak Spanish.\\r\\n2. All Spanish speakers are trained.\\r\\n3. Most volunteers work weekends.\\r\\n4. Most volunteers are students.\\r\\n5. Most weekend workers are trained.\\r\\n\\r\\nFirst, diagram each statement. Then answer these without looking below:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Which two statements prove that **some volunteers are trained**?\\r\\n2. Which two statements prove that **some students work weekends**?\\r\\n3. Do statements 3 and 5 prove that **most volunteers are trained**? Explain the gap or draw a counterexample.\\r\\n4. Can you write either valid **some** conclusion in the reverse order?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details><summary>Show the diagrams and worked answers</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\n1. Volunteers       ←some→  Spanish speakers\\r\\n2. Spanish speakers →       Trained people\\r\\n3. Volunteers       ─most→  Weekend workers\\r\\n4. Volunteers       ─most→  Students\\r\\n5. Weekend workers  ─most→  Trained people\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**1. Statements 1 and 2.** At least one volunteer speaks Spanish. Every Spanish speaker is trained. That volunteer is trained, so **some volunteers are trained**.\\r\\n\\r\\n**2. Statements 3 and 4.** Both majorities count the volunteers. The weekend workers and students must share at least one volunteer. So **some students work weekends**.\\r\\n\\r\\n**3. No.** Statement 3 says most volunteers work weekends. Statement 5 counts all weekend workers, a different group. The volunteers who work weekends could be among the untrained weekend workers. Nothing requires most volunteers to be trained.\\r\\n\\r\\n**4. Yes.** A some statement describes an overlap in either direction: **some trained people are volunteers**, and **some weekend workers are students**.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n"}}}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 6.3 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"b99a8c","wall_time_seconds":5.327718,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":2365,"output":"---\\r\\nname: frontend-design\\r\\ndescription: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don\'t read as templated defaults.\\r\\nlicense: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Frontend Design\\r\\n\\r\\nApproach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else\'s. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Ground your designs in the subject matter\\r\\n\\r\\nIf the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design\'s audience, and the design\'s primary job, as a proposal. If there\'s any information in your memory about the client\'s preferences or context about what they\'re building, use that as a hint. The subject\'s industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief\'s real content and subject matter throughout.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Design principles\\r\\n\\r\\nFor web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject\'s world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that\'s truly the best option.\\r\\n\\r\\nTypography carries the personality of the page. You don\'t need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.\\r\\n\\r\\nChoose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.\\r\\n\\r\\nDefault to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.\\r\\n\\r\\nAvoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:\\r\\n- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.\\r\\n- Using all caps for labels.\\r\\n- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.\\r\\n\\r\\nVisual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that\'s only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.\\r\\n\\r\\nUse non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person\'s action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.\\r\\n\\r\\nConsider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it\'s up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique\\r\\n\\r\\nFor calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:\\r\\n1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic\'s own Codex-interaction accent, so on a user\'s brief it reads as a tell);\\r\\n2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;\\r\\n3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;\\r\\n4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;\\r\\n5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots (\'A · B · C\'); labels built as \'WORD — fragment\' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a \'→\' appended to link and button text.\\r\\n\\r\\nAll traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief\'s own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don\'t spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there\'s often a careful balance between doing what you\'re good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.\\r\\n\\r\\nWork in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client\'s design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.\\r\\n- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.\\r\\n- Type: the typefaces and their roles.\\r\\n- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?\\r\\n- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.\\r\\n\\r\\nThen review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you\'ve confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It\'s easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Restraint and self-critique\\r\\n\\r\\nSpend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel\'s advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you\'ve tried, it can help you in future passes.\\r\\n\\r\\n## More on writing in design\\r\\n\\r\\nWords appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.\\r\\n\\r\\nWrite from the end user\'s perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.\\r\\n\\r\\nUse active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: \\"Save changes,\\" not \\"Submit.\\" An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says \\"Publish\\" produces a toast that says \\"Published.\\" The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.\\r\\n\\r\\nTreat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface\'s voice rather than a person\'s. Errors don\'t apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.\\r\\n"}'}]

What must be true? What could still be true? I tell you that  some of the books are hardcover . How many hardcover books must there be?\n\t\t29 container\n\t\t\t30 text At least  one . There could be one, four, or all eight. “Some” rules out zero. It does not rule out “most” or “all.”\n\t\t31 image Eight books showing that one hardcover book and eight hardcover books both satisfy some.\n\t\t32 text This is easy to miss because in ordinary conversation “some” often suggests “some, but not all.” On the LSAT, that extra phrase is not part of the statement. If all eight books are hardcover, it is still true that some are hardcover.\n\t\t33 container\n\t\t\t34 text Try it “Some applicants received an interview.” Could every applicant have received one? Does the sentence tell us that anyone was denied an interview?\n\t\t\t35 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t36 text Check your answer\n\t\t37 container\n\t\t\t38 text Whenever you read  some , replace it with  at least one  in your head. That tells you exactly what the sentence guarantees:\n\t\t39 container\n\t\t\t40 text Some of the books are hardcover.\n\t\t\t41 text At least one of the books is hardcover.\n\t\t42 text Now focus on that one book. It belongs to both groups: it is a book, and it is hardcover. If we describe the same object from the hardcover side, we can say:\n\t\t43 container\n\t\t\t44 text Some hardcover items are books.\n\t\t\t45 text At least one hardcover item is a book.\n\t\t46 container\n\t\t\t47 text We have not found a new object. We have described the same overlap in the other direction. That is why a  some  statement works both ways:\n\t\t48 text Books  ←some→  Hardcover\n\n\t\t49 text The double arrow tells us that at least one thing belongs to both groups. It does not tell us that every book is hardcover or that every hardcover item is a book.\n\t\t50 heading 02 Most guarantees more than half, Value: 2, ID: most\n\t\t\t51 text 02 Most guarantees more than half\n\t\t52 container\n\t\t\t53 text Now I tell you that  most of the eight books are hardcover . We need at least  five  hardcover books. Four would be exactly half, and half is not most. Five, six, seven, or eight could satisfy the sentence.\n\t\t54 image Eight books showing that five hardcover books and eight hardcover books both satisfy most.\n\t\t55 text Notice that all eight could still be hardcover. “Most” does not tell us that an exception exists.\n\t\t56 container\n\t\t\t57 text Try it If most of the eight books are hardcover, must some of them be hardcover? Must any be paperback?\n\t\t\t58 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t59 text Check your answer\n\t\t60 container\n\t\t\t61 text Here is where the direction of the statement matters. From “most books are hardcover,” we know that  some hardcover things are books . We cannot say that  most hardcover things are books . The original sentence counts the books on this shelf. The reversed sentence would count every hardcover thing, including things outside that group.\n\t\t62 text Books  ─most→  Hardcover\nHardcover  ←some→  Books\n\n\t\t63 container\n\t\t\t64 text The first arrow gives the majority claim. The second line is the overlap that the majority guarantees. When we read a most statement backward, the word becomes  some .\n\t\t65 heading 03 All leaves no exception, Value: 2, ID: all\n\t\t\t66 text 03 All leaves no exception\n\t\t67 container\n\t\t\t68 text If  all eight books are hardcover , every book on the shelf is hardcover. One paperback on that shelf would make the statement false.\n\t\t69 image Eight books showing that all eight must be hardcover to satisfy all.\n\t\t70 container\n\t\t\t71 text An all statement gives us a rule:  if it is a book on this shelf, then it is hardcover .\n\t\t72 text Book on this shelf  →  Hardcover\nNot hardcover       →  Not a book on this shelf\n\n\t\t73 text The second line is the contrapositive. Both lines go with the same rule. We cannot turn the first line around and conclude that every hardcover thing is a book on this shelf.\n\t\t74 container\n\t\t\t75 text Try it You pick up a paperback. What does the rule tell you? What if you pick up a hardcover notebook?\n\t\t\t76 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t77 text Check your answer\n\t\t78 text There is a small qualification. “All A are B” gives a rule about A. By itself, it does not tell us that any A exist. When we already know the group exists, all also guarantees most and some.\n\t\t79 heading Put the three statements side by side, Value: 2\n\t\t\t80 text Put the three statements side by side\n\t\t81 text The same shelf can help us see the whole range.\n\t\t82 image For eight existing books: some permits one through eight hardcover, most permits five through eight, and all requires eight.\n\t\t83 text Read the implications in one direction:\n\t\t84 text ALL  →  MOST  →  SOME       (when the group exists)\n\n\t\t85 container\n\t\t\t86 text If all eight books are hardcover, then most are, and some are. If only “some” is given, all eight  could  be hardcover, but we cannot conclude that they  are . Keep the distinction between a possible situation and a required one.\n\t\t87 heading Carry a claim through an all rule, Value: 2, ID: inferences\n\t\t\t88 text Carry a claim through an all rule\n\t\t89 container\n\t\t\t90 text Now we can combine statements. Suppose  some library books are mysteries  and  all mysteries are fiction . We have at least one book that is a mystery. The all rule applies to every mystery, including that one. So  some library books are fiction .\n\t\t91 text Library books  ←some→  Mysteries  →  Fiction\nLibrary books  ←some→  Fiction\n\n\t\t92 container\n\t\t\t93 text The all arrow points  away from  the mystery group we reached. That is why the chain works. If the second sentence said only “most mysteries are fiction,” the mystery books we found could be among the exceptions.\n\t\t94 text The same reasoning preserves the first quantity word:\n\t\t95 table\n\t\t\t96 row\n\t\t\t\t97 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t98 text First statement\n\t\t\t\t99 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t100 text Rule\n\t\t\t\t101 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t102 text What follows\n\t\t\t103 row\n\t\t\t\t104 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t105 text Some library books are mysteries.\n\t\t\t\t106 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t107 text All mysteries are fiction.\n\t\t\t\t108 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t109 text Some library books are fiction.\n\t\t\t110 row\n\t\t\t\t111 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t112 text Most library books are mysteries.\n\t\t\t\t113 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t114 text All mysteries are fiction.\n\t\t\t\t115 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t116 text Most library books are fiction.\n\t\t\t117 row\n\t\t\t\t118 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t119 text All library books are mysteries.\n\t\t\t\t120 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t121 text All mysteries are fiction.\n\t\t\t\t122 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t123 text All library books are fiction.\n\t\t124 container\n\t\t\t125 text Try it “Most library books are mysteries. All fiction is mystery.” Can we conclude that most library books are fiction?\n\t\t\t126 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t127 text Check your answer\n\t\t128 heading Two majorities of the same group must meet, Value: 2\n\t\t\t129 text Two majorities of the same group must meet\n\t\t130 container\n\t\t\t131 text Suppose a club has ten members.  Most members study law , and  most members work part time . Each “most” needs at least six of the ten members. Those two sets cannot fit inside the club without sharing at least two people.\n\t\t132 image Ten club members. Six study law, six work part time, and at least two do both.\n\t\t133 container\n\t\t\t134 text So  some law students work part time . We can also say  some part-time workers study law . These are the same people, described from opposite sides of a some statement.\n\t\t135 text Club members  ─most→  Law students\nClub members  ─most→  Part-time workers\nLaw students  ←some→  Part-time workers\n\n\t\t136 container\n\t\t\t137 text The two most arrows begin with the  same group . That shared starting point is what forces the overlap. The conclusion is  some , not most. We know the two groups meet; we do not know what fraction of either group lies in the overlap.\n\t\t138 container\n\t\t\t139 text Try it If most club members study law and most club members work part time, could the two groups of members be completely separate?\n\t\t\t140 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t141 text Check your answer\n\t\t142 heading A second way two most statements can work, Value: 2\n\t\t\t143 text A second way two most statements can work\n\t\t144 container\n\t\t\t145 text Here is a different comparison.  Most debate team members are seniors , but  most seniors are not on the debate team . The seniors on the team are more than half of the team and less than half of the seniors. The same overlap takes up a larger share of the team than of the senior class. Therefore,  there are more seniors than debate team members .\n\t\t146 image An example in which six of ten debate team members are seniors, while six of twenty seniors are on the team.\n\t\t147 text The numbers in the picture are one possible case. The conclusion follows from the two majority claims, not from those particular numbers.\n\t\t148 heading Similar chains can leave a gap, Value: 2\n\t\t\t149 text Similar chains can leave a gap\n\t\t150 text Two some statements need not describe the same person or thing:\n\t\t151 text Some volunteers speak Spanish.\nSome Spanish speakers are trained.\n\n\t\t152 text The trained Spanish speakers could all be people who do not volunteer. We cannot conclude that any volunteers are trained.\n\t\t153 text Replacing the second “some” with “most” does not fix the gap. The Spanish-speaking volunteers could sit in the untrained minority. Even two most statements chained through different starting groups do not automatically produce a new majority claim.\n\t\t154 container\n\t\t\t155 text Before drawing a conclusion, ask:  Am I carrying a known group through an all rule? Or do two majorities count the same group?  If neither is true, check whether the groups could miss each other.\n\t\t156 container\n\t\t\t157 heading The moves to keep, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t158 text The moves to keep\n\t\t\t159 table\n\t\t\t\t160 row\n\t\t\t\t\t161 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t162 text What you have\n\t\t\t\t\t163 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t164 text What you may conclude\n\t\t\t\t165 row\n\t\t\t\t\t166 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t167 text Some A are B\n\t\t\t\t\t168 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t169 text Some B are A\n\t\t\t\t170 row\n\t\t\t\t\t171 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t172 text Most A are B\n\t\t\t\t\t173 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t174 text Some A are B, and some B are A\n\t\t\t\t175 row\n\t\t\t\t\t176 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t177 text All A are B\n\t\t\t\t\t178 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t179 text A → B, and not B → not A\n\t\t\t\t180 row\n\t\t\t\t\t181 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t182 text Some/most/all A are B; all B are C\n\t\t\t\t\t183 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t184 text The same first quantity of A are C\n\t\t\t\t185 row\n\t\t\t\t\t186 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t187 text Most A are B; most A are C\n\t\t\t\t\t188 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t189 text Some B are C\n\t\t\t190 text These are the useful moves. The arrows show exactly where each one is allowed to go.\n\t\t191 container\n\t\t\t192 heading Short drill: diagram, combine, decide, Value: 2, ID: drill\n\t\t\t\t193 text Short drill: diagram, combine, decide\n\t\t\t194 text Here are five statements about one volunteer program. \n\t\t\t195 text Volunteer\n\t\t\t196 text , \n\t\t\t197 text Spanish speaker\n\t\t\t198 text , \n\t\t\t199 text trained person\n\t\t\t200 text , \n\t\t\t201 text weekend worker\n\t\t\t202 text , and \n\t\t\t203 text student\n\t\t\t204 text  name groups of people. Treat each sentence as true.\n\t\t\t205 content list\n\t\t\t\t206 container\n\t\t\t\t\t207 text 1 . Some volunteers speak Spanish.\n\t\t\t\t208 container\n\t\t\t\t\t209 text 2 . All Spanish speakers are trained.\n\t\t\t\t210 container\n\t\t\t\t\t211 text 3 . Most volunteers work weekends.\n\t\t\t\t212 container\n\t\t\t\t\t213 text 4 . Most volunteers are students.\n\t\t\t\t214 container\n\t\t\t\t\t215 text 5 . Most weekend workers are trained.\n\t\t\t216 text First, diagram each statement. Then answer these without looking below:\n\t\t\t217 content list\n\t\t\t\t218 container\n\t\t\t\t\t219 text 1 . Which two statements prove that  some volunteers are trained ?\n\t\t\t\t220 container\n\t\t\t\t\t221 text 2 .
