If only “some” is given, all eight **could** be hardcover, but we cannot conclude that they **are**. Keep the distinction between a possible situation and a required one.\r\n\r\n## Carry a claim through an all rule\r\n\r\nNow we can combine statements. Suppose **some library books are mysteries** and **all mysteries are fiction**. We have at least one book that is a mystery. The all rule applies to every mystery, including that one. So **some library books are fiction**.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nLibrary books  ←some→  Mysteries  →  Fiction\r\nLibrary books  ←some→  Fiction\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe all arrow points **away from** the mystery group we reached. That is why the chain works. If the second sentence said only “most mysteries are fiction,” the mystery books we found could be among the exceptions.\r\n\r\nThe same reasoning preserves the first quantity word:\r\n\r\n| First statement | Rule | What follows |\r\n|---|---|---|\r\n| Some library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Some library books are fiction. |\r\n| Most library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Most library books are fiction. |\r\n| All library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | All library books are fiction. |\r\n\r\n**Try it:** “Most library books are mysteries. All fiction is mystery.” Can we conclude that most library books are fiction?\r\n\r\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\r\n\r\nNo. The all arrow goes from fiction to mystery. We cannot start at mystery and travel backward to fiction.\r\n\r\n</details>\r\n\r\n## Two majorities of the same group must meet\r\n\r\nSuppose a club has ten members. **Most members study law**, and **most members work part time**. Each “most” needs at least six of the ten members. Those two sets cannot fit inside the club without sharing at least two people.\r\n\r\n![Ten club members. Six study law, six work part time, and at least two do both.](./assets/club-majority-overlap.svg)\r\n\r\nSo **some law students work part time**. We can also say **some part-time workers study law**. These are the same people, described from opposite sides of a some statement.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nClub members  ─most→  Law students\r\nClub members  ─most→  Part-time workers\r\nLaw students  ←some→  Part-time workers\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe two most arrows begin with the **same group**. That shared starting point is what forces the overlap. The conclusion is **some**, not most. We know the two groups meet; we do not know what fraction of either group lies in the overlap.\r\n\r\n**Try it:** If most club members study law and most club members work part time, could the two groups of members be completely separate?\r\n\r\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\r\n\r\nNo. Two separate majorities would require more members than the club has. At least one member must have both traits.\r\n\r\n</details>\r\n\r\n## A second way two most statements can work\r\n\r\nHere is a different comparison. **Most debate team members are seniors**, but **most seniors are not on the debate team**. The seniors on the team are more than half of the team and less than half of the seniors. The same overlap takes up a larger share of the team than of the senior class. Therefore, **there are more seniors than debate team members**.\r\n\r\n![An example in which six of ten debate team members are seniors, while six of twenty seniors are on the team.](./assets/group-size-comparison.svg)\r\n\r\nThe numbers in the picture are one possible case. The conclusion follows from the two majority claims, not from those particular numbers.\r\n\r\n## Similar chains can leave a gap\r\n\r\nTwo some statements need not describe the same person or thing:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nSome volunteers speak Spanish.\r\nSome Spanish speakers are trained.\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe trained Spanish speakers could all be people who do not volunteer. We cannot conclude that any volunteers are trained.\r\n\r\nReplacing the second “some” with “most” does not fix the gap. The Spanish-speaking volunteers could sit in the untrained minority. Even two most statements chained through different starting groups do not automatically produce a new majority claim.\r\n\r\nBefore drawing a conclusion, ask: **Am I carrying a known group through an all rule? Or do two majorities count the same group?** If neither is true, check whether the groups could miss each other.\r\n\r\n## The moves to keep\r\n\r\n| What you have | What you may conclude |\r\n|---|---|\r\n| Some A are B | Some B are A |\r\n| Most A are B | Some A are B, and some B are A |\r\n| All A are B | A → B, and not B → not A |\r\n| Some/most/all A are B; all B are C | The same first quantity of A are C |\r\n| Most A are B; most A are C | Some B are C |\r\n\r\nThese are the useful moves. The arrows show exactly where each one is allowed to go.\r\n\r\n## Short drill: diagram, combine, decide\r\n\r\nHere are five statements about one volunteer program. **Volunteer**, **Spanish speaker**, **trained person**, **weekend worker**, and **student** name groups of people. Treat each sentence as true.\r\n\r\n1. Some volunteers speak Spanish.\r\n2. All Spanish speakers are trained.\r\n3. Most volunteers work weekends.\r\n4. Most volunteers are students.\r\n5. Most weekend workers are trained.\r\n\r\nFirst, diagram each statement. Then answer these without looking below:\r\n\r\n1. Which two statements prove that **some volunteers are trained**?\r\n2. Which two statements prove that **some students work weekends**?\r\n3. Do statements 3 and 5 prove that **most volunteers are trained**? Explain the gap or draw a counterexample.\r\n4. Can you write either valid **some** conclusion in the reverse order?\r\n\r\n<details><summary>Show the diagrams and worked answers</summary>\r\n\r\n```text\r\n1. Volunteers       ←some→  Spanish speakers\r\n2. Spanish speakers →       Trained people\r\n3. Volunteers       ─most→  Weekend workers\r\n4. Volunteers       ─most→  Students\r\n5. Weekend workers  ─most→  Trained people\r\n```\r\n'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 1.9 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '# Some, Most, and All\r\n\r\nQuantity statements tell us whether a claim applies to some members of a group, most of them, or all of them. Suppose a class has been assigned a case to read. “Some students read it,” “most students read it,” and “all students read it” are three different claims about that same class. We do not need an exact headcount to understand the difference.\r\n\r\nFor each sentence, ask: **What must be true? What could still be true?** The answer changes with the word we use.\r\n\r\n## Some guarantees at least one\r\n\r\nImagine a shelf with eight books. I tell you that **some of the books are hardcover**. How many hardcover books must there be?\r\n\r\nAt least **one**. There could be one, four, or all eight. “Some” rules out zero. It does not rule out “most” or “all.”\r\n\r\n![Eight books showing that one hardcover book and eight hardcover books both satisfy some.](./assets/some-books.svg)\r\n\r\nThis is easy to miss because in ordinary conversation “some” often suggests “some, but not all.” On the LSAT, that extra phrase is not part of the statement. If all eight books are hardcover, it is still true that some are hardcover.\r\n\r\n**Try it:** “Some applicants received an interview.” Could every applicant have received one? Does the sentence tell us that anyone was denied an interview?\r\n\r\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\r\n\r\nEvery applicant could have received an interview. The sentence does not tell us that anyone was denied one. “Some” guarantees at least one applicant received an interview, but it leaves open how many others did.\r\n\r\n</details>\r\n\r\nWhenever you read **some**, replace it with **at least one** in your head. That tells you exactly what the sentence guarantees:\r\n\r\n> **Some of the books are hardcover.**\r\n>\r\n> **At least one of the books is hardcover.**\r\n\r\nNow focus on that one book. It belongs to both groups: it is a book, and it is hardcover. If we describe the same object from the hardcover side, we can say:\r\n\r\n> **Some hardcover items are books.**\r\n>\r\n> **At least one hardcover item is a book.**\r\n\r\nWe have not found a new object. We have described the same overlap in the other direction. That is why a **some** statement works both ways:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nBooks  ←some→  Hardcover\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe double arrow tells us that at least one thing belongs to both groups. It does not tell us that every book is hardcover or that every hardcover item is a book.\r\n\r\n## Most guarantees more than half\r\n\r\nNow I tell you that **most of the eight books are hardcover**. We need at least **five** hardcover books. Four would be exactly half, and half is not most. Five, six, seven, or eight could satisfy the sentence.\r\n\r\n![Eight books showing that five hardcover books and eight hardcover books both satisfy most.](./assets/most-books.svg)\r\n\r\nNotice that all eight could still be hardcover. “Most” does not tell us that an exception exists.\r\n\r\n**Try it:** If most of the eight books are hardcover, must some of them be hardcover? Must any be paperback?\r\n\r\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\r\n\r\nAt least five are hardcover, so **some are hardcover**. No paperback book is required. All eight could be hardcover.\r\n\r\n</details>\r\n\r\nHere is where the direction of the statement matters. From “most books are hardcover,” we know that **some hardcover things are books**. We cannot say that **most hardcover things are books**. The original sentence counts the books on this shelf. The reversed sentence would count every hardcover thing, including things outside that group.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nBooks  ─most→  Hardcover\r\nHardcover  ←some→  Books\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe first arrow gives the majority claim. The second line is the overlap that the majority guarantees. When we read a most statement backward, the word becomes **some**.\r\n\r\n## All leaves no exception\r\n\r\nIf **all eight books are hardcover**, every book on the shelf is hardcover. One paperback on that shelf would make the statement false.\r\n\r\n![Eight books showing that all eight must be hardcover to satisfy all.](./assets/all-books.svg)\r\n\r\nAn all statement gives us a rule: **if it is a book on this shelf, then it is hardcover**.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nBook on this shelf  →  Hardcover\r\nNot hardcover       →  Not a book on this shelf\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe second line is the contrapositive. Both lines go with the same rule. We cannot turn the first line around and conclude that every hardcover thing is a book on this shelf.\r\n\r\n**Try it:** You pick up a paperback. What does the rule tell you? What if you pick up a hardcover notebook?\r\n\r\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\r\n\r\nThe paperback cannot be one of these books. The hardcover notebook tells us nothing about whether it is one of these books. Being hardcover is required of the books, but it is not enough to identify one.\r\n\r\n</details>\r\n\r\nThere is a small qualification. “All A are B” gives a rule about A. By itself, it does not tell us that any A exist. When we already know the group exists, all also guarantees most and some.\r\n\r\n## Put the three statements side by side\r\n\r\nThe same shelf can help us see the whole range.\r\n\r\n![For eight existing books: some permits one through eight hardcover, most permits five through eight, and all requires eight.](./assets/book-quantity-ranges.svg)\r\n\r\nRead the implications in one direction:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nALL  →  MOST  →  SOME       (when the group exists)\r\n```\r\n\r\nIf all eight books are hardcover, then most are, and some are. If only “some” is given, all eight **could** be hardcover, but we cannot conclude that they **are**. Keep the distinction between a possible situation and a required one.\r\n\r\n## Carry a claim through an all rule\r\n\r\nNow we can combine statements. Suppose **some library books are mysteries** and **all mysteries are fiction**. We have at least one book that is a mystery. The all rule applies to every mystery, including that one. So **some library books are fiction**.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nLibrary books  ←some→  Mysteries  →  Fiction\r\nLibrary books  ←some→  Fiction\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe all arrow points **away from** the mystery group we reached. That is why the chain works. If the second sentence said only “most mysteries are fiction,” the mystery books we found could be among the exceptions.\r\n\r\nThe same reasoning preserves the first quantity word:\r\n\r\n| First statement | Rule | What follows |\r\n|---|---|---|\r\n| Some library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Some library books are fiction. |\r\n| Most library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Most library books are fiction. |\r\n| All library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | All library books are fiction. |\r\n\r\n**Try it:** “Most library books are mysteries. All fiction is mystery.” Can we conclude that most library books are fiction?\r\n\r\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\r\n\r\nNo. The all arrow goes from fiction to mystery. We cannot start at mystery and travel backward to fiction.\r\n\r\n</details>\r\n\r\n## Two majorities of the same group must meet\r\n\r\nSuppose a club has ten members. **Most members study law**, and **most members work part time**. Each “most” needs at least six of the ten members. Those two sets cannot fit inside the club without sharing at least two people.\r\n\r\n![Ten club members. Six study law, six work part time, and at least two do both.](./assets/club-majority-overlap.svg)\r\n\r\nSo **some law students work part time**. We can also say **some part-time workers study law**. These are the same people, described from opposite sides of a some statement.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nClub members  ─most→  Law students\r\nClub members  ─most→  Part-time workers\r\nLaw students  ←some→  Part-time workers\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe two most arrows begin with the **same group**. That shared starting point is what forces the overlap. The conclusion is **some**, not most. We know the two groups meet; we do not know what fraction of either group lies in the overlap.\r\n\r\n**Try it:** If most club members study law and most club members work part time, could the two groups of members be completely separate?\r\n\r\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\r\n\r\nNo. Two separate majorities would require more members than the club has. At least one member must have both traits.\r\n\r\n</details>\r\n\r\n### When all describes that same group\r\n\r\nThere is another way to guarantee an overlap. Suppose **most club members study law**, and **all club members work part time**. We already know there are law students in the club. The all rule tells us that *each one of those members* also works part time. So **some law students work part time**.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nClub members  ─most→  Law students\r\nClub members  →        Part-time workers\r\nLaw students  ←some→  Part-time workers\r\n```\r\n\r\nWe can make the same move with **some**. If **some club members study law** and **all club members work part time**, take the member guaranteed by “some.” That person has both traits. Again, **some law students work part time**. The sentences can be stated in the other order: **all club members work part time; some club members study law**. The same person still proves the overlap.\r\n\r\n![An all rule covers every club member. A highlighted law student is therefore also a part-time worker.](./assets/all-and-overlap.svg)\r\n\r\n**Try it:** All club members study law. All club members work part time. Must some law students work part time?\r\n\r\n<details><summary>Check your answer</summary>\r\n\r\nNot yet. The two all rules tell us what is true **if** someone is in the club, but neither tells us that the club has a member. Add “at least one person belongs to the club,” and the overlap follows.\r\n\r\n</details>\r\n\r\n## A second way two most statements can work\r\n\r\nHere is a different comparison. **Most debate team members are seniors**, but **most seniors are not on the debate team**. The seniors on the team are more than half of the team and less than half of the seniors. The same overlap takes up a larger share of the team than of the senior class. Therefore, **there are more seniors than debate team members**.\r\n\r\n![An example in which six of ten debate team members are seniors, while six of twenty seniors are on the team.](./assets/group-size-comparison.svg)\r\n\r\nThe numbers in the picture are one possible case. The conclusion follows from the two majority claims, not from those particular numbers.\r\n\r\n## Similar chains can leave a gap\r\n\r\nTwo some statements need not describe the same person or thing:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nSome volunteers speak Spanish.\r\nSome Spanish speakers are trained.\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe trained Spanish speakers could all be people who do not volunteer. We cannot conclude that any volunteers are trained.\r\n\r\nReplacing the second “some” with “most” does not fix the gap. The Spanish-speaking volunteers could sit in the untrained minority. Even two most statements chained through different starting groups do not automatically produce a new majority claim.\r\n\r\nBefore drawing a conclusion, ask: **Am I carrying a known group through an all rule? Or do two majorities count the same group?** If neither is true, check whether the groups could miss each other.\r\n\r\n## The moves to keep\r\n\r\n| What you have | What you may conclude |\r\n|---|---|\r\n| Some A are B | Some B are A |\r\n| Most A are B | Some A are B, and some B are A |\r\n| All A are B | A → B, and not B → not A |\r\n| Some/most/all A are B; all B are C | The same first quantity of A are C |\r\n| Most A are B; most A are C | Some B are C |\r\n| Most A are B; all A are C | Some B are C |\r\n| Some A are B; all A are C | Some B are C |\r\n\r\nTwo **all** claims about A guarantee that every A has both traits. They guarantee **some B are C** only when we also know that at least one A exists.\r\n\r\nThese are the useful moves. The arrows show exactly where each one is allowed to go.\r\n\r\n## Short drill: diagram, combine, decide\r\n\r\nHere are five statements about one volunteer program. **Volunteer**, **Spanish speaker**, **trained person**, **weekend worker**, and **student** name groups of people. Treat each sentence as true.\r\n\r\n1. Some volunteers speak Spanish.\r\n2. All Spanish speakers are trained.\r\n3. Most volunteers work weekends.\r\n4. Most volunteers are students.\r\n5. Most weekend workers are trained.\r\n\r\nFirst, diagram each statement. Then answer these without looking below:\r\n\r\n1. Which two statements prove that **some volunteers are trained**?\r\n2. Which two statements prove that **some students work weekends**?\r\n3. Do statements 3 and 5 prove that **most volunteers are trained**? Explain the gap or draw a counterexample.\r\n4. Can you write either valid **some** conclusion in the reverse order?\r\n\r\n<details><summary>Show the diagrams and worked answers</summary>\r\n\r\n```text\r\n1. Volunteers       ←some→  Spanish speakers\r\n2. Spanish speakers →       Trained people\r\n3. Volunteers       ─most→  Weekend workers\r\n4. Volunteers       ─most→  Students\r\n5. Weekend workers  ─most→  Trained people\r\n```\r\n\r\n**1. Statements 1 and 2.** At least one volunteer speaks Spanish. Every Spanish speaker is trained. That volunteer is trained, so **some volunteers are trained**.\r\n\r\n**2. Statements 3 and 4.** Both majorities count the volunteers. The weekend workers and students must share at least one volunteer. So **some students work weekends**.\r\n\r\n**3. No.** Statement 3 says most volunteers work weekends. Statement 5 counts all weekend workers, a different group. The volunteers who work weekends could be among the untrained weekend workers. Nothing requires most volunteers to be trained.\r\n\r\n**4. Yes.** A some statement describes an overlap in either direction: **some trained people are volunteers**, and **some weekend workers are students**.\r\n\r\n</details>\r\n'}]

Answers "who/what/why".\r\n- **DESIGN.md** (visual): visual theme, color palette, typography, components, layout. Follows the [Google Stitch DESIGN.md format](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/design-md/format/). Answers "how it looks".\r\n\r\nEvery other impeccable command reads these files before doing any work.\r\n\r\n## Step 1: Load current state\r\n\r\nRun the shared loader first so you know what already exists:\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nnode .agents/skills/impeccable/scripts/load-context.mjs\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe output tells you whether PRODUCT.md and/or DESIGN.md already exist. If `migrated: true`, legacy `.impeccable.md` was auto-renamed to `PRODUCT.md`. Infer a hypothesis from the codebase (see Step 2), confirm with the user, write the field.\r\n- **Both exist**: STOP and use Codex\'s structured user-input/question tool when available; if unavailable, ask directly in chat to clarify what you cannot infer. Ask which file to refresh. Skip the one the user doesn\'t want changed.\r\n- **Just DESIGN.md exists (unusual)**: do Steps 2-4 to produce PRODUCT.md.\r\n\r\nNever silently overwrite an existing file. Always confirm first.\r\n\r\nIf teach was invoked as a setup blocker by another command, such as `$impeccable craft landing page`, pause that command here. Complete teach, re-run the loader, then resume the original command with the freshly loaded context. For craft, resume into shape next; teach creates project context, but it is not a substitute for the task-specific shape interview and confirmed design brief.\r\n\r\n## Step 2: Explore the codebase\r\n\r\nBefore asking questions, thoroughly scan the project to discover what you can:\r\n\r\n- **README and docs**: Project purpose, target audience, any stated goals\r\n- **Package.json / config files**: Tech stack, dependencies, existing design libraries\r\n- **Existing components**: Current design patterns, spacing, typography in use\r\n- **Brand assets**: Logos, favicons, color values already defined\r\n- **Design tokens / CSS variables**: Existing color palettes, font stacks, spacing scales\r\n- **Any style guides or brand documentation**\r\n\r\nAlso form a **register hypothesis** from what you find:\r\n\r\n- Brand signals: `/`, `/about`, `/pricing`, `/blog/*`, `/docs/*`, hero sections, big typography, scroll-driven sections, landing-page-shaped content.\r\n- Product signals: `/app/*`, `/dashboard`, `/settings`, `/(auth)`, forms, data tables, side/top nav, app-shell components.\r\n\r\nRegister is a hypothesis at this point, not a decision — Step 3 confirms it.\r\n\r\nNote what you\'ve learned and what remains unclear. This exploration feeds both PRODUCT.md and DESIGN.md.\r\n\r\n## Step 3: Ask strategic questions (for PRODUCT.md)\r\n\r\nSTOP and use Codex\'s structured user-input/question tool when available; if unavailable, ask directly in chat to clarify what you cannot infer. Ask only about what you couldn\'t infer from the codebase.\r\n\r\n### Interview mode, not confirmation mode\r\n\r\nIf the repo is empty or the user\'s brief is sparse, run a short interview before proposing PRODUCT.md. Do **not** turn a one-sentence request into a complete inferred PRODUCT.md and ask for blanket confirmation.\r\n\r\n- Use the harness\'s structured question tool when one exists. Otherwise, ask directly in chat and stop.\r\n- Ask **2-3 questions per round**, then wait for answers.\r\n- Use inferred answers as hypotheses or options, not as finished facts.\r\n- Complete at least one real user-answer round before drafting PRODUCT.md, unless every required answer is directly discoverable from repo docs.\r\n- Round 1 should establish register, users/purpose, and desired outcome.\r\n- Round 2 should establish brand personality or references, anti-references, and accessibility needs.\r\n\r\n### Minimum viable interview\r\n\r\nAsk enough to complete PRODUCT.md. At minimum, cover register confirmation, users and purpose, brand personality, anti-references, and accessibility needs unless each answer is directly discoverable from repo context. After at least one interview round, you may propose inferred answers, but the user must confirm them before you write PRODUCT.md. Never synthesize PRODUCT.md from the original task prompt alone.\r\n\r\n### Register (ask first — it shapes everything below)\r\n\r\nEvery design task is either **brand** (marketing, landing, campaign, long-form content, portfolio — design IS the product) or **product** (app UI, admin, dashboards, tools — design SERVES the product).\r\n\r\nIf Step 2 produced a clear hypothesis, lead with it: *"From the codebase, this looks like a [brand / product] surface — does that match your intent, or should we treat it differently?"*\r\n\r\nIf the signal is genuinely split (e.g. a product with a big marketing landing), STOP and use Codex\'s structured user-input/question tool when available; if unavailable, ask directly in chat to clarify what you cannot infer. Ask which register describes the **primary** surface. The register can be overridden per task later, but PRODUCT.md carries one default.\r\n\r\n### Users & Purpose\r\n- Who uses this? What\'s their context when using it?\r\n- What job are they trying to get done?\r\n- For brand: what emotions should the interface evoke? (confidence, delight, calm, urgency)\r\n- For product: what workflow are they in? What\'s the primary task on any given screen?\r\n\r\n### Brand & Personality\r\n- How would you describe the brand personality in 3 words?\r\n- Reference sites or apps that capture the right feel? What specifically about them?\r\n  - For brand, push for real-world references in the right lane (tech-minimal, editorial-magazine, consumer-warm, brutalist-grid, etc.) — not generic "modern" adjectives.\r\n  - For product, push for category best-tool references (Linear, Figma, Notion, Raycast, Stripe).\r\n- What should this explicitly NOT look like? Any anti-references?\r\n\r\n### Accessibility & Inclusion\r\n- Specific accessibility requirements? (WCAG level, known user needs)\r\n- Considerations for reduced motion, color blindness, or other accommodations?\r\n\r\nSkip questions where the answer is already clear. **Do NOT ask about colors, fonts, radii, or visual styling here** — those belong in DESIGN.md, not PRODUCT.md.\r\n\r\n## Step 4: Write PRODUCT.md\r\n\r\nWrite PRODUCT.md only after the user has confirmed the strategic answers from Step 3. If an inferred answer is uncertain or unconfirmed, ask before writing.\r\n\r\nSynthesize into a strategic document:\r\n\r\n```markdown\r\n# Product\r\n\r\n## Register\r\n\r\nproduct\r\n\r\n## Users\r\n[Who they are, their context, the job to be done]\r\n\r\n## Product Purpose\r\n[What this product does, why it exists, what success looks like]\r\n\r\n## Brand Personality\r\n[Voice, tone, 3-word personality, emotional goals]\r\n\r\n## Anti-references\r\n[What this should NOT look like. Specific bad-example sites or patterns to avoid.]\r\n\r\n## Design Principles\r\n[3-5 strategic principles derived from the conversation. Principles like "practice what you preach", "show, don\'t tell", "expert confidence" — NOT visual rules like "use OKLCH" or "magenta accent".]\r\n\r\n## Accessibility & Inclusion\r\n[WCAG level, known user needs, considerations]\r\n```\r\n\r\nRegister is either `brand` or `product` as a bare value. No prose, no commentary.\r\n\r\nWrite to `PROJECT_ROOT/PRODUCT.md`. If `.impeccable.md` existed, the loader already renamed it — merge into that content rather than starting from scratch.\r\n\r\n## Step 5: Decide on DESIGN.md\r\n\r\nOffer `$impeccable document` either way. Two paths:\r\n\r\n- **Code exists** (CSS tokens, components, a running site): "I can generate a DESIGN.md that captures your visual system (colors, typography, components) so variants stay on-brand. Want to do that now?"\r\n- **Pre-implementation** (empty project): "I can seed a starter DESIGN.md from five quick questions about color strategy, type direction, motion energy, and references. Load its reference and follow that flow.\r\n\r\nIf the user prefers to skip, mention they can run `$impeccable document` any time later.\r\n\r\n## Step 6: Confirm and wrap up\r\n\r\nSummarize:\r\n- Register captured (brand / product)\r\n- What was written (PRODUCT.md, DESIGN.md, or both)\r\n- The 3-5 strategic principles from PRODUCT.md that will guide future work\r\n- If DESIGN.md is pending, remind the user how to generate it later\r\n\r\n**Critical: re-run the loader to refresh session context.** After writing PRODUCT.md, run `node .agents/skills/impeccable/scripts/load-context.mjs` one final time and let its full JSON output land in conversation. This ensures subsequent commands in this session use the freshly-written PRODUCT.md, not a stale earlier version.\r\n\r\nIf teach was invoked as a blocker by another impeccable command (e.g. the user ran `$impeccable polish` with no PRODUCT.md), resume that original task now with the fresh context.\r\n\r\nOptionally STOP and use Codex\'s structured user-input/question tool when available; if unavailable, ask directly in chat to clarify what you cannot infer. [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 5.4 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Warning: truncated output (original token count: 8281)\nTotal output lines: 10\n\n{\n  "hasProduct": true,\n  "product": "# Product\\n\\n<!-- impeccable:product-schema 1 -->\\n\\n## Scope\\n\\nApp-wide only. Every statement in this file must be true of all of LSAT U.\\n\\nA rule that binds one surface does not belong here. It goes in that surface\'s brief under `.impeccable/surfaces/`. This split is deliberate and is the correction to a real failure: the previous PRODUCT.md was written on 2026-05-02 for the Intro to LR bootcamp alone, then widened app-wide on 2026-05-08 in a commit whose stated purpose was adding messenger principles. Bootcamp anti-references silently became binding on the drills, and stayed binding for four months. A one-surface rule written into an app-wide file has no boundary that can hold it. Keeping the file app-wide only removes the mechanism.\\n\\nThe repo already carries eight bounded contexts with their own glossaries (`CONTEXT-MAP.md`). Surface-specific product truth follows those boundaries, not this file.\\n\\n## Platform\\n\\nweb\\n\\n## Users\\n\\n**Primary: Aspiring Attorneys clients.** Students who are paying Joshua for one-to-one LSAT coaching. They have consultations, scheduled sessions, transcripts, assigned work, and a real back-and-forth with him. The platform is where their coaching lives between sessions. They arrive already knowing who their coach is, and design decisions are made for them first.\\n\\n**Secondary: independent self-study learners.** Students using the platform without an active coaching relationship. They are served by the same surfaces but are not the audience a tradeoff is resolved in favour of.\\n\\n**Operator: Joshua.** The sole instructor and the product, voice, and content authority. He assigns work, publishes material, reviews student activity, and answers messages. He works from any device at any hour, so operator surfaces are as responsive as student surfaces.\\n\\n## Product Purpose\\n\\nLSAT U is the operational platform for Joshua\'s coaching practice. It delivers the method, holds the student\'s work, and keeps the coaching relationship live between sessions.\\n\\nFor a student: one place that knows what they have done, what they got wrong, and what to do next.\\n\\nFor Joshua: one workspace to assign, publish, review, and reply without losing the one-to-one feel that his practice is sold on.\\n\\nSuccess is a student who logs in without being chased, knows the next action without asking, and can point to what improved.\\n\\n## Positioning\\n\\n**A real coach is in it.**\\n\\nThe claim a competing product cannot truthfully copy is that a named human being is on the other side of the platform, has met this student, and has looked at this student\'s work. Assignments come from him. Messages are answered by him. The material was authored by him. Nothing in the product should be built in a way that would still be true if the coach were removed, and nothing should imply a coach is present where one is not.\\n\\n## Operating Context\\n\\nThe platform sits inside a coaching practice that runs partly outside it. Future work must not assume the app is the whole system.\\n\\n- Coaching sessions happen on video and are transcribed. Session records, notes, and recaps originate outside the app.\\n- Booking and payment run through their own flow (packages, booking passes, a public booking microsite, single sessions).\\n- Students also practice on third-party platforms. Work done elsewhere is real work, and the app is not the only record of a student\'s effort.\\n- Joshua authors material ahead of time and assigns it, rather than the system generating it on demand.\\n- Students use both desktop and mobile, in focused study blocks and in short check-ins.\\n\\n## Capabilities and Constraints\\n\\nConfirmed surfaces: authentication and onboarding, the foyer, the classroom, guided drills and the question bank, full-passage Reading Comprehension, the Activity Centre, the Testing Centre and practice test runs, the wrong answer journal, saved sets, analytics and history, scheduling and booking, the inbox, the bootcamps, and an admin and teacher workspace.\\n\\nTechnical constraints:\\n\\n- React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, shadcn/ui and Radix primitives, React Router, TanStack Query, Supabase.\\n- One motion library (`framer-motion`). One primary icon library (`lucide-react`). New work composes existing primitives before introducing a new dependency.\\n- Deployment is not a side effect of pushing to `main`. Production at lsatprep.study requires an explicit publish step.\\n- Database migrations in `supabase/migrations/` are an archive, not an applied ledger. Production schema changes go through their own path, and UI must not assume a table exists because a migration file does.\\n\\nTerminology is not defined here. It is defined per bounded context and mapped by `CONTEXT-MAP.md`. A word can carry different weight in different contexts, and collapsing them has already caused real bugs (a **flag** is not a **wrong answer**; **Set** and **Position** were separated for this reason).\\n\\n## Brand Commitments\\n\\n- **Name:** LSAT U, operating under Aspiring Attorneys. Production domain lsatprep.study.\\n- **No em-dashes in anything a student or prospect reads.** Joshua does not type them. A stray em-dash reads as machine-written and costs trust. This binds computed copy, utility copy, and authored copy alike.\\n- **Voice: undecided, deliberately.** The previous record carried a \\"coach voice, not industry voice\\" principle and two named voice registers (R1 procedural, R2 metaphor-led). Both were removed on 2026-09-05 by Joshua\'s decision, on the grounds that they were not stated clearly enough to be usable. They are being redone. Route student-facing copy to Joshua.\\n\\n## Evidence on Hand\\n\\nReal:\\n\\n- A live production deployment at lsatprep.study with real enrolled students.\\n- Authored LSAT curriculum: bootcamp modules, guided drill banks, RC passages with per-question explanations, and practice test content.\\n- Real student work in the database: attempts, sessions, flags, wrong answers, assignments.\\n- A real named instructor with a real coaching practice behind the product.\\n\\nAbsent, and never to be fabricated:\\n\\n- No testimonials, case studies, press coverage, score-improvement statistics, or named customer references exist in this repo. The Hall is a serif institution: an optical serif for its headings and an inscriptional face for its few carved lines. The split is the whole typographic idea. Inside, type gets out of the way; at the door, type is the architecture.\\n\\n### Hierarchy\\n\\n- **Title** (600, 24px, line-height 1, tracking -0.025em): card and section headings in the Workroom.\\n- **Body** (400, 14px rising to 16px at 640px and above, line-height 1.6): everything a student reads in the Workroom chrome.\\n- **Question** (400, 16px, line-height 1.6, Outfit): LSAT stimulus and answer choices. Hierarchy is built from size, weight and space. A second family inside the Workroom is a defect unless it is the Outfit question lock.\\n\\n**The Question Never Moves Rule.** LSAT question text is font-locked. A serif appearing in the Workroom chrome means the seam has leaked.\\n\\n## Layout\\n\\nThe Workroom is a centred single column with generous side gutters. The container centres by default, carries 32px of horizontal padding, and stops widening at 1400px.\\n\\nBreakpoints are the framework defaults up to 1280px, with the largest step pulled in to 1400px. The container\'s maximum is a ceiling for layout, never a licence for prose.\\n\\n## Elevation & Depth\\n\\n**Flat, with hairline separation.** Surfaces sit on the page rather than above it. There is no second border weight in the Workroom.\\n\\n### Named Rules\\n\\n**The Hairline Rule.** One pixel, always. The test is: would a user fluent in the category\'s best tools (Linear, Figma, Notion, Raycast, Stripe come to mind) sit down and trust this interface, or pause at every subtly-off component?\r\n\r\nProduct UI\'s failure mode isn\'t flatness, it\'s strangeness without purpose: over-decorated buttons, mismatched form controls, gratuitous motion, display fonts where labels should be, invented affordances for standard tasks. The bar is earned familiarity. The tool should disappear into the task.\r\n\r\n## Typography\r\n\r\n- **System fonts are legitimate.** `-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", system-ui, sans-serif` gives you native feel on every platform. Inter is the common cross-platform default for a reason.\r\n- **One family is often right.** Product UIs don\'t need display/body pairing. A well-tuned sans carries headings, buttons, labels, body, data.\r\n- **Fixed rem scale, not fluid.** Clamp-sized headings don\'t serve product UI. Users view at consistent DPI, and a fluid h1 that shrinks in a sidebar looks worse, not better.\r\n- **Tighter scale ratio.** 1.125–1.2 between steps is typical. More type elements here than on brand surfaces; exaggerated contrast creates noise.\r\n- **Line length still applies for prose** (65–75ch). Data and compact UI can run denser — tables at 120ch+ are fine.\r\n\r\n## Color\r\n\r\nProduct defaults to Restrained. A single surface can earn Committed — a dashboard where one category color carries a report, an onboarding flow with a drenched welcome screen — but Restrained is the floor.\r\n\r\n- State-rich semantic vocabulary: hover, focus, active, disabled, selected, loading, error, warning, success, info. Standardize these.\r\n- Accent color used for primary actions, current selection, and state indicators only — not decoration.\r\n- A second neutral layer for sidebars, toolbars, and panels (slightly cooler or warmer than the content surface).\r\n\r\n## Layout\r\n\r\n- Predictable grids. Consistency IS an affordance — users navigate faster when the structure is expected.\r\n- Familiar patterns are features. Standard navigation (top bar, side nav), breadcrumbs, tabs, and form layouts have established user expectations. Don\'t reinvent for flavor.\r\n- Responsive behavior is structural (collapse sidebar, responsive table, breakpoint-driven columns), not fluid typography.\r\n\r\n## Components\r\n\r\nEvery interactive component has: default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error. Don\'t ship with half of these.\r\n\r\n- Skeleton states for loading, not spinners in the middle of content.\r\n- Empty states that teach the interface, not "nothing here."\r\n- Consistent affordances across the surface. Same button shape. Same form-control vocabulary. Same icon style.\r\n\r\n## Motion\r\n\r\n- 150–250 ms on most transitions. Users are in flow — don\'t make them wait for choreography.\r\n- Motion conveys state, not decoration. Move the book slider: the books respond, and **some**, **most**, and **all** light up only when each claim becomes true. Newly activated states give one brief warm pulse. I softened the heavy callout styling and gave the new questions a consistent visual treatment. I checked the thresholds at 0, 1, 4, 5, and 8 books, the answer reveals, image loading, and mobile width. Reduced-motion settings stop the pulses.

This is a **local preview** of the lesson. The interactive treatment is not yet part of the posted LSAT U page.

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 1.9 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': "Use the sentence behind each arrow to check what it guarantees.\r\n\r\n## Nearby words need a closer look\r\n\r\nSome test sentences use less exact language. **Many**, **often**, **few**, and **not many** tell us something about frequency or size, but they do not set a universal numerical cutoff. A hundred menu items could make five feel like few; in a menu of six, five would not feel like few. Do not quietly replace these words with a fixed number.\r\n\r\n**Most** is different: it crosses a precise line, **more than half**. Words such as **the majority** plainly express that idea. Words such as **usually**, **typically**, **likely**, and **probably** can suggest it in context, but pay attention to what the sentence actually counts. “Probably” about one event, for example, is a likelihood claim, not a headcount of a group.\r\n\r\n**Not all** *does* give us a precise minimum: at least one exception. “Not all club members are lawyers” means **at least one club member is not a lawyer**. It does not tell us whether the other members are lawyers.\r\n\r\n**Quick check:** A menu lists 100 beers. “Many are Belgian,” “few are Belgian,” and “not many are Belgian” are three claims. Can you assign each one an exact minimum and maximum? What does “not all are Belgian” guarantee?\r\n\r\n<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>\r\n\r\nThe first three do **not** have fixed numerical boundaries. “Many” suggests more than an isolated example, while “few” and “not many” suggest a small number relative to the context. None alone licenses a specific cutoff such as five or ten. “Not all” is exact about one thing: **at least one beer is not Belgian**.\r\n\r\n</details>\r\n\r\n### Pop quiz: decide whether the overlap follows\r\n\r\nFor each pair, decide whether it guarantees **some A are C**. Draw a witness or explain where the groups could miss each other before opening the answers.\r\n\r\n1. Some A are B. All B are C.\r\n2. Some A are B. Most A are C.\r\n3. All A are B. Some B are C.\r\n4. Some A are B. Most B are C.\r\n5. Some A are B. Some B are C.\r\n6. Most A are B. Most A are C.\r\n7. All A are B. All A are C.\r\n\r\n<details><summary>Show the worked answers</summary>\r\n\r\n1. **Yes.** The A that is B must also be C because every B is C.\r\n2. **No.** The A that is B could be outside the majority of A that is C.\r\n3. **No.** The B that is C could be outside A. The all rule runs from A to B, not back from B to A.\r\n4. **No.** The known A that is B could be among the B that are not C.\r\n5. **No.** The B in the first statement could differ from the B in the second.\r\n6. **Yes.** Two majorities of the same A group must share at least one member, who is both B and C.\r\n7. **Not from these statements alone.** Every A would be both B and C, but the statements do not establish that an A exists. If at least one A exists, the answer becomes yes.\r\n\r\n“No” here means **no guaranteed A–C overlap**. The premises may still imply a different, smaller fact. For example, statement 3's “some B are C” is already given.\r\n\r\n</details>\r\n\r\n## Short drill: diagram, combine, decide\r\n\r\nHere are five statements about one volunteer program. **Volunteer**, **Spanish speaker**, **trained person**, **weekend worker**, and **student** name groups of people. Treat each sentence as true.\r\n\r\n1. Some volunteers speak Spanish.\r\n2. All Spanish speakers are trained.\r\n3. Most volunteers work weekends.\r\n4. Most volunteers are students.\r\n5. Most weekend workers are trained.\r\n\r\nFirst, diagram each statement. Then answer these without looking below:\r\n\r\n1. Which two statements prove that **some volunteers are trained**?\r\n2. Which two statements prove that **some students work weekends**?\r\n3. Do statements 3 and 5 prove that **most volunteers are trained**? Explain the gap or draw a counterexample.\r\n4. Can you write either valid **some** conclusion in the reverse order?\r\n\r\n<details><summary>Show the diagrams and worked answers</summary>\r\n\r\n```text\r\n1. Volunteers       ←some→  Spanish speakers\r\n2. Spanish speakers →       Trained people\r\n3. Volunteers       ─most→  Weekend workers\r\n4. Volunteers       ─most→  Students\r\n5. Weekend workers  ─most→  Trained people\r\n```\r\n\r\n**1. Statements 1 and 2.** At least one volunteer speaks Spanish. Every Spanish speaker is trained. That volunteer is trained, so **some volunteers are trained**.\r\n\r\n**2. Statements 3 and 4.** Both majorities count the volunteers. The weekend workers and students must share at least one volunteer. So **some students work weekends**.\r\n\r\n**3. No.** Statement 3 says most volunteers work weekends. Statement 5 counts all weekend workers, a different group. The volunteers who work weekends could be among the untrained weekend workers. Nothing requires most volunteers to be trained.\r\n\r\n**4. Yes.** A some statement describes an overlap in either direction: **some trained people are volunteers**, and **some weekend workers are students**.\r\n\r\n</details>\r\n"}]

That tells you exactly what the sentence guarantees:\r\n\r\n> **Some of the books are hardcover.**\r\n>\r\n> **At least one of the books is hardcover.**\r\n\r\nNow focus on that one book. It belongs to both groups: it is a book, and it is hardcover. If we describe the same object from the hardcover side, we can say:\r\n\r\n> **Some hardcover items are books.**\r\n>\r\n> **At least one hardcover item is a book.**\r\n\r\nWe have not found a new object. We have described the same overlap in the other direction. That is why a **some** statement works both ways:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nBooks  ←some→  Hardcover\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe double arrow tells us that at least one thing belongs to both groups. It does not tell us that every book is hardcover or that every hardcover item is a book.\r\n\r\n## Most guarantees more than half\r\n\r\nNow I tell you that **most of the eight books are hardcover**. We need at least **five** hardcover books. Four would be exactly half, and half is not most. Five, six, seven, or eight could satisfy the sentence.\r\n\r\n'}]

What must be true? What could still be true? The answer changes with the word we use.\n\t\t\t19 container Explore quantity statements with eight books\n\t\t\t\t20 text A LITTLE EXPERIMENT\n\t\t\t\t21 container\n\t\t\t\t\t22 text 1\n\t\t\t\t\t23 text  of 8 books are hardcover\n\t\t\t\t24 text Move the count. Watch which statements become true.\n\t\t\t\t25 slider (settable, integer) Description: Number of hardcover books, Value: 1, ID: quantity-slider\n\t\t\t\t26 container\n\t\t\t\t\t27 text Some Most All\n\t\t28 container Jump through the lesson\n\t\t\t29 link Description: Some, Value: 127.0.0.1:8765/brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/08-quantity-statements-visual-preview.html#some\n\t\t\t30 link Description: Most, Value: 127.0.0.1:8765/brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/08-quantity-statements-visual-preview.html#most\n\t\t\t31 link Description: All, Value: 127.0.0.1:8765/brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/08-quantity-statements-visual-preview.html#all\n\t\t\t32 link Description: Inferences, Value: 127.0.0.1:8765/brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/08-quantity-statements-visual-preview.html#inferences\n\t\t\t33 link Description: Drill, Value: 127.0.0.1:8765/brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/08-quantity-statements-visual-preview.html#drill\n\t\t34 heading 01 Some guarantees at least one, Value: 2, ID: some\n\t\t\t35 text 01 Some guarantees at least one\n\t\t36 container\n\t\t\t37 text Imagine a shelf with eight books. I tell you that  some of the books are hardcover . How many hardcover books must there be?\n\t\t38 container\n\t\t\t39 text At least  one . There could be one, four, or all eight. “Some” rules out zero. It does not rule out “most” or “all.”\n\t\t40 image Eight books showing that one hardcover book and eight hardcover books both satisfy some.\n\t\t41 text This is easy to miss because in ordinary conversation “some” often suggests “some, but not all.” On the LSAT, that extra phrase is not part of the statement. If all eight books are hardcover, it is still true that some are hardcover.\n\t\t42 container\n\t\t\t43 text Try it “Some applicants received an interview.” Could every applicant have received one? Does the sentence tell us that anyone was denied an interview?\n\t\t\t44 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t45 text Check your answer\n\t\t46 container\n\t\t\t47 text Whenever you read  some , replace it with  at least one  in your head. That tells you exactly what the sentence guarantees:\n\t\t48 container\n\t\t\t49 text Some of the books are hardcover.\n\t\t\t50 text At least one of the books is hardcover.\n\t\t51 text Now focus on that one book. It belongs to both groups: it is a book, and it is hardcover. If we describe the same object from the hardcover side, we can say:\n\t\t52 container\n\t\t\t53 text Some hardcover items are books.\n\t\t\t54 text At least one hardcover item is a book.\n\t\t55 container\n\t\t\t56 text We have not found a new object. We have described the same overlap in the other direction. That is why a  some  statement works both ways:\n\t\t57 text Books  ←some→  Hardcover\n\n\t\t58 text The double arrow tells us that at least one thing belongs to both groups. It does not tell us that every book is hardcover or that every hardcover item is a book.\n\t\t59 heading 02 Most guarantees more than half, Value: 2, ID: most\n\t\t\t60 text 02 Most guarantees more than half\n\t\t61 container\n\t\t\t62 text Now I tell you that  most of the eight books are hardcover . We need at least  five  hardcover books. Four would be exactly half, and half is not most. Five, six, seven, or eight could satisfy the sentence.\n\t\t63 image Eight books showing that five hardcover books and eight hardcover books both satisfy most.\n\t\t64 text Notice that all eight could still be hardcover. “Most” does not tell us that an exception exists.\n\t\t65 container\n\t\t\t66 text Try it If most of the eight books are hardcover, must some of them be hardcover? Must any be paperback?\n\t\t\t67 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t68 text Check your answer\n\t\t69 container\n\t\t\t70 text Here is where the direction of the statement matters. From “most books are hardcover,” we know that  some hardcover things are books . We cannot say that  most hardcover things are books . The original sentence counts the books on this shelf. The reversed sentence would count every hardcover thing, including things outside that group.\n\t\t71 text Books  ─most→  Hardcover\nHardcover  ←some→  Books\n\n\t\t72 container\n\t\t\t73 text The first arrow gives the majority claim. The second line is the overlap that the majority guarantees. When we read a most statement backward, the word becomes  some .\n\t\t74 container\n\t\t\t75 text Quick check A program has 100 applicants. Most speak Spanish. What is the smallest possible number who speak Spanish? What is the largest?\n\t\t\t76 button (collapsed) Show the answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t77 text Show the answer\n\t\t78 heading 03 All leaves no exception, Value: 2, ID: all\n\t\t\t79 text 03 All leaves no exception\n\t\t80 container\n\t\t\t81 text If  all eight books are hardcover , every book on the shelf is hardcover. One paperback on that shelf would make the statement false.\n\t\t82 image Eight books showing that all eight must be hardcover to satisfy all.\n\t\t83 container\n\t\t\t84 text An all statement gives us a rule:  if it is a book on this shelf, then it is hardcover .\n\t\t85 text Book on this shelf  →  Hardcover\nNot hardcover       →  Not a book on this shelf\n\n\t\t86 text The second line is the contrapositive. Both lines go with the same rule. We cannot turn the first line around and conclude that every hardcover thing is a book on this shelf.\n\t\t87 container\n\t\t\t88 text Try it You pick up a paperback. What does the rule tell you? What if you pick up a hardcover notebook?\n\t\t\t89 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t90 text Check your answer\n\t\t91 text There is a small qualification. “All A are B” gives a rule about A. By itself, it does not tell us that any A exist. When we already know the group exists, all also guarantees most and some.\n\t\t92 heading Put the three statements side by side, Value: 2\n\t\t\t93 text Put the three statements side by side\n\t\t94 text The same shelf can help us see the whole range.\n\t\t95 image For eight existing books: some permits one through eight hardcover, most permits five through eight, and all requires eight.\n\t\t96 text Read the implications in one direction:\n\t\t97 text ALL  →  MOST  →  SOME       (when the group exists)\n\n\t\t98 container\n\t\t\t99 text If all eight books are hardcover, then most are, and some are. If only “some” is given, all eight  could  be hardcover, but we cannot conclude that they  are . Keep the distinction between a possible situation and a required one.\n\t\t100 heading Carry a claim through an all rule, Value: 2, ID: inferences\n\t\t\t101 text Carry a claim through an all rule\n\t\t102 container\n\t\t\t103 text Now we can combine statements. Suppose  some library books are mysteries  and  all mysteries are fiction . We have at least one book that is a mystery. The all rule applies to every mystery, including that one. So  some library books are fiction .\n\t\t104 text Library books  ←some→  Mysteries  →  Fiction\nLibrary books  ←some→  Fiction\n\n\t\t105 container\n\t\t\t106 text The all arrow points  away from  the mystery group we reached. That is why the chain works. If the second sentence said only “most mysteries are fiction,” the mystery books we found could be among the exceptions.\n\t\t107 container\n\t\t\t108 text Quick check Some archive documents are letters. All letters are handwritten. What follows?\n\t\t\t109 button (collapsed) Show the answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t110 text Show the answer\n\t\t111 text The same reasoning preserves the first quantity word:\n\t\t112 table\n\t\t\t113 row\n\t\t\t\t114 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t115 text First statement\n\t\t\t\t116 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t117 text Rule\n\t\t\t\t118 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t119 text What follows\n\t\t\t120 row\n\t\t\t\t121 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t122 text Some library books are mysteries.\n\t\t\t\t123 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t124 text All mysteries are fiction.\n\t\t\t\t125 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t126 text Some library books are fiction.\n\t\t\t127 row\n\t\t\t\t128 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t129 text Most library books are mysteries.\n\t\t\t\t130 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t131 text All mysteries are fiction.\n\t\t\t\t132 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t133 text Most library books are fiction.\n\t\t\t134 row\n\t\t\t\t135 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t136 text All library books are mysteries.\n\t\t\t\t137 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t138 text All mysteries are fiction.\n\t\t\t\t139 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t140 text All library books are fiction.\n\t\t141 container\n\t\t\t142 text Try it “Most library books are mysteries. All fiction is mystery.” Can we conclude that most library books are fiction?\n\t\t\t143 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t144 text Check your answer\n\t\t145 heading Two majorities of the same group must meet, Value: 2\n\t\t\t146 text Two majorities of the same group must meet\n\t\t147 container\n\t\t\t148 text Suppose a club has ten members.  Most members study law , and  most members work part time . Each “most” needs at least six of the ten members. Those two sets cannot fit inside the club without sharing at least two people.\n\t\t149 image Ten club members. Six study law, six work part time, and at least two do both.\n\t\t150 container\n\t\t\t151 text So  some law students work part time . We can also say  some part-time workers study law . These are the same people, described from opposite sides of a some statement.\n\t\t152 text Club members  ─most→  Law students\nClub members  ─most→  Part-time workers\nLaw students  ←some→  Part-time workers\n\n\t\t153 container\n\t\t\t154 text The two most arrows begin with the  same group . That shared starting point is what forces the overlap. The conclusion is  some , not most. We know the two groups meet; we do not know what fraction of either group lies in the overlap.\n\t\t155 container\n\t\t\t156 text Quick check A club has 25 members. Most are lawyers, and most have criminal records. What is the smallest possible number of members who are both?\n\t\t\t157 button (collapsed) Show the answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t158 text Show the answer\n\t\t159 container\n\t\t\t160 text Try it If most club members study law and most club members work part time, could the two groups of members be completely separate?\n\t\t\t161 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t162 text Check your answer\n\t\t163 heading When all describes that same group, Value: 3\n\t\t\t164 text When all describes that same group\n\t\t165 container\n\t\t\t166 text There is another way to guarantee an overlap. Suppose  most club members study law , and  all club members work part time . We already know there are law students in the club. The all rule tells us that  each one of those members  also works part time. So  some law students work part time .\n\t\t167 text Club members  ─most→  Law students\nClub members  →        Part-time workers\nLaw students  ←some→  Part-time workers\n\n\t\t168 container\n\t\t\t169 text We can make the same move with  some . If  some club members study law  and  all club members work part time , take the member guaranteed by “some.” That person has both traits. Again,  some law students work part time . The sentences can be stated in the other order:  all club members work part time; some club members study law . The same person still proves the overlap.\n\t\t170 image An all rule covers every club member. A highlighted law student is therefore also a part-time worker.\n\t\t171 container\n\t\t\t172 text Try it All club members study law. All club members work part time. Must some law students work part time?\n\t\t\t173 button (collapsed) Check your answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t174 text Check your answer\n\t\t175 heading A second way two most statements can work, Value: 2\n\t\t\t176 text A second way two most statements can work\n\t\t177 container\n\t\t\t178 text Here is a different comparison.  Most debate team members are seniors , but  most seniors are not on the debate team . The seniors on the team are more than half of the team and less than half of the seniors. The same overlap takes up a larger share of the team than of the senior class. Therefore,  there are more seniors than debate team members .\n\t\t179 image An example in which six of ten debate team members are seniors, while six of twenty seniors are on the team.\n\t\t180 text The numbers in the picture are one possible case. The conclusion follows from the two majority claims, not from those particular numbers.\n\t\t181 heading Similar chains can leave a gap, Value: 2\n\t\t\t182 text Similar chains can leave a gap\n\t\t183 text Two some statements need not describe the same person or thing:\n\t\t184 text Some volunteers speak Spanish.\nSome Spanish speakers are trained.\n\n\t\t185 text The trained Spanish speakers could all be people who do not volunteer. We cannot conclude that any volunteers are trained.\n\t\t186 text Replacing the second “some” with “most” does not fix the gap. The Spanish-speaking volunteers could sit in the untrained minority. Even two most statements chained through different starting groups do not automatically produce a new majority claim.\n\t\t187 container\n\t\t\t188 text Before drawing a conclusion, ask:  Am I carrying a known group through an all rule? Or do two majorities count the same group?  If neither is true, check whether the groups could miss each other.\n\t\t189 container\n\t\t\t190 text Quick check A club has 13 members. Most are women, and some are dancers. How many female dancers are guaranteed? How many are possible?\n\t\t\t191 button (collapsed) Show the answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t192 text Show the answer\n\t\t193 container\n\t\t\t194 heading The moves to keep, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t195 text The moves to keep\n\t\t\t196 table\n\t\t\t\t197 row\n\t\t\t\t\t198 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t199 text What you have\n\t\t\t\t\t200 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t201 text What you may conclude\n\t\t\t\t202 row\n\t\t\t\t\t203 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t204 text Some A are B\n\t\t\t\t\t205 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t206 text Some B are A\n\t\t\t\t207 row\n\t\t\t\t\t208 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t209 text Most A are B\n\t\t\t\t\t210 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t211 text Some A are B, and some B are A\n\t\t\t\t212 row\n\t\t\t\t\t213 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t214 text All A are B\n\t\t\t\t\t215 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t216 text A → B, and not B → not A\n\t\t\t\t217 row\n\t\t\t\t\t218 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t219 text Some/most/all A are B; all B are C\n\t\t\t\t\t220 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t221 text The same first quantity of A are C\n\t\t\t\t222 row\n\t\t\t\t\t223 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t224 text Most A are B; most A are C\n\t\t\t\t\t225 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t226 text Some B are C\n\t\t\t\t227 row\n\t\t\t\t\t228 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t229 text Most A are B; all A are C\n\t\t\t\t\t230 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t231 text Some B are C\n\t\t\t\t232 row\n\t\t\t\t\t233 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t234 text Some A are B; all A are C\n\t\t\t\t\t235 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t\t236 text Some B are C\n\t\t\t237 text Two \n\t\t\t238 text all\n\t\t\t239 text  claims about A guarantee that every A has both traits. They guarantee \n\t\t\t240 text some B are C\n\t\t\t241 text  only when we also know that at least one A exists. These are the useful moves. The arrows show exactly where each one is allowed to go.\n\t\t\t242 heading Nearby words need a closer look, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t243 text Nearby words need a closer look\n\t\t\t244 text Some test sentences use less exact language. \n\t\t\t245 text Many\n\t\t\t246 text , \n\t\t\t247 text often\n\t\t\t248 text , \n\t\t\t249 text few\n\t\t\t250 text , and \n\t\t\t251 text not many\n\t\t\t252 text  tell us something about frequency or size, but they do not set a universal numerical cutoff. A hundred menu items could make five feel like few; in a menu of six, five would not feel like few. Do not quietly replace these words with a fixed number.\n\t\t\t253 text Most\n\t\t\t254 text  is different: it crosses a precise line, \n\t\t\t255 text more than half\n\t\t\t256 text . Words such as \n\t\t\t257 text the majority\n\t\t\t258 text  plainly express that idea. Words such as \n\t\t\t259 text usually\n\t\t\t260 text , \n\t\t\t261 text typically\n\t\t\t262 text , \n\t\t\t263 text likely\n\t\t\t264 text , and \n\t\t\t265 text probably\n\t\t\t266 text  can suggest it in context, but pay attention to what the sentence actually counts. “Probably” about one event, for example, is a likelihood claim, not a headcount of a group.\n\t\t\t267 text Not all\n\t\t\t268 text does\n\t\t\t269 text  give us a precise minimum: at least one exception. “Not all club members are lawyers” means \n\t\t\t270 text at least one club member is not a lawyer\n\t\t\t271 text . It does not tell us whether the other members are lawyers. Quick check A menu lists 100 beers. “Many are Belgian,” “few are Belgian,” and “not many are Belgian” are three claims. Can you assign each one an exact minimum and maximum? What does “not all are Belgian” guarantee?\n\t\t\t272 button (collapsed) Show the answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t273 text Show the answer\n\t\t\t274 heading Pop quiz: decide whether the overlap follows, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t275 text Pop quiz: decide whether the overlap follows\n\t\t\t276 text For each pair, decide whether it guarantees \n\t\t\t277 text some A are C\n\t\t\t278 text . Draw a witness or explain where the groups could miss each other before opening the answers.\n\t\t\t279 content list\n\t\t\t\t280 container\n\t\t\t\t\t281 AXListMarker 1. \n\t\t\t\t\t282 text Some A are B. All B are C.\n\t\t\t\t283 container\n\t\t\t\t\t284 AXListMarker 2. \n\t\t\t\t\t285 text Some A are B. Most A are C.\n\t\t\t\t286 container\n\t\t\t\t\t287 AXListMarker 3. \n\t\t\t\t\t288 text All A are B. Some B are C.\n\t\t\t\t289 container\n\t\t\t\t\t290 AXListMarker 4. \n\t\t\t\t\t291 text Some A are B. Most B are C.\n\t\t\t\t292 container\n\t\t\t\t\t293 AXListMarker 5. \n\t\t\t\t\t294 text Some A are B. Some B are C.\n\t\t\t\t295 container\n\t\t\t\t\t296 AXListMarker 6. \n\t\t\t\t\t297 text Most A are B. Most A are C.\n\t\t\t\t298 container\n\t\t\t\t\t299 AXListMarker 7. \n\t\t\t\t\t300 text All A are B. All A are C.\n\t\t\t301 button (collapsed) Show the worked answers, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t302 text Show the worked answers\n\t\t303 container\n\t\t\t304 heading Short drill: diagram, combine, decide, Value: 2, ID: drill\n\t\t\t\t305 text Short drill: diagram, combine, decide\n\t\t\t306 text Here are five statements about one volunteer program. \n\t\t\t307 text Volunteer\n\t\t\t308 text , \n\t\t\t309 text Spanish speaker\n\t\t\t310 text , \n\t\t\t311 text trained person\n\t\t\t312 text , \n\t\t\t313 text weekend worker\n\t\t\t314 text , and \n\t\t\t315 text student\n\t\t\t316 text  name groups of people. Treat each sentence as true.\n\t\t\t317 content list\n\t\t\t\t318 container\n\t\t\t\t\t319 text 1 . Some volunteers speak Spanish.\n\t\t\t\t320 container\n\t\t\t\t\t321 text 2 . All Spanish speakers are trained.\n\t\t\t\t322 container\n\t\t\t\t\t323 text 3 . Most volunteers work weekends.\n\t\t\t\t324 container\n\t\t\t\t\t325 text 4 . Most volunteers are students.\n\t\t\t\t326 container\n\t\t\t\t\t327 text 5 . Most weekend workers are trained.\n\t\t\t328 text First, diagram each statement. Then answer these without looking below:\n\t\t\t329 content list\n\t\t\t\t330 container\n\t\t\t\t\t331 text 1 . Which two statements prove that  some volunteers are trained ?\n\t\t\t\t332 container\n\t\t\t\t\t333 text 2 . Which two statements prove that  some students work weekends ?\n\t\t\t\t334 container\n\t\t\t\t\t335 text 3 . Do statements 3 and 5 prove that  most volunteers are trained ? Explain the gap or draw a counterexample.\n\t\t\t\t336 container\n\t\t\t\t\t337 text 4 . Can you write either valid  some  conclusion in the reverse order?\n\t\t\t338 button (collapsed) Show the diagrams and worked answers, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t\t339 text Show the diagrams and worked answers\n\t\t340 button (disabled) Ask\n\t\t341 button (disabled) Back to notes\n\nThe focused UI element is 0 AXWebArea Some, Most, and All | LSAT U visual study, URL: 127.0.0.1:8765/brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/08-quantity-statements-visual-preview.html'}]
