These are three different claims about that same class:</p>\r\n  <div class="quantity-claims" aria-label="Three claims about the same class">\r\n    <div class="quantity-claim"><b>Some</b><span>students read it.</span></div>\r\n    <div class="quantity-claim"><b>Most</b><span>students read it.</span></div>\r\n    <div class="quantity-claim"><b>All</b><span>students read it.</span></div>\r\n  </div>\r\n  <p class="quantity-scenario">We do not need an exact headcount to understand the difference.</p>\r\n  <div class="quantity-opening-question"><p>What must be true?</p><p>What could still be true?</p><small>The answer changes with the word we use.</small></div>\r\n  </div>\r\n  <div class="quantity-lab" aria-label="Explore quantity statements with eight books">\r\n    <div class="quantity-lab-head"><span class="quantity-lab-kicker">A little experiment</span><span class="quantity-lab-count" aria-live="polite"><b id="quantity-count">1</b> of 8 books are hardcover</span></div>\r\n    <div class="quantity-lab-books" aria-hidden="true"><span class="quantity-lab-book is-hardcover"><i></i></span><span class="quantity-lab-book"><i></i></span><span class="quantity-lab-book"><i></i></span><span class="quantity-lab-book"><i></i></span><span class="quantity-lab-book"><i></i></span><span class="quantity-lab-book"><i></i></span><span class="quantity-lab-book"><i></i></span><span class="quantity-lab-book"><i></i></span></div>\r\n    <label class="quantity-lab-instruction" for="quantity-slider">Move the count. Watch which statements become true.</label>\r\n    <input id="quantity-slider" class="quantity-lab-slider" type="range" min="0" max="8" value="1" aria-label="Number of hardcover books">\r\n    <div class="quantity-lab-verdicts" aria-live="polite"><span data-rule="some" class="is-true"><i></i><b>Some</b><small>1–8</small></span><span data-rule="most"><i></i><b>Most</b><small>5–8</small></span><span data-rule="all"><i></i><b>All</b><small>8</small></span></div>\r\n  </div>\r\n</header>\r\n<nav class="quantity-jump" aria-label="Jump through the lesson"><a href="#some">Some</a><a href="#most">Most</a><a href="#all">All</a><a href="#inferences">Inferences</a><a href="#quantity-quiz">Practice</a><a href="#drill">Drill</a></nav><h2 id="some" class="quantity-chapter"><span class="quantity-chapter-number">01</span>Some guarantees at least one</h2>\r\n<p>Imagine a shelf with eight books. I tell you that <strong>some of the books are hardcover</strong>. How many hardcover books must there be?</p>\r\n<p>At least <strong>one</strong>. There could be one, four, or all eight. “Some” rules out zero. It does not rule out “most” or “all.”</p>\r\n<figure class="quantity-figure"><img src="./assets/some-books.svg" alt="Eight books showing that one hardcover book and eight hardcover books both satisfy some."></figure>\r\n<p>This is easy to miss because in ordinary conversation “some” often suggests “some, but not all.” On the LSAT, that extra phrase is not part of the statement. If all eight books are hardcover, it is still true that some are hardcover.</p>\r\n<aside class="quantity-check" data-check="0"><div class="quantity-check-top"><span>Try it</span><span>01</span></div><p class="quantity-check-question"> “Some applicants received an interview.” Could every applicant have received one? Does the sentence tell us that anyone was denied an interview?</p><form class="quantity-check-form"><label for="quantity-check-0">Your answer</label><textarea id="quantity-check-0" rows="2" placeholder="Write your answer here…" required></textarea><button type="submit">Check my answer <span aria-hidden="true">↗</span></button></form><div class="quantity-check-result" hidden aria-live="polite"><strong></strong><div class="quantity-check-worked"><div class="quantity-answer-body"><p>Every applicant could have received an interview. The sentence does not tell us that anyone was denied one. “Some” guarantees at least one applicant received an interview, but it leaves open how many others did.</p>\r\n</div></div><button type="button" class="quantity-check-again">Edit my answer</button></div></aside>\r\n\r\n<p>Whenever you read <strong>some</strong>, replace it with <strong>at least one</strong> in your head. That tells you exactly what the sentence guarantees:</p>\r\n<blockquote>\r\n<p><strong>Some of the books are hardcover.</strong></p>\r\n<p><strong>At least one of the books is hardcover.</strong></p>\r\n</blockquote>\r\n<p>Now focus on that one book. It belongs to both groups: it is a book, and it is hardcover. If we describe the same object from the hardcover side, we can say:</p>\r\n<blockquote>\r\n<p><strong>Some hardcover items are books.</strong></p>\r\n<p><strong>At least one hardcover item is a book.</strong></p>\r\n</blockquote>\r\n<p>We have not found a new object. We have described the same overlap in the other direction. That is why a <strong>some</strong> statement works both ways:</p>\r\n<pre><code class="language-text">Books  ←some→  Hardcover\r\n</code></pre>\r\n<p>The double arrow tells us that at least one thing belongs to both groups. It does not tell us that every book is hardcover or that every hardcover item is a book.</p>\r\n<h3>What would make “some” false?</h3>\r\n<p>If <strong>some books are hardcover</strong> is false, then <strong>no books are hardcover</strong>. There is not even one book in both groups. Notice the difference between <strong>no books are hardcover</strong> and <strong>some books are not hardcover</strong>. The second sentence still allows other books to be hardcover, so it does not negate “some.”</p>\r\n<h2 id="most" class="quantity-chapter"><span class="quantity-chapter-number">02</span>Most guarantees more than half</h2>\r\n<p>Now I tell you that <strong>most of the eight books are hardcover</strong>. We need at least <strong>five</strong> hardcover books. Four would be exactly half, and half is not most. Five, six, seven, or eight could satisfy the sentence.</p>\r\n<figure class="quantity-figure"><img src="./assets/most-books.svg" alt="Eight books showing that five hardcover books and eight hardcover books both satisfy most."></figure>\r\n<p>Notice that all eight could still be hardcover. “Most” does not tell us that an exception exists.</p>\r\n<aside class="quantity-check" data-check="1"><div class="quantity-check-top"><span>Try it</span><span>02</span></div><p class="quantity-check-question"> If most of the eight books are hardcover, must some of them be hardcover? Must any be paperback?</p><form class="quantity-check-form"><label for="quantity-check-1">Your answer</label><textarea id="quantity-check-1" rows="2" placeholder="Write your answer here…" required></textarea><button type="submit">Check my answer <span aria-hidden="true">↗</span></button></form><div class="quantity-check-result" hidden aria-live="polite"><strong></strong><div class="quantity-check-worked"><div class="quantity-answer-body"><p>At least five are hardcover, so <strong>some are hardcover</strong>. No paperback book is required. All eight could be hardcover.</p>\r\n</div></div><button type="button" class="quantity-check-again">Edit my answer</button></div></aside>\r\n\r\n<p>Here is where the direction of the statement matters. From “most books are hardcover,” we know that <strong>some hardcover things are books</strong>. We cannot say that <strong>most hardcover things are books</strong>. Five of our eight shelf books could be hardcover, while a library holds hundreds of other hardcover items. The first statement counts the eight books; the reversed statement counts a different group.</p>\r\n<pre><code class="language-text">Books  ─most→  Hardcover\r\nHardcover  ←some→  Books\r\n</code></pre>\r\n<p>The first arrow gives the majority claim. The second line is the overlap that the majority guarantees. When we read a most statement backward, the word becomes <strong>some</strong>.</p>\r\n<aside class="quantity-check" data-check="2"><div class="quantity-check-top"><span>Quick check</span><span>03</span></div><p class="quantity-check-question"> A program has 100 applicants. Most speak Spanish. What is the smallest possible number who speak Spanish? What is the largest?</p><form class="quantity-check-form"><label for="quantity-check-2">Your answer</label><textarea id="quantity-check-2" rows="2" placeholder="Write your answer here…" required></textarea><button type="submit">Check my answer <span aria-hidden="true">↗</span></button></form><div class="quantity-check-result" hidden aria-live="polite"><strong></strong><div class="quantity-check-worked"><div class="quantity-answer-body"><p><strong>51 to 100.</strong> Fifty is only half. “Most” also permits all 100, so it does not establish an exception.</p>\r\n</div></div><button type="button" class="quantity-check-again">Edit my answer</button></div></aside>\r\n\r\n<h3>What would make “most” false?</h3>\r\n<p>“Most of the eight books are hardcover” needs at least five hardcover books. Its negation permits <strong>four or fewer</strong>. Four is exactly half, so it already makes “most” false. The opposite of “most are hardcover” is <strong>half or fewer are hardcover</strong>, not “most are paperback.” Both kinds could make up exactly half.</p>\r\n<h2 id="all" class="quantity-chapter"><span class="quantity-chapter-number">03</span>All leaves no exception</h2>\r\n<p>If <strong>all eight books are hardcover</strong>, every book on the shelf is hardcover. One paperback on that shelf would make the statement false.</p>\r\n<figure class="quantity-figure"><img src="./assets/all-books.svg" alt="Eight books showing that all eight must be hardcover to satisfy all."></figure>\r\n<p>An all statement gives us a rule: <strong>if it is one of these eight books, then it is hardcover</strong>.</p>\r\n<pre><code class="language-text">One of these books  →  Hardcover\r\nNot hardcover       →  Not one of these books\r\n</code></pre>\r\n<p>The second line is the contrapositive. Both lines go with the same rule. We cannot turn the first line around and conclude that every hardcover thing is a book on this shelf.</p>\r\n<aside class="quantity-check" data-check="3"><div class="quantity-check-top"><span>Try it</span><span>04</span></div><p class="quantity-check-question"> You pick up a paperback. What does the rule tell you? What if you pick up a hardcover book from another shelf?</p><form class="quantity-check-form"><label for="quantity-check-3">Your answer</label><textarea id="quantity-check-3" rows="2" placeholder="Write your answer here…" required></textarea><button type="submit">Check my answer <span aria-hidden="true">↗</span></button></form><div class="quantity-check-result" hidden aria-live="polite"><strong></strong><div class="quantity-check-worked"><div class="quantity-answer-body"><p>The paperback cannot be one of these eight books. A hardcover book from another shelf does not become one of these eight just because it is hardcover. Being hardcover is required, but it is not enough to identify one of these books.</p>\r\n</div></div><button type="button" class="quantity-check-again">Edit my answer</button></div></aside>\r\n\r\n<p>There is a small qualification. “All A are B” gives a rule about A. By itself, it does not tell us that any A exist. When we already know the group exists, all also guarantees most and some.</p>\r\n<h3>What would make “all” false?</h3>\r\n<p>One exception is enough. “Not all eight books are hardcover” means <strong>at least one of the eight is not hardcover</strong>. The other seven could still be hardcover. This is the negation of the all claim. By contrast, “not hardcover → not one of these eight books” is its <strong>contrapositive</strong>: another way to state the original rule, not a way to deny it.</p>\r\n<h2 class="quantity-chapter"><span class="quantity-chapter-number">04</span>Put the three statements side by side</h2>\r\n<p>The same shelf can help us see the whole range.</p>\r\n<figure class="quantity-figure"><img src="./assets/book-quantity-ranges.svg" alt="For eight existing books: some permits one through eight hardcover, most permits five through eight, and all requires eight."></figure>\r\n<p>Read the implications in one direction:</p>\r\n<pre><code class="language-text">ALL  →  MOST  →  SOME       (when the group exists)\r\n</code></pre>\r\n<p>If all eight books are hardcover, then most are, and some are. If only “some” is given, all eight <strong>could</strong> be hardcover, but we cannot conclude that they <strong>are</strong>. Keep the distinction between a possible situation and a required one.</p>\r\n<h2 id="inferences" class="quantity-chapter"><span class="quantity-chapter-number">05</span>Carry a claim through an all rule</h2>\r\n<p>Now we can combine statements. Suppose <strong>some library books are mysteries</strong> and <strong>all mysteries are fiction</strong>. We have at least one book that is a mystery. The all rule applies to every mystery, including that one. So <strong>some library books are fiction</strong>.</p>\r\n<pre><code class="language-text">Library books  ←some→  Mysteries  →  Fiction\r\nLibrary books  ←some→  Fiction\r\n</code></pre>\r\n'}]

These are three different claims about that same class:\n\t\t4 container Three claims about the same class\n\t\t\t5 text Some\n\t\t\t6 text students read it.\n\t\t\t7 text Most\n\t\t\t8 text students read it.\n\t\t\t9 text All\n\t\t\t10 text students read it.\n\t\t11 text We do not need an exact headcount to understand the difference.\n\t\t12 text What must be true?\n\t\t13 text What could still be true?\n\t\t14 text The answer changes with the word we use.\n\t\t15 text One shelf. Three thresholds.\n\t\t16 text Some  1â€“8 Most  5â€“8 All  8\n\t\t17 text Number of hardcover books out of eight.\n\t\t18 heading 01Some guarantees at least one, Value: 2, ID: some\n\t\t\t19 text 01 Some guarantees at least one\n\t\t20 text Imagine a shelf with eight books. I tell you that \n\t\t21 text some of the books are hardcover\n\t\t22 text . How many hardcover books must there be? At least \n\t\t23 text one\n\t\t24 text . There could be one, four, or all eight. â€œSomeâ€\x9d rules out zero. It does not rule out â€œmostâ€\x9d or â€œall.â€\x9d\n\t\t25 container Eight books showing that one hardcover book and eight hardcover books both satisfy some.\n\t\t26 text This is easy to miss because in ordinary conversation â€œsomeâ€\x9d often suggests â€œsome, but not all.â€\x9d On the LSAT, that extra phrase is not part of the statement. If all eight books are hardcover, it is still true that some are hardcover. TRY IT 01\n\t\t27 text â€œSome applicants received an interview.â€\x9d Could every applicant have received one? Does the sentence tell us that anyone was denied an interview?\n\t\t28 button (collapsed) Show the worked answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t29 text Show the worked answer\n\t\t30 text Whenever you read \n\t\t31 text some\n\t\t32 text , replace it with \n\t\t33 text at least one\n\t\t34 text  in your head. That tells you exactly what the sentence guarantees:\n\t\t35 text Some of the books are hardcover.\n\t\t36 text At least one of the books is hardcover.\n\t\t37 text Now focus on that one book. It belongs to both groups: it is a book, and it is hardcover. If we describe the same object from the hardcover side, we can say:\n\t\t38 text Some hardcover items are books.\n\t\t39 text At least one hardcover item is a book.\n\t\t40 text We have not found a new object. We have described the same overlap in the other direction. That is why a \n\t\t41 text some\n\t\t42 text  statement works both ways:\n\t\t43 text Books  â†\x90someâ†’  Hardcover\n\n\t\t44 text The double arrow tells us that at least one thing belongs to both groups. It does not tell us that every book is hardcover or that every hardcover item is a book.\n\t\t45 heading What would make â€œsomeâ€\x9d false?, Value: 3\n\t\t\t46 text What would make â€œsomeâ€\x9d false?\n\t\t47 text If \n\t\t48 text some books are hardcover\n\t\t49 text  is false, then \n\t\t50 text no books are hardcover\n\t\t51 text . There is not even one book in both groups. Notice the difference between \n\t\t52 text no books are hardcover\n\t\t53 text  and \n\t\t54 text some books are not hardcover\n\t\t55 text . The second sentence still allows other books to be hardcover, so it does not negate â€œsome.â€\x9d\n\t\t56 heading 02Most guarantees more than half, Value: 2, ID: most\n\t\t\t57 text 02 Most guarantees more than half\n\t\t58 text Now I tell you that \n\t\t59 text most of the eight books are hardcover\n\t\t60 text . We need at least \n\t\t61 text five\n\t\t62 text  hardcover books. Four would be exactly half, and half is not most. Five, six, seven, or eight could satisfy the sentence.\n\t\t63 container Eight books showing that five hardcover books and eight hardcover books both satisfy most.\n\t\t64 text Notice that all eight could still be hardcover. â€œMostâ€\x9d does not tell us that an exception exists. TRY IT 02\n\t\t65 text If most of the eight books are hardcover, must some of them be hardcover? Must any be paperback?\n\t\t66 button (collapsed) Show the worked answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t67 text Show the worked answer\n\t\t68 text Here is where the direction of the statement matters. From â€œmost books are hardcover,â€\x9d we know that \n\t\t69 text some hardcover things are books\n\t\t70 text . We cannot say that \n\t\t71 text most hardcover things are books\n\t\t72 text . Five of our eight shelf books could be hardcover, while a library holds hundreds of other hardcover items. The first statement counts the eight books; the reversed statement counts a different group.\n\t\t73 text Books  â”€mostâ†’  Hardcover\nHardcover  â†\x90someâ†’  Books\n\n\t\t74 text The first arrow gives the majority claim. The second line is the overlap that the majority guarantees. When we read a most statement backward, the word becomes \n\t\t75 text some\n\t\t76 text . QUICK CHECK 03\n\t\t77 text A program has 100 applicants. Most speak Spanish. What is the smallest possible number who speak Spanish? What is the largest?\n\t\t78 button (collapsed) Show the worked answer, Secondary Actions: Expand\n\t\t\t79 text Show the worked answer\n\t\t80 heading What would make â€œmostâ€\x9d false?, Value: 3\n\t\t\t81 text What would make â€œmostâ€\x9d false?\n\t\t82 text â€œMost of the eight books are hardcoverâ€\x9d needs at least five hardcover books. Its negation permits \n\t\t83 text four or fewer\n\t\t84 text . Four is exactly half, so it already makes â€œmostâ€\x9d false. The opposite of â€œmost are hardcoverâ€\x9d is \n\t\t85 text half or fewer are hardcover\n\t\t86 text , not â€œmost are paperback.â€\x9d Both kinds could make up exactly half.\n\t\t87 heading 03All leaves no exception, Value: 2, ID: all\n\t\t\t88 text 03 All leaves no exception\n\t\t89 text If \n\t\t90 text all eight books are hardcover\n\t\t91 text , every book on the shelf is hardcover. One paperback on that shelf would make the statement false.\n\t\t92 container Eight books showing that all eight must be hardcover to satisfy all.\n\t\t93 text An all statement gives us a rule: \n\t\t94 text if it is one of these eight books, then it is hardcover\n\t\t95 text .\n\t\t96 text One of these books  â†’  Hardcover\nNot hardcover       â†’  Not one of these books\n\n\t\t97 text The second line is the contrapositive. Both lines go with the same rule. We cannot turn the first line around and conclude that every hardcover thing is a book on this shelf. TRY IT 04\n\t\t98 text You pick up a paperback. The conclusion follows from the two majority claims, not from those particular numbers.\n\t\t263 heading 08Similar chains can leave a gap, Value: 2\n\t\t\t264 text 08 Similar chains can leave a gap\n\t\t265 text Two some statements need not describe the same person or thing:\n\t\t266 text Some volunteers speak Spanish.\nSome Spanish speakers are trained.\n\n\t\t267 text The trained Spanish speakers could all be people who do not volunteer. We cannot conclude that any volunteers are trained.\n\t\t268 container Two different Spanish speakers satisfy the two some claims without any volunteer being trained.\n\t\t269 text Replacing the second â€œsomeâ€\x9d with â€œmostâ€\x9d does not fix the gap. The Spanish-speaking volunteers could sit in the untrained minority. Even two most statements that count different groups do not automatically produce a new majority claim. Before drawing a conclusion, ask: \n\t\t270 text Am I carrying a known group through an all rule? They imply at least one.\n\t\t\t349 row\n\t\t\t\t350 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t351 text Most\n\t\t\t\t\t352 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t353 text more than half\n\t\t\t\t\t354 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t355 text a majority of\n\t\t\t\t356 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t357 text Strictly more than half of the named group fit.\n\t\t\t358 row\n\t\t\t\t359 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t360 text All\n\t\t\t\t\t361 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t362 text every\n\t\t\t\t\t363 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t364 text each\n\t\t\t\t\t365 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t366 text without exception\n\t\t\t\t367 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t368 text Every member of the named group fits. No exact numerical boundary follows.\n\t\t\t378 row\n\t\t\t\t379 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t380 text No\n\t\t\t\t\t381 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t382 text none\n\t\t\t\t\t383 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t384 text zero\n\t\t\t\t385 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t386 text Not a single member fits.\n\t\t\t387 row\n\t\t\t\t388 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t389 text Not all\n\t\t\t\t390 cell\n\t\t\t\t\t391 text At least one member does \n\t\t\t\t\t392 text not\n\t\t\t\t\t393 text  fit.\n\t\t394 container\n\t\t\t395 text Few  is worth separating from  a few . â€œA few books are hardcoverâ€\x9d affirms that at least some are. â€œFew books are hardcoverâ€\x9d stresses how small the number is. It often suggests some in ordinary speech, but it does not set a dependable numerical minimum. â€œNot manyâ€\x9d can include zero. A hundred menu items could make five feel like few; in a menu of six, five would not feel like few. Do not quietly replace any of these phrases with a fixed number.\n\t\t396 container\n\t\t\t397 text Most  is different: it crosses a precise line,  more than half . Words such as  the majority  plainly express that idea. Words such as  usually ,  typically ,  generally ,  commonly ,  frequently ,  often ,  likely , and  probably  can suggest prevalence in context, but pay attention to what the sentence actually counts. â€œProbablyâ€\x9d about one event, for example, is a likelihood claim, not a headcount of a group.\n\t\t398 container\n\t\t\t399 text Not all does  give us a precise minimum: at least one exception. â€œNot all club members are lawyersâ€\x9d means  at least one club member is not a lawyer . [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Wall time: 0.6264 seconds\nOutput:'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Browser tab: 1116362009, Title: "Classroom transfer", URL: "http://127.0.0.1:8765/brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/09-quantity-statements-transfer.html".\n1 AXWebArea Classroom transfer, URL: 127.0.0.1:8765/brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/09-quantity-statements-transfer.html\n\t2 container\n\t\t3 text entry area (settable) Quantity statements tell us whether a claim applies to some members of a group, most of them, or all of them. Suppose a class has been assigned a case to read. “Some students read it,” “most students read it,” and “all students read it” are three different claims about that same class. We do not need an exact headcount to understand the difference.\n\nFor each sentence, ask: **What must be true? What could still be true?** The answer changes with the word we use.\n\n## Some guarantees at least one\n\nImagine a shelf with eight books. I tell you that **some of the books are hardcover**. How many hardcover books must there be?\n\nAt least **one**. There could be one, four, or all eight. “Some” rules out zero. It does not rule out “most” or “all.”\n\n> **Visual:** Eight books showing that one hardcover book and eight hardcover books both satisfy some.\n\nThis is easy to miss because in ordinary conversation “some” often suggests “some, but not all.” On the LSAT, that extra phrase is not part of the statement. If all eight books are hardcover, it is still true that some are hardcover.\n\n**Try it:** “Some applicants received an interview.” Could every applicant have received one? Does the sentence tell us that anyone was denied an interview?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nEvery applicant could have received an interview. The sentence does not tell us that anyone was denied one. “Some” guarantees at least one applicant received an interview, but it leaves open how many others did.\n\nWhenever you read **some**, replace it with **at least one** in your head. That tells you exactly what the sentence guarantees:\n\n> **Some of the books are hardcover.**\n>\n> **At least one of the books is hardcover.**\n\nNow focus on that one book. It belongs to both groups: it is a book, and it is hardcover. If we describe the same object from the hardcover side, we can say:\n\n> **Some hardcover items are books.**\n>\n> **At least one hardcover item is a book.**\n\nWe have not found a new object. We have described the same overlap in the other direction. That is why a **some** statement works both ways:\n\n```text\nBooks  ←some→  Hardcover\n```\n\nThe double arrow tells us that at least one thing belongs to both groups. It does not tell us that every book is hardcover or that every hardcover item is a book.\n\n### What would make “some” false?\n\nIf **some books are hardcover** is false, then **no books are hardcover**. There is not even one book in both groups. Notice the difference between **no books are hardcover** and **some books are not hardcover**. The second sentence still allows other books to be hardcover, so it does not negate “some.”\n\n## Most guarantees more than half\n\nNow I tell you that **most of the eight books are hardcover**. We need at least **five** hardcover books. Four would be exactly half, and half is not most. Five, six, seven, or eight could satisfy the sentence.\n\n> **Visual:** Eight books showing that five hardcover books and eight hardcover books both satisfy most.\n\nNotice that all eight could still be hardcover. “Most” does not tell us that an exception exists.\n\n**Try it:** If most of the eight books are hardcover, must some of them be hardcover? Must any be paperback?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nAt least five are hardcover, so **some are hardcover**. No paperback book is required. All eight could be hardcover.\n\nHere is where the direction of the statement matters. From “most books are hardcover,” we know that **some hardcover things are books**. We cannot say that **most hardcover things are books**. Five of our eight shelf books could be hardcover, while a library holds hundreds of other hardcover items. The first statement counts the eight books; the reversed statement counts a different group.\n\n```text\nBooks  ─most→  Hardcover\nHardcover  ←some→  Books\n```\n\nThe first arrow gives the majority claim. The second line is the overlap that the majority guarantees. When we read a most statement backward, the word becomes **some**.\n\n**Quick check:** A program has 100 applicants. Most speak Spanish. What is the smallest possible number who speak Spanish? What is the largest?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n**51 to 100.** Fifty is only half. “Most” also permits all 100, so it does not establish an exception.\n\n### What would make “most” false?\n\n“Most of the eight books are hardcover” needs at least five hardcover books. Its negation permits **four or fewer**. Four is exactly half, so it already makes “most” false. The opposite of “most are hardcover” is **half or fewer are hardcover**, not “most are paperback.” Both kinds could make up exactly half.\n\n## All leaves no exception\n\nIf **all eight books are hardcover**, every book on the shelf is hardcover. One paperback on that shelf would make the statement false.\n\n> **Visual:** Eight books showing that all eight must be hardcover to satisfy all.\n\nAn all statement gives us a rule: **if it is one of these eight books, then it is hardcover**.\n\n```text\nOne of these books  →  Hardcover\nNot hardcover       →  Not one of these books\n```\n\nThe second line is the contrapositive. Both lines go with the same rule. We cannot turn the first line around and conclude that every hardcover thing is a book on this shelf.\n\n**Try it:** You pick up a paperback. What does the rule tell you? What if you pick up a hardcover book from another shelf?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nThe paperback cannot be one of these eight books. A hardcover book from another shelf does not become one of these eight just because it is hardcover. Being hardcover is required, but it is not enough to identify one of these books.\n\nThere is a small qualification. “All A are B” gives a rule about A. By itself, it does not tell us that any A exist. When we already know the group exists, all also guarantees most and some.\n\n### What would make “all” false?\n\nOne exception is enough. “Not all eight books are hardcover” means **at least one of the eight is not hardcover**. The other seven could still be hardcover. This is the negation of the all claim. By contrast, “not hardcover → not one of these eight books” is its **contrapositive**: another way to state the original rule, not a way to deny it.\n\n## Put the three statements side by side\n\nThe same shelf can help us see the whole range.\n\n> **Visual:** For eight existing books: some permits one through eight hardcover, most permits five through eight, and all requires eight.\n\nRead the implications in one direction:\n\n```text\nALL  →  MOST  →  SOME       (when the group exists)\n```\n\nIf all eight books are hardcover, then most are, and some are. If only “some” is given, all eight **could** be hardcover, but we cannot conclude that they **are**. Keep the distinction between a possible situation and a required one.\n\n## Carry a claim through an all rule\n\nNow we can combine statements. Suppose **some library books are mysteries** and **all mysteries are fiction**. We have at least one book that is a mystery. The all rule applies to every mystery, including that one. So **some library books are fiction**.\n\n```text\nLibrary books  ←some→  Mysteries  →  Fiction\nLibrary books  ←some→  Fiction\n```\n\nThe all arrow points **away from** the mystery group we reached. That is why the chain works. If the second sentence said only “most mysteries are fiction,” the mystery books we found could be among the exceptions.\n\n> **Visual:** A marked library book is inside the mysteries group, which is entirely inside the fiction group.\n\n**Quick check:** Some archive documents are letters. All letters are handwritten. What follows?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n**Some archive documents are handwritten.** Take a document guaranteed to be a letter. The all rule applies to that document.\n\nThe same reasoning preserves the first quantity word:\n\n| First statement | Rule | What follows |\n|---|---|---|\n| Some library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Some library books are fiction. |\n| Most library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Most library books are fiction. |\n| All library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | All library books are fiction. |\n\n**Try it:** “Most library books are mysteries. All fiction is mystery.” Can we conclude that most library books are fiction?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nNo. The all arrow goes from fiction to mystery. We cannot start at mystery and travel backward to fiction.\n\n## Two majorities of the same group must meet\n\nSuppose a club has ten members. **Most members study law**, and **most members work part time**. Each “most” needs at least six of the ten members. Those two sets cannot fit inside the club without sharing at least two people.\n\n> **Visual:** Ten club members. Six study law, six work part time, and at least two do both.\n\n**What is given?** More than half of the *same ten members* study law. More than half of those same ten work part time. The claims count club members, not all law students or all part-time workers everywhere.\n\n**Why must they meet?** Each group needs at least six members. If the groups were separate, we would need twelve different club members. There are only ten. At least two members must be in both groups.\n\n**What follows?** **Some law students work part time.** We can reverse that some claim: **some part-time workers study law**. Both sentences describe the same overlapping members. We know at least one exists; we do not know that most law students or most part-time workers have the other trait.\n\n```text\nGiven:       Most club members study law.\n             Most club members work part time.\nMust follow: Some law students work part time.\nWhy:         Both majorities count the same club members.\n```\n\n**Quick check:** A club has 25 members. Most are lawyers, and most play an instrument. What is the smallest possible number who are both lawyers and play an instrument?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n**One.** Each majority needs at least 13 members. If none overlapped, those groups would require 26 different people, but the club has only 25. All 25 could also have both traits.\n\n**Try it:** If most club members study law and most club members work part time, could the two groups of members be completely separate?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nNo. Two separate majorities would require more members than the club has. At least one member must have both traits.\n\n### When all describes that same group\n\nThere is another way to guarantee an overlap. Suppose **most club members study law**, and **all club members work part time**. We already know there are law students in the club. The all rule tells us that *each one of those members* also works part time. So **some law students work part time**.\n\n```text\nGiven:       Most club members study law.\n             All club members work part time.\nMust follow: Some law students work part time.\nWhy:         The law students already found are club members,\n             so the all rule applies to each of them.\n```\n\nWe can make the same move with **some**. If **some club members study law** and **all club members work part time**, take the member guaranteed by “some.” That person has both traits. Again, **some law students work part time**. The sentences can be stated in the other order: **all club members work part time; some club members study law**. The same person still proves the overlap.\n\n> **Visual:** An all rule covers every club member. A highlighted law student is therefore also a part-time worker.\n\n**Try it:** All A are B. All A are C. Must some B be C?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nNot yet. The two all rules tell us what is true **if** something is A, but neither tells us that any A exists. Add “at least one A exists,” and the overlap follows.\n\n## Two majorities can also compare group sizes\n\nHere is a different comparison. **Most debate team members are seniors**, but **most seniors are not on the debate team**. The seniors on the team are more than half of the team and less than half of the seniors. The same overlap takes up a larger share of the team than of the senior class. Therefore, **there are more seniors than debate team members**.\n\n> **Visual:** An example in which six of ten debate team members are seniors, while six of twenty seniors are on the team.\n\nThe numbers in the picture are one possible case. The conclusion follows from the two majority claims, not from those particular numbers.\n\n## Similar chains can leave a gap\n\nTwo some statements need not describe the same person or thing:\n\n```text\nSome volunteers speak Spanish.\nSome Spanish speakers are trained.\n```\n\nThe trained Spanish speakers could all be people who do not volunteer. We cannot conclude that any volunteers are trained.\n\n> **Visual:** Two different Spanish speakers satisfy the two some claims without any volunteer being trained.\n\nReplacing the second “some” with “most” does not fix the gap. The Spanish-speaking volunteers could sit in the untrained minority. Even two most statements that count different groups do not automatically produce a new majority claim.\n\nBefore drawing a conclusion, ask: **Am I carrying a known group through an all rule? Or do two majorities count the same group?** If neither is true, check whether the groups could miss each other.\n\n**Quick check:** A club has 13 members. Most are women, and some are dancers. How many female dancers are guaranteed? How many are possible?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n**Zero are guaranteed; as many as 13 are possible.** Seven women and one dancer meet the statements even if that dancer is one of the six men. Both traits could also belong to every member. A most claim and a some claim about the same group do not force the two traits to meet.\n\n## The moves to keep\n\n| What you have | What you may conclude |\n|---|---|\n| Some A are B | Some B are A |\n| Most A are B | Some A are B, and some B are A |\n| All A are B | A → B, and not B → not A |\n| Some/most/all A are B; all B are C | The same first quantity of A are C |\n| Most A are B; most A are C | Some B are C |\n| Most A are B; all A are C | Some B are C |\n| Some A are B; all A are C | Some B are C |\n\nTwo **all** claims about A guarantee that every A has both traits. They guarantee **some B are C** only when we also know that at least one A exists.\n\nUse the sentence behind each arrow to check what it guarantees.\n\n## Nearby words need a closer look\n\nThe words around a quantity statement can look familiar without making the same promise. Sort them by **what they guarantee**, then check the sentence in front of you:\n\n| Word or phrase | What it guarantees |\n|---|---|\n| **Some**, **at least one**, **one or more** | One or more members fit. All may fit too. |\n| **A few**, **several**, **many** | A positive number in ordinary use, but no universal cutoff. They imply at least one. |\n| **Most**, **more than half**, **a majority of** | Strictly more than half of the named group fit. |\n| **All**, **every**, **each**, **without exception** | Every member of the named group fits. The group may still need a separate existence premise. |\n| **Few**, **not many**, **not often** | A small number or low frequency in context. No exact numerical boundary follows. |\n| **No**, **none**, **zero** | Not a single member fits. |\n| **Not all** | At least one member does **not** fit. |\n\n**Few** is worth separating from **a few**. “A few books are hardcover” affirms that at least some are. “Few books are hardcover” stresses how small the number is. It often suggests some in ordinary speech, but it does not set a dependable numerical minimum. “Not many” can include zero. A hundred menu items could make five feel like few; in a menu of six, five would not feel like few. Do not quietly replace any of these phrases with a fixed number.\n\n**Most** is different: it crosses a precise line, **more than half**. Words such as **the majority** plainly express that idea. Words such as **usually**, **typically**, **generally**, **commonly**, **frequently**, **often**, **likely**, and **probably** can suggest prevalence in context, but pay attention to what the sentence actually counts. “Probably” about one event, for example, is a likelihood claim, not a headcount of a group.\n\n**Not all** *does* give us a precise minimum: at least one exception. “Not all club members are lawyers” means **at least one club member is not a lawyer**. It does not tell us whether the other members are lawyers.\n\n**Quick check:** A menu lists 100 beers. “Many are Belgian,” “few are Belgian,” and “not many are Belgian” are three claims. Can you assign each one an exact minimum and maximum? What does “not all are Belgian” guarantee?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nThe first three do **not** have fixed numerical boundaries. “Many” suggests more than an isolated example, while “few” and “not many” suggest a small number relative to the context. None alone licenses a specific cutoff such as five or ten. “Not all” is exact about one thing: **at least one beer is not Belgian**.\n\n### Pop quiz: decide whether the overlap follows\n\nFor each pair, decide whether it guarantees **some A are C**. Draw a witness or explain where the groups could miss each other before opening the answers.\n\n1. Some A are B. All B are C.\n2. Some A are B. Most A are C.\n3. All A are B. Some B are C.\n4. Some A are B. Most B are C.\n5. Some A are B. Some B are C.\n6. Most A are B. Most A are C.\n7. All A are B. All A are C.\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n1. **Yes.** The A that is B must also be C because every B is C.\n2. **No.** The A that is B could be outside the majority of A that is C.\n3. **No.** The B that is C could be outside A. The all rule runs from A to B, not back from B to A.\n4. **No.** The known A that is B could be among the B that are not C.\n5. **No.** The B in the first statement could differ from the B in the second.\n6. **Yes.** Two majorities of the same A group must share at least one member, who is both B and C.\n7. **Not from these statements alone.** Every A would be both B and C, but the statements do not establish that an A exists. If at least one A exists, the answer becomes yes.\n\n“No” here means **no guaranteed A–C overlap**. The premises may still imply a different, smaller fact. For example, statement 3\'s “some B are C” is already given.\n\n## Short drill: diagram, combine, decide\n\nHere are five statements about one volunteer program. **Volunteer**, **Spanish speaker**, **trained person**, **weekend worker**, and **student** name groups of people. Treat each sentence as true.\n\n1. Some volunteers speak Spanish.\n2. All Spanish speakers are trained.\n3. Most volunteers work weekends.\n4. Most volunteers are students.\n5. Most weekend workers are trained.\n\nFirst, diagram each statement. Then answer these without looking below:\n\n1. Which two statements prove that **some volunteers are trained**?\n2. Which two statements prove that **some students work weekends**?\n3. Do statements 3 and 5 prove that **most volunteers are trained**? Explain the gap or draw a counterexample.\n4. Can you write either valid **some** conclusion in the reverse order?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n```text\n1. Volunteers       ←some→  Spanish speakers\n2. Spanish speakers →       Trained people\n3. Volunteers       ─most→  Weekend workers\n4. Volunteers       ─most→  Students\n5. Weekend workers  ─most→  Trained people\n```\n\n**1. Statements 1 and 2.** At least one volunteer speaks Spanish. Every Spanish speaker is trained. That volunteer is trained, so **some volunteers are trained**.\n\n**2. Statements 3 and 4.** Both majorities count the volunteers. The weekend workers and students must share at least one volunteer. So **some students work weekends**.\n\n**3. No.** Statement 3 says most volunteers work weekends. Statement 5 counts all weekend workers, a different group. The volunteers who work weekends could be among the untrained weekend workers. Nothing requires most volunteers to be trained.\n\n**4. Yes.** A some statement describes an overlap in either direction: **some trained people are volunteers**, and **some weekend workers are students**.\n\n\nThe focused UI element is 1 AXWebArea Classroom transfer, URL: 127.0.0.1:8765/brainstorms/2026-09-28-recap-format/09-quantity-statements-transfer.html'}]

"Post a session recap" above puts one in their Classroom.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t80 heading NOTES AND UPLOADS, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t81 text NOTES AND UPLOADS\n\t\t\t\t\t\t82 text NOTES\n\t\t\t\t\t\t83 button Create note\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t84 image\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t85 text Create note\n\t\t\t\t\t\t86 text No notes yet.
