Use the attachment bar in the chat to add files, screenshots, or transcripts.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t89 container Post a session recap\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t90 heading Post a session recap, Value: 3, ID: recap-composer-title\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t91 text Post a session recap\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t92 text Posts immediately to the student\'s Classroom under Notes and recaps.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t93 text Title\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t94 text field (settable) Title, Value: Some, Most, and All, ID: recap-title\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t95 text Body\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t96 checkbox Preview, Value: 0\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t101 text entry area (settable) Body, ID: recap-body, Value: Quantity statements tell us whether a claim applies to some members of a group, most of them, or all of them. Suppose a class has been assigned a case to read. “Some students read it,” “most students read it,” and “all students read it” are three different claims about that same class. We do not need an exact headcount to understand the difference.\n\nFor each sentence, ask: **What must be true? What could still be true?** The answer changes with the word we use.\n\n## Some guarantees at least one\n\nImagine a shelf with eight books. I tell you that **some of the books are hardcover**. How many hardcover books must there be?\n\nAt least **one**. There could be one, four, or all eight. “Some” rules out zero. It does not rule out “most” or “all.”\n\n> **Visual:** Eight books showing that one hardcover book and eight hardcover books both satisfy some.\n\nThis is easy to miss because in ordinary conversation “some” often suggests “some, but not all.” On the LSAT, that extra phrase is not part of the statement. If all eight books are hardcover, it is still true that some are hardcover.\n\n**Try it:** “Some applicants received an interview.” Could every applicant have received one? Does the sentence tell us that anyone was denied an interview?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nEvery applicant could have received an interview. The sentence does not tell us that anyone was denied one. “Some” guarantees at least one applicant received an interview, but it leaves open how many others did.\n\nWhenever you read **some**, replace it with **at least one** in your head. That tells you exactly what the sentence guarantees:\n\n> **Some of the books are hardcover.**\n>\n> **At least one of the books is hardcover.**\n\nNow focus on that one book. It belongs to both groups: it is a book, and it is hardcover. If we describe the same object from the hardcover side, we can say:\n\n> **Some hardcover items are books.**\n>\n> **At least one hardcover item is a book.**\n\nWe have not found a new object. We have described the same overlap in the other direction. That is why a **some** statement works both ways:\n\n```text\nBooks  ←some→  Hardcover\n```\n\nThe double arrow tells us that at least one thing belongs to both groups. It does not tell us that every book is hardcover or that every hardcover item is a book.\n\n### What would make “some” false?\n\nIf **some books are hardcover** is false, then **no books are hardcover**. There is not even one book in both groups. Notice the difference between **no books are hardcover** and **some books are not hardcover**. The second sentence still allows other books to be hardcover, so it does not negate “some.”\n\n## Most guarantees more than half\n\nNow I tell you that **most of the eight books are hardcover**. We need at least **five** hardcover books. Four would be exactly half, and half is not most. Five, six, seven, or eight could satisfy the sentence.\n\n> **Visual:** Eight books showing that five hardcover books and eight hardcover books both satisfy most.\n\nNotice that all eight could still be hardcover. “Most” does not tell us that an exception exists.\n\n**Try it:** If most of the eight books are hardcover, must some of them be hardcover? Must any be paperback?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nAt least five are hardcover, so **some are hardcover**. No paperback book is required. All eight could be hardcover.\n\nHere is where the direction of the statement matters. From “most books are hardcover,” we know that **some hardcover things are books**. We cannot say that **most hardcover things are books**. Five of our eight shelf books could be hardcover, while a library holds hundreds of other hardcover items. The first statement counts the eight books; the reversed statement counts a different group.\n\n```text\nBooks  ─most→  Hardcover\nHardcover  ←some→  Books\n```\n\nThe first arrow gives the majority claim. The second line is the overlap that the majority guarantees. When we read a most statement backward, the word becomes **some**.\n\n**Quick check:** A program has 100 applicants. Most speak Spanish. What is the smallest possible number who speak Spanish? What is the largest?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n**51 to 100.** Fifty is only half. “Most” also permits all 100, so it does not establish an exception.\n\n### What would make “most” false?\n\n“Most of the eight books are hardcover” needs at least five hardcover books. Its negation permits **four or fewer**. Four is exactly half, so it already makes “most” false. The opposite of “most are hardcover” is **half or fewer are hardcover**, not “most are paperback.” Both kinds could make up exactly half.\n\n## All leaves no exception\n\nIf **all eight books are hardcover**, every book on the shelf is hardcover. One paperback on that shelf would make the statement false.\n\n> **Visual:** Eight books showing that all eight must be hardcover to satisfy all.\n\nAn all statement gives us a rule: **if it is one of these eight books, then it is hardcover**.\n\n```text\nOne of these books  →  Hardcover\nNot hardcover       →  Not one of these books\n```\n\nThe second line is the contrapositive. Both lines go with the same rule. We cannot turn the first line around and conclude that every hardcover thing is a book on this shelf.\n\n**Try it:** You pick up a paperback. What does the rule tell you? What if you pick up a hardcover book from another shelf?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nThe paperback cannot be one of these eight books. A hardcover book from another shelf does not become one of these eight just because it is hardcover. Being hardcover is required, but it is not enough to identify one of these books.\n\nThere is a small qualification. “All A are B” gives a rule about A. By itself, it does not tell us that any A exist. When we already know the group exists, all also guarantees most and some.\n\n### What would make “all” false?\n\nOne exception is enough. “Not all eight books are hardcover” means **at least one of the eight is not hardcover**. The other seven could still be hardcover. This is the negation of the all claim. By contrast, “not hardcover → not one of these eight books” is its **contrapositive**: another way to state the original rule, not a way to deny it.\n\n## Put the three statements side by side\n\nThe same shelf can help us see the whole range.\n\n> **Visual:** For eight existing books: some permits one through eight hardcover, most permits five through eight, and all requires eight.\n\nRead the implications in one direction:\n\n```text\nALL  →  MOST  →  SOME       (when the group exists)\n```\n\nIf all eight books are hardcover, then most are, and some are. If only “some” is given, all eight **could** be hardcover, but we cannot conclude that they **are**. Keep the distinction between a possible situation and a required one.\n\n## Carry a claim through an all rule\n\nNow we can combine statements. Suppose **some library books are mysteries** and **all mysteries are fiction**. We have at least one book that is a mystery. The all rule applies to every mystery, including that one. So **some library books are fiction**.\n\n```text\nLibrary books  ←some→  Mysteries  →  Fiction\nLibrary books  ←some→  Fiction\n```\n\nThe all arrow points **away from** the mystery group we reached. That is why the chain works. If the second sentence said only “most mysteries are fiction,” the mystery books we found could be among the exceptions.\n\n> **Visual:** A marked library book is inside the mysteries group, which is entirely inside the fiction group.\n\n**Quick check:** Some archive documents are letters. All letters are handwritten. What follows?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n**Some archive documents are handwritten.** Take a document guaranteed to be a letter. The all rule applies to that document.\n\nThe same reasoning preserves the first quantity word:\n\n| First statement | Rule | What follows |\n|---|---|---|\n| Some library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Some library books are fiction. |\n| Most library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Most library books are fiction. |\n| All library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | All library books are fiction. |\n\n**Try it:** “Most library books are mysteries. All fiction is mystery.” Can we conclude that most library books are fiction?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nNo. The all arrow goes from fiction to mystery. We cannot start at mystery and travel backward to fiction.\n\n## Two majorities of the same group must meet\n\nSuppose a club has ten members. **Most members study law**, and **most members work part time**. Each “most” needs at least six of the ten members. Those two sets cannot fit inside the club without sharing at least two people.\n\n> **Visual:** Ten club members. Six study law, six work part time, and at least two do both.\n\n**What is given?** More than half of the *same ten members* study law. More than half of those same ten work part time. The claims count club members, not all law students or all part-time workers everywhere.\n\n**Why must they meet?** Each group needs at least six members. If the groups were separate, we would need twelve different club members. There are only ten. At least two members must be in both groups.\n\n**What follows?** **Some law students work part time.** We can reverse that some claim: **some part-time workers study law**. Both sentences describe the same overlapping members. We know at least one exists; we do not know that most law students or most part-time workers have the other trait.\n\n```text\nGiven:       Most club members study law.\n             Most club members work part time.\nMust follow: Some law students work part time.\nWhy:         Both majorities count the same club members.\n```\n\n**Quick check:** A club has 25 members. Most are lawyers, and most play an instrument. What is the smallest possible number who are both lawyers and play an instrument?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n**One.** Each majority needs at least 13 members. If none overlapped, those groups would require 26 different people, but the club has only 25. All 25 could also have both traits.\n\n**Try it:** If most club members study law and most club members work part time, could the two groups of members be completely separate?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nNo. Two separate majorities would require more members than the club has. At least one member must have both traits.\n\n### When all describes that same group\n\nThere is another way to guarantee an overlap. Suppose **most club members study law**, and **all club members work part time**. We already know there are law students in the club. The all rule tells us that *each one of those members* also works part time. So **some law students work part time**.\n\n```text\nGiven:       Most club members study law.\n             All club members work part time.\nMust follow: Some law students work part time.\nWhy:         The law students already found are club members,\n             so the all rule applies to each of them.\n```\n\nWe can make the same move with **some**. If **some club members study law** and **all club members work part time**, take the member guaranteed by “some.” That person has both traits. Again, **some law students work part time**. The sentences can be stated in the other order: **all club members work part time; some club members study law**. The same person still proves the overlap.\n\n> **Visual:** An all rule covers every club member. A highlighted law student is therefore also a part-time worker.\n\n**Try it:** All A are B. All A are C. Must some B be C?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nNot yet. The two all rules tell us what is true **if** something is A, but neither tells us that any A exists. Add “at least one A exists,” and the overlap follows.\n\n## Two majorities can also compare group sizes\n\nHere is a different comparison. **Most debate team members are seniors**, but **most seniors are not on the debate team**. The seniors on the team are more than half of the team and less than half of the seniors. The same overlap takes up a larger share of the team than of the senior class. Therefore, **there are more seniors than debate team members**.\n\n> **Visual:** An example in which six of ten debate team members are seniors, while six of twenty seniors are on the team.\n\nThe numbers in the picture are one possible case. The conclusion follows from the two majority claims, not from those particular numbers.\n\n## Similar chains can leave a gap\n\nTwo some statements need not describe the same person or thing:\n\n```text\nSome volunteers speak Spanish.\nSome Spanish speakers are trained.\n```\n\nThe trained Spanish speakers could all be people who do not volunteer. We cannot conclude that any volunteers are trained.\n\n> **Visual:** Two different Spanish speakers satisfy the two some claims without any volunteer being trained.\n\nReplacing the second “some” with “most” does not fix the gap. The Spanish-speaking volunteers could sit in the untrained minority. Even two most statements that count different groups do not automatically produce a new majority claim.\n\nBefore drawing a conclusion, ask: **Am I carrying a known group through an all rule? Or do two majorities count the same group?** If neither is true, check whether the groups could miss each other.\n\n**Quick check:** A club has 13 members. Most are women, and some are dancers. How many female dancers are guaranteed? How many are possible?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n**Zero are guaranteed; as many as 13 are possible.** Seven women and one dancer meet the statements even if that dancer is one of the six men. Both traits could also belong to every member. A most claim and a some claim about the same group do not force the two traits to meet.\n\n## The moves to keep\n\n| What you have | What you may conclude |\n|---|---|\n| Some A are B | Some B are A |\n| Most A are B | Some A are B, and some B are A |\n| All A are B | A → B, and not B → not A |\n| Some/most/all A are B; all B are C | The same first quantity of A are C |\n| Most A are B; most A are C | Some B are C |\n| Most A are B; all A are C | Some B are C |\n| Some A are B; all A are C | Some B are C |\n\nTwo **all** claims about A guarantee that every A has both traits. They guarantee **some B are C** only when we also know that at least one A exists.\n\nUse the sentence behind each arrow to check what it guarantees.\n\n## Nearby words need a closer look\n\nThe words around a quantity statement can look familiar without making the same promise. Sort them by **what they guarantee**, then check the sentence in front of you:\n\n| Word or phrase | What it guarantees |\n|---|---|\n| **Some**, **at least one**, **one or more** | One or more members fit. All may fit too. |\n| **A few**, **several**, **many** | A positive number in ordinary use, but no universal cutoff. They imply at least one. |\n| **Most**, **more than half**, **a majority of** | Strictly more than half of the named group fit. |\n| **All**, **every**, **each**, **without exception** | Every member of the named group fits. The group may still need a separate existence premise. |\n| **Few**, **not many**, **not often** | A small number or low frequency in context. No exact numerical boundary follows. |\n| **No**, **none**, **zero** | Not a single member fits. |\n| **Not all** | At least one member does **not** fit. |\n\n**Few** is worth separating from **a few**. “A few books are hardcover” affirms that at least some are. “Few books are hardcover” stresses how small the number is. It often suggests some in ordinary speech, but it does not set a dependable numerical minimum. “Not many” can include zero. A hundred menu items could make five feel like few; in a menu of six, five would not feel like few. Do not quietly replace any of these phrases with a fixed number.\n\n**Most** is different: it crosses a precise line, **more than half**. Words such as **the majority** plainly express that idea. Words such as **usually**, **typically**, **generally**, **commonly**, **frequently**, **often**, **likely**, and **probably** can suggest prevalence in context, but pay attention to what the sentence actually counts. “Probably” about one event, for example, is a likelihood claim, not a headcount of a group.\n\n**Not all** *does* give us a precise minimum: at least one exception. “Not all club members are lawyers” means **at least one club member is not a lawyer**. It does not tell us whether the other members are lawyers.\n\n**Quick check:** A menu lists 100 beers. “Many are Belgian,” “few are Belgian,” and “not many are Belgian” are three claims. Can you assign each one an exact minimum and maximum? What does “not all are Belgian” guarantee?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nThe first three do **not** have fixed numerical boundaries. “Many” suggests more than an isolated example, while “few” and “not many” suggest a small number relative to the context. None alone licenses a specific cutoff such as five or ten. “Not all” is exact about one thing: **at least one beer is not Belgian**.\n\n### Pop quiz: decide whether the overlap follows\n\nFor each pair, decide whether it guarantees **some A are C**. Draw a witness or explain where the groups could miss each other before opening the answers.\n\n1. Some A are B. All B are C.\n2. Some A are B. Most A are C.\n3. All A are B. Some B are C.\n4. Some A are B. Most B are C.\n5. Some A are B. Some B are C.\n6. Most A are B. Most A are C.\n7. All A are B. All A are C.\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n1. **Yes.** The A that is B must also be C because every B is C.\n2. **No.** The A that is B could be outside the majority of A that is C.\n3. **No.** The B that is C could be outside A. The all rule runs from A to B, not back from B to A.\n4. **No.** The known A that is B could be among the B that are not C.\n5. **No.** The B in the first statement could differ from the B in the second.\n6. **Yes.** Two majorities of the same A group must share at least one member, who is both B and C.\n7. **Not from these statements alone.** Every A would be both B and C, but the statements do not establish that an A exists. If at least one A exists, the answer becomes yes.\n\n“No” here means **no guaranteed A–C overlap**. The premises may still imply a different, smaller fact. For example, statement 3\'s “some B are C” is already given.\n\n## Short drill: diagram, combine, decide\n\nHere are five statements about one volunteer program. **Volunteer**, **Spanish speaker**, **trained person**, **weekend worker**, and **student** name groups of people. Treat each sentence as true.\n\n1. Some volunteers speak Spanish.\n2. All Spanish speakers are trained.\n3. Most volunteers work weekends.\n4. Most volunteers are students.\n5. Most weekend workers are trained.\n\nFirst, diagram each statement. Then answer these without looking below:\n\n1. Which two statements prove that **some volunteers are trained**?\n2. Which two statements prove that **some students work weekends**?\n3. Do statements 3 and 5 prove that **most volunteers are trained**? Explain the gap or draw a counterexample.\n4. Can you write either valid **some** conclusion in the reverse order?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n```text\n1. Volunteers       ←some→  Spanish speakers\n2. Spanish speakers →       Trained people\n3. Volunteers       ─most→  Weekend workers\n4. Volunteers       ─most→  Students\n5. Weekend workers  ─most→  Trained people\n```\n\n**1. Statements 1 and 2.** At least one volunteer speaks Spanish. Every Spanish speaker is trained. That volunteer is trained, so **some volunteers are trained**.\n\n**2. Statements 3 and 4.** Both majorities count the volunteers. The weekend workers and students must share at least one volunteer. So **some students work weekends**.\n\n**3. No.** Statement 3 says most volunteers work weekends. Statement 5 counts all weekend workers, a different group. The volunteers who work weekends could be among the untrained weekend workers. Nothing requires most volunteers to be trained.\n\n**4. Yes.** A some statement describes an overlap in either direction: **some trained people are volunteers**, and **some weekend workers are students**.\n\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t98 text Markdown: ## for a heading, - for a bullet, **bold**.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t99 button Cancel\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t100 button Post recap\n\nThe focused UI element is 101 text entry area (settable) Body, ID: recap-body, Value: Quantity statements tell us whether a claim applies to some members of a group, most of them, or all of them. Suppose a class has been assigned a case to read. “Some students read it,” “most students read it,” and “all students read it” are three different claims about that same class. We do not need an exact headcount to understand the difference.\n\nFor each sentence, ask: **What must be true? What could still be true?** The answer changes with the word we use.\n\n## Some guarantees at least one\n\nImagine a shelf with eight books. I tell you that **some of the books are hardcover**. How many hardcover books must there be?\n\nAt least **one**. There could be one, four, or all eight. “Some” rules out zero. It does not rule out “most” or “all.”\n\n> **Visual:** Eight books showing that one hardcover book and eight hardcover books both satisfy some.\n\nThis is easy to miss because in ordinary conversation “some” often suggests “some, but not all.” On the LSAT, that extra phrase is not part of the statement. If all eight books are hardcover, it is still true that some are hardcover.\n\n**Try it:** “Some applicants received an interview.” Could every applicant have received one? Does the sentence tell us that anyone was denied an interview?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nEvery applicant could have received an interview. The sentence does not tell us that anyone was denied one. “Some” guarantees at least one applicant received an interview, but it leaves open how many others did.\n\nWhenever you read **some**, replace it with **at least one** in your head. That tells you exactly what the sentence guarantees:\n\n> **Some of the books are hardcover.**\n>\n> **At least one of the books is hardcover.**\n\nNow focus on that one book. It belongs to both groups: it is a book, and it is hardcover. If we describe the same object from the hardcover side, we can say:\n\n> **Some hardcover items are books.**\n>\n> **At least one hardcover item is a book.**\n\nWe have not found a new object. We have described the same overlap in the other direction. That is why a **some** statement works both ways:\n\n```text\nBooks  ←some→  Hardcover\n```\n\nThe double arrow tells us that at least one thing belongs to both groups. It does not tell us that every book is hardcover or that every hardcover item is a book.\n\n### What would make “some” false?\n\nIf **some books are hardcover** is false, then **no books are hardcover**. There is not even one book in both groups. Notice the difference between **no books are hardcover** and **some books are not hardcover**. The second sentence still allows other books to be hardcover, so it does not negate “some.”\n\n## Most guarantees more than half\n\nNow I tell you that **most of the eight books are hardcover**. We need at least **five** hardcover books. Four would be exactly half, and half is not most. Five, six, seven, or eight could satisfy the sentence.\n\n> **Visual:** Eight books showing that five hardcover books and eight hardcover books both satisfy most.\n\nNotice that all eight could still be hardcover. “Most” does not tell us that an exception exists.\n\n**Try it:** If most of the eight books are hardcover, must some of them be hardcover? Must any be paperback?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nAt least five are hardcover, so **some are hardcover**. No paperback book is required. All eight could be hardcover.\n\nHere is where the direction of the statement matters. From “most books are hardcover,” we know that **some hardcover things are books**. We cannot say that **most hardcover things are books**. Five of our eight shelf books could be hardcover, while a library holds hundreds of other hardcover items. The first statement counts the eight books; the reversed statement counts a different group.\n\n```text\nBooks  ─most→  Hardcover\nHardcover  ←some→  Books\n```\n\nThe first arrow gives the majority claim. The second line is the overlap that the majority guarantees. When we read a most statement backward, the word becomes **some**.\n\n**Quick check:** A program has 100 applicants. Most speak Spanish. What is the smallest possible number who speak Spanish? What is the largest?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n**51 to 100.** Fifty is only half. “Most” also permits all 100, so it does not establish an exception.\n\n### What would make “most” false?\n\n“Most of the eight books are hardcover” needs at least five hardcover books. Its negation permits **four or fewer**. Four is exactly half, so it already makes “most” false. The opposite of “most are hardcover” is **half or fewer are hardcover**, not “most are paperback.” Both kinds could make up exactly half.\n\n## All leaves no exception\n\nIf **all eight books are hardcover**, every book on the shelf is hardcover. One paperback on that shelf would make the statement false.\n\n> **Visual:** Eight books showing that all eight must be hardcover to satisfy all.\n\nAn all statement gives us a rule: **if it is one of these eight books, then it is hardcover**.\n\n```text\nOne of these books  →  Hardcover\nNot hardcover       →  Not one of these books\n```\n\nThe second line is the contrapositive. Both lines go with the same rule. We cannot turn the first line around and conclude that every hardcover thing is a book on this shelf.\n\n**Try it:** You pick up a paperback. What does the rule tell you? What if you pick up a hardcover book from another shelf?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nThe paperback cannot be one of these eight books. A hardcover book from another shelf does not become one of these eight just because it is hardcover. Being hardcover is required, but it is not enough to identify one of these books.\n\nThere is a small qualification. “All A are B” gives a rule about A. By itself, it does not tell us that any A exist. When we already know the group exists, all also guarantees most and some.\n\n### What would make “all” false?\n\nOne exception is enough. “Not all eight books are hardcover” means **at least one of the eight is not hardcover**. The other seven could still be hardcover. This is the negation of the all claim. By contrast, “not hardcover → not one of these eight books” is its **contrapositive**: another way to state the original rule, not a way to deny it.\n\n## Put the three statements side by side\n\nThe same shelf can help us see the whole range.\n\n> **Visual:** For eight existing books: some permits one through eight hardcover, most permits five through eight, and all requires eight.\n\nRead the implications in one direction:\n\n```text\nALL  →  MOST  →  SOME       (when the group exists)\n```\n\nIf all eight books are hardcover, then most are, and some are. If only “some” is given, all eight **could** be hardcover, but we cannot conclude that they **are**. Keep the distinction between a possible situation and a required one.\n\n## Carry a claim through an all rule\n\nNow we can combine statements. Suppose **some library books are mysteries** and **all mysteries are fiction**. We have at least one book that is a mystery. The all rule applies to every mystery, including that one. So **some library books are fiction**.\n\n```text\nLibrary books  ←some→  Mysteries  →  Fiction\nLibrary books  ←some→  Fiction\n```\n\nThe all arrow points **away from** the mystery group we reached. That is why the chain works. If the second sentence said only “most mysteries are fiction,” the mystery books we found could be among the exceptions.\n\n> **Visual:** A marked library book is inside the mysteries group, which is entirely inside the fiction group.\n\n**Quick check:** Some archive documents are letters. All letters are handwritten. What follows?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n**Some archive documents are handwritten.** Take a document guaranteed to be a letter. The all rule applies to that document.\n\nThe same reasoning preserves the first quantity word:\n\n| First statement | Rule | What follows |\n|---|---|---|\n| Some library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Some library books are fiction. |\n| Most library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Most library books are fiction. |\n| All library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | All library books are fiction. |\n\n**Try it:** “Most library books are mysteries. All fiction is mystery.” Can we conclude that most library books are fiction?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nNo. The all arrow goes from fiction to mystery. We cannot start at mystery and travel backward to fiction.\n\n## Two majorities of the same group must meet\n\nSuppose a club has ten members. **Most members study law**, and **most members work part time**. Each “most” needs at least six of the ten members. Those two sets cannot fit inside the club without sharing at least two people.\n\n> **Visual:** Ten club members. Six study law, six work part time, and at least two do both.\n\n**What is given?** More than half of the *same ten members* study law. More than half of those same ten work part time. The claims count club members, not all law students or all part-time workers everywhere.\n\n**Why must they meet?** Each group needs at least six members. If the groups were separate, we would need twelve different club members. There are only ten. At least two members must be in both groups.\n\n**What follows?** **Some law students work part time.** We can reverse that some claim: **some part-time workers study law**. Both sentences describe the same overlapping members. We know at least one exists; we do not know that most law students or most part-time workers have the other trait.\n\n```text\nGiven:       Most club members study law.\n             Most club members work part time.\nMust follow: Some law students work part time.\nWhy:         Both majorities count the same club members.\n```\n\n**Quick check:** A club has 25 members. Most are lawyers, and most play an instrument. What is the smallest possible number who are both lawyers and play an instrument?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n**One.** Each majority needs at least 13 members. If none overlapped, those groups would require 26 different people, but the club has only 25. All 25 could also have both traits.\n\n**Try it:** If most club members study law and most club members work part time, could the two groups of members be completely separate?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nNo. Two separate majorities would require more members than the club has. At least one member must have both traits.\n\n### When all describes that same group\n\nThere is another way to guarantee an overlap. Suppose **most club members study law**, and **all club members work part time**. We already know there are law students in the club. The all rule tells us that *each one of those members* also works part time. So **some law students work part time**.\n\n```text\nGiven:       Most club members study law.\n             All club members work part time.\nMust follow: Some law students work part time.\nWhy:         The law students already found are club members,\n             so the all rule applies to each of them.\n```\n\nWe can make the same move with **some**. If **some club members study law** and **all club members work part time**, take the member guaranteed by “some.” That person has both traits. Again, **some law students work part time**. The sentences can be stated in the other order: **all club members work part time; some club members study law**. The same person still proves the overlap.\n\n> **Visual:** An all rule covers every club member. A highlighted law student is therefore also a part-time worker.\n\n**Try it:** All A are B. All A are C. Must some B be C?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nNot yet. The two all rules tell us what is true **if** something is A, but neither tells us that any A exists. Add “at least one A exists,” and the overlap follows.\n\n## Two majorities can also compare group sizes\n\nHere is a different comparison. **Most debate team members are seniors**, but **most seniors are not on the debate team**. The seniors on the team are more than half of the team and less than half of the seniors. The same overlap takes up a larger share of the team than of the senior class. Therefore, **there are more seniors than debate team members**.\n\n> **Visual:** An example in which six of ten debate team members are seniors, while six of twenty seniors are on the team.\n\nThe numbers in the picture are one possible case. The conclusion follows from the two majority claims, not from those particular numbers.\n\n## Similar chains can leave a gap\n\nTwo some statements need not describe the same person or thing:\n\n```text\nSome volunteers speak Spanish.\nSome Spanish speakers are trained.\n```\n\nThe trained Spanish speakers could all be people who do not volunteer. We cannot conclude that any volunteers are trained.\n\n> **Visual:** Two different Spanish speakers satisfy the two some claims without any volunteer being trained.\n\nReplacing the second “some” with “most” does not fix the gap. The Spanish-speaking volunteers could sit in the untrained minority. Even two most statements that count different groups do not automatically produce a new majority claim.\n\nBefore drawing a conclusion, ask: **Am I carrying a known group through an all rule? Or do two majorities count the same group?** If neither is true, check whether the groups could miss each other.\n\n**Quick check:** A club has 13 members. Most are women, and some are dancers. How many female dancers are guaranteed? How many are possible?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n**Zero are guaranteed; as many as 13 are possible.** Seven women and one dancer meet the statements even if that dancer is one of the six men. Both traits could also belong to every member. A most claim and a some claim about the same group do not force the two traits to meet.\n\n## The moves to keep\n\n| What you have | What you may conclude |\n|---|---|\n| Some A are B | Some B are A |\n| Most A are B | Some A are B, and some B are A |\n| All A are B | A → B, and not B → not A |\n| Some/most/all A are B; all B are C | The same first quantity of A are C |\n| Most A are B; most A are C | Some B are C |\n| Most A are B; all A are C | Some B are C |\n| Some A are B; all A are C | Some B are C |\n\nTwo **all** claims about A guarantee that every A has both traits. They guarantee **some B are C** only when we also know that at least one A exists.\n\nUse the sentence behind each arrow to check what it guarantees.\n\n## Nearby words need a closer look\n\nThe words around a quantity statement can look familiar without making the same promise. Sort them by **what they guarantee**, then check the sentence in front of you:\n\n| Word or phrase | What it guarantees |\n|---|---|\n| **Some**, **at least one**, **one or more** | One or more members fit. All may fit too. |\n| **A few**, **several**, **many** | A positive number in ordinary use, but no universal cutoff. They imply at least one. |\n| **Most**, **more than half**, **a majority of** | Strictly more than half of the named group fit. |\n| **All**, **every**, **each**, **without exception** | Every member of the named group fits. The group may still need a separate existence premise. |\n| **Few**, **not many**, **not often** | A small number or low frequency in context. No exact numerical boundary follows. |\n| **No**, **none**, **zero** | Not a single member fits. |\n| **Not all** | At least one member does **not** fit. |\n\n**Few** is worth separating from **a few**. “A few books are hardcover” affirms that at least some are. “Few books are hardcover” stresses how small the number is. It often suggests some in ordinary speech, but it does not set a dependable numerical minimum. “Not many” can include zero. A hundred menu items could make five feel like few; in a menu of six, five would not feel like few. Do not quietly replace any of these phrases with a fixed number.\n\n**Most** is different: it crosses a precise line, **more than half**. Words such as **the majority** plainly express that idea. Words such as **usually**, **typically**, **generally**, **commonly**, **frequently**, **often**, **likely**, and **probably** can suggest prevalence in context, but pay attention to what the sentence actually counts. “Probably” about one event, for example, is a likelihood claim, not a headcount of a group.\n\n**Not all** *does* give us a precise minimum: at least one exception. “Not all club members are lawyers” means **at least one club member is not a lawyer**. It does not tell us whether the other members are lawyers.\n\n**Quick check:** A menu lists 100 beers. “Many are Belgian,” “few are Belgian,” and “not many are Belgian” are three claims. Can you assign each one an exact minimum and maximum? What does “not all are Belgian” guarantee?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\nThe first three do **not** have fixed numerical boundaries. “Many” suggests more than an isolated example, while “few” and “not many” suggest a small number relative to the context. None alone licenses a specific cutoff such as five or ten. “Not all” is exact about one thing: **at least one beer is not Belgian**.\n\n### Pop quiz: decide whether the overlap follows\n\nFor each pair, decide whether it guarantees **some A are C**. Draw a witness or explain where the groups could miss each other before opening the answers.\n\n1. Some A are B. All B are C.\n2. Some A are B. Most A are C.\n3. All A are B. Some B are C.\n4. Some A are B. Most B are C.\n5. Some A are B. Some B are C.\n6. Most A are B. Most A are C.\n7. All A are B. All A are C.\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n1. **Yes.** The A that is B must also be C because every B is C.\n2. **No.** The A that is B could be outside the majority of A that is C.\n3. **No.** The B that is C could be outside A. The all rule runs from A to B, not back from B to A.\n4. **No.** The known A that is B could be among the B that are not C.\n5. **No.** The B in the first statement could differ from the B in the second.\n6. **Yes.** Two majorities of the same A group must share at least one member, who is both B and C.\n7. **Not from these statements alone.** Every A would be both B and C, but the statements do not establish that an A exists. If at least one A exists, the answer becomes yes.\n\n“No” here means **no guaranteed A–C overlap**. The premises may still imply a different, smaller fact. For example, statement 3\'s “some B are C” is already given.\n\n## Short drill: diagram, combine, decide\n\nHere are five statements about one volunteer program. **Volunteer**, **Spanish speaker**, **trained person**, **weekend worker**, and **student** name groups of people. Treat each sentence as true.\n\n1. Some volunteers speak Spanish.\n2. All Spanish speakers are trained.\n3. Most volunteers work weekends.\n4. Most volunteers are students.\n5. Most weekend workers are trained.\n\nFirst, diagram each statement. Then answer these without looking below:\n\n1. Which two statements prove that **some volunteers are trained**?\n2. Which two statements prove that **some students work weekends**?\n3. Do statements 3 and 5 prove that **most volunteers are trained**? Explain the gap or draw a counterexample.\n4. Can you write either valid **some** conclusion in the reverse order?\n\n**Worked answer**\n\n```text\n1. Volunteers       ←some→  Spanish speakers\n2. Spanish speakers →       Trained people\n3. Volunteers       ─most→  Weekend workers\n4. Volunteers       ─most→  Students\n5. Weekend workers  ─most→  Trained people\n```\n\n**1. Statements 1 and 2.** At least one volunteer speaks Spanish. Every Spanish speaker is trained. That volunteer is trained, so **some volunteers are trained**.\n\n**2. Statements 3 and 4.** Both majorities count the volunteers. The weekend workers and students must share at least one volunteer. So **some students work weekends**.\n\n**3. No.** Statement 3 says most volunteers work weekends. Statement 5 counts all weekend workers, a different group. The volunteers who work weekends could be among the untrained weekend workers. Nothing requires most volunteers to be trained.\n\n**4. Yes.** A some statement describes an overlap in either direction: **some trained people are volunteers**, and **some weekend workers are students**.\n'}]

Use "Create note" above or the chat attachment bar.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t87 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t88 text UPLOADS No uploads yet. Use the attachment bar in the chat to add files, screenshots, or transcripts.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t89 container Post a session recap\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t90 heading Post a session recap, Value: 3, ID: recap-composer-title\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t91 text Post a session recap\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t92 text Posts immediately to the student\'s Classroom under Notes and recaps.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t93 text Title\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t94 text field (settable) Title, Value: Some, Most, and All, ID: recap-title\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t95 text Body\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t96 checkbox Back to writing, Value: 1\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t101 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t102 text Quantity statements tell us whether a claim applies to some members of a group, most of them, or all of them. Suppose a class has been assigned a case to read. “Some students read it,” “most students read it,” and “all students read it” are three different claims about that same class. We do not need an exact headcount to understand the difference. For each sentence, ask: \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t103 text What must be true? What could still be true?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t104 text  The answer changes with the word we use.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t105 heading Some guarantees at least one, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t106 text Some guarantees at least one\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t107 text Imagine a shelf with eight books. I tell you that \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t108 text some of the books are hardcover\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t109 text . How many hardcover books must there be? At least \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t110 text one\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t111 text . There could be one, four, or all eight. “Some” rules out zero. It does not rule out “most” or “all.”\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t112 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t113 text Visual:  Eight books showing that one hardcover book and eight hardcover books both satisfy some.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t114 text This is easy to miss because in ordinary conversation “some” often suggests “some, but not all.” On the LSAT, that extra phrase is not part of the statement. If all eight books are hardcover, it is still true that some are hardcover.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t115 text Try it:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t116 text  “Some applicants received an interview.” Could every applicant have received one? Does the sentence tell us that anyone was denied an interview?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t117 text Worked answer\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t118 text Every applicant could have received an interview. The sentence does not tell us that anyone was denied one. “Some” guarantees at least one applicant received an interview, but it leaves open how many others did. Whenever you read \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t119 text some\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t120 text , replace it with \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t121 text at least one\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t122 text  in your head. That tells you exactly what the sentence guarantees:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t123 text Some of the books are hardcover.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t124 text At least one of the books is hardcover.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t125 text Now focus on that one book. It belongs to both groups: it is a book, and it is hardcover. If we describe the same object from the hardcover side, we can say:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t126 text Some hardcover items are books.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t127 text At least one hardcover item is a book.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t128 text We have not found a new object. We have described the same overlap in the other direction. That is why a \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t129 text some\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t130 text  statement works both ways:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t131 text Books  ←some→  Hardcover\n\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t132 text The double arrow tells us that at least one thing belongs to both groups. It does not tell us that every book is hardcover or that every hardcover item is a book.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t133 heading What would make “some” false?, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t134 text What would make “some” false?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t135 text If \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t136 text some books are hardcover\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t137 text  is false, then \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t138 text no books are hardcover\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t139 text . There is not even one book in both groups. Notice the difference between \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t140 text no books are hardcover\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t141 text  and \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t142 text some books are not hardcover\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t143 text . The second sentence still allows other books to be hardcover, so it does not negate “some.”\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t144 heading Most guarantees more than half, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t145 text Most guarantees more than half\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t146 text Now I tell you that \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t147 text most of the eight books are hardcover\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t148 text . We need at least \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t149 text five\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t150 text  hardcover books. Four would be exactly half, and half is not most. Five, six, seven, or eight could satisfy the sentence.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t151 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t152 text Visual:  Eight books showing that five hardcover books and eight hardcover books both satisfy most.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t153 text Notice that all eight could still be hardcover. “Most” does not tell us that an exception exists.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t154 text Try it:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t155 text  If most of the eight books are hardcover, must some of them be hardcover? Must any be paperback?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t156 text Worked answer\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t157 text At least five are hardcover, so \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t158 text some are hardcover\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t159 text . No paperback book is required. All eight could be hardcover. Here is where the direction of the statement matters. From “most books are hardcover,” we know that \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t160 text some hardcover things are books\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t161 text . We cannot say that \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t162 text most hardcover things are books\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t163 text . Five of our eight shelf books could be hardcover, while a library holds hundreds of other hardcover items. The first statement counts the eight books; the reversed statement counts a different group.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t164 text Books  ─most→  Hardcover\nHardcover  ←some→  Books\n\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t165 text The first arrow gives the majority claim. The second line is the overlap that the majority guarantees. When we read a most statement backward, the word becomes \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t166 text some\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t167 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t168 text Quick check:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t169 text  A program has 100 applicants. Most speak Spanish. What is the smallest possible number who speak Spanish? What is the largest?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t170 text Worked answer\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t171 text 51 to 100.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t172 text  Fifty is only half. “Most” also permits all 100, so it does not establish an exception.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t173 heading What would make “most” false?, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t174 text What would make “most” false?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t175 text “Most of the eight books are hardcover” needs at least five hardcover books. Its negation permits \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t176 text four or fewer\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t177 text . Four is exactly half, so it already makes “most” false. The opposite of “most are hardcover” is \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t178 text half or fewer are hardcover\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t179 text , not “most are paperback.” Both kinds could make up exactly half.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t180 heading All leaves no exception, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t181 text All leaves no exception\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t182 text If \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t183 text all eight books are hardcover\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t184 text , every book on the shelf is hardcover. One paperback on that shelf would make the statement false.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t185 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t186 text Visual:  Eight books showing that all eight must be hardcover to satisfy all.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t187 text An all statement gives us a rule: \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t188 text if it is one of these eight books, then it is hardcover\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t189 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t190 text One of these books  →  Hardcover\nNot hardcover       →  Not one of these books\n\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t191 text The second line is the contrapositive. Both lines go with the same rule. We cannot turn the first line around and conclude that every hardcover thing is a book on this shelf.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t192 text Try it:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t193 text  You pick up a paperback. What does the rule tell you? What if you pick up a hardcover book from another shelf?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t194 text Worked answer\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t195 text The paperback cannot be one of these eight books. A hardcover book from another shelf does not become one of these eight just because it is hardcover. Being hardcover is required, but it is not enough to identify one of these books. There is a small qualification. “All A are B” gives a rule about A. By itself, it does not tell us that any A exist. When we already know the group exists, all also guarantees most and some.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t196 heading What would make “all” false?, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t197 text What would make “all” false?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t198 text One exception is enough. “Not all eight books are hardcover” means \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t199 text at least one of the eight is not hardcover\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t200 text . The other seven could still be hardcover. This is the negation of the all claim. By contrast, “not hardcover → not one of these eight books” is its \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t201 text contrapositive\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t202 text : another way to state the original rule, not a way to deny it.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t203 heading Put the three statements side by side, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t204 text Put the three statements side by side\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t205 text The same shelf can help us see the whole range.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t206 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t207 text Visual:  For eight existing books: some permits one through eight hardcover, most permits five through eight, and all requires eight.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t208 text Read the implications in one direction:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t209 text ALL  →  MOST  →  SOME       (when the group exists)\n\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t210 text If all eight books are hardcover, then most are, and some are. If only “some” is given, all eight \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t211 text could\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t212 text  be hardcover, but we cannot conclude that they \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t213 text are\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t214 text . Keep the distinction between a possible situation and a required one.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t215 heading Carry a claim through an all rule, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t216 text Carry a claim through an all rule\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t217 text Now we can combine statements. Suppose \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t218 text some library books are mysteries\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t219 text  and \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t220 text all mysteries are fiction\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t221 text . We have at least one book that is a mystery. The all rule applies to every mystery, including that one. So \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t222 text some library books are fiction\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t223 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t224 text Library books  ←some→  Mysteries  →  Fiction\nLibrary books  ←some→  Fiction\n\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t225 text The all arrow points \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t226 text away from\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t227 text  the mystery group we reached. That is why the chain works. If the second sentence said only “most mysteries are fiction,” the mystery books we found could be among the exceptions.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t228 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t229 text Visual:  A marked library book is inside the mysteries group, which is entirely inside the fiction group.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t230 text Quick check:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t231 text  Some archive documents are letters. All letters are handwritten. What follows?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t232 text Worked answer\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t233 text Some archive documents are handwritten.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t234 text  Take a document guaranteed to be a letter. The all rule applies to that document. The same reasoning preserves the first quantity word: | First statement | Rule | What follows | |---|---|---| | Some library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Some library books are fiction. | | Most library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | Most library books are fiction. | | All library books are mysteries. | All mysteries are fiction. | All library books are fiction. |\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t235 text Try it:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t236 text  “Most library books are mysteries. All fiction is mystery.” Can we conclude that most library books are fiction?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t237 text Worked answer\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t238 text No. The all arrow goes from fiction to mystery. We cannot start at mystery and travel backward to fiction.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t239 heading Two majorities of the same group must meet, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t240 text Two majorities of the same group must meet\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t241 text Suppose a club has ten members. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t242 text Most members study law\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t243 text , and \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t244 text most members work part time\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t245 text . Each “most” needs at least six of the ten members. Those two sets cannot fit inside the club without sharing at least two people.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t246 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t247 text Visual:  Ten club members. Six study law, six work part time, and at least two do both.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t248 text What is given?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t249 text  More than half of the \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t250 text same ten members\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t251 text  study law. More than half of those same ten work part time. The claims count club members, not all law students or all part-time workers everywhere.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t252 text Why must they meet?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t253 text  Each group needs at least six members. If the groups were separate, we would need twelve different club members. There are only ten. At least two members must be in both groups.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t254 text What follows?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t255 text Some law students work part time.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t256 text  We can reverse that some claim: \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t257 text some part-time workers study law\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t258 text . Both sentences describe the same overlapping members. We know at least one exists; we do not know that most law students or most part-time workers have the other trait.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t259 text Given:       Most club members study law.\n             Most club members work part time.\nMust follow: Some law students work part time.\nWhy:         Both majorities count the same club members.\n\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t260 text Quick check:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t261 text  A club has 25 members. Most are lawyers, and most play an instrument. What is the smallest possible number who are both lawyers and play an instrument?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t262 text Worked answer\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t263 text One.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t264 text  Each majority needs at least 13 members. If none overlapped, those groups would require 26 different people, but the club has only 25. All 25 could also have both traits.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t265 text Try it:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t266 text  If most club members study law and most club members work part time, could the two groups of members be completely separate?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t267 text Worked answer\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t268 text No. Two separate majorities would require more members than the club has. At least one member must have both traits.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t269 heading When all describes that same group, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t270 text When all describes that same group\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t271 text There is another way to guarantee an overlap. Suppose \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t272 text most club members study law\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t273 text , and \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t274 text all club members work part time\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t275 text . We already know there are law students in the club. The all rule tells us that \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t276 text each one of those members\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t277 text  also works part time. So \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t278 text some law students work part time\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t279 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t280 text Given:       Most club members study law.\n             All club members work part time.\nMust follow: Some law students work part time.\nWhy:         The law students already found are club members,\n             so the all rule applies to each of them.\n\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t281 text We can make the same move with \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t282 text some\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t283 text . If \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t284 text some club members study law\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t285 text  and \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t286 text all club members work part time\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t287 text , take the member guaranteed by “some.” That person has both traits. Again, \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t288 text some law students work part time\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t289 text . The sentences can be stated in the other order: \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t290 text all club members work part time; some club members study law\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t291 text . The same person still proves the overlap.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t292 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t293 text Visual:  An all rule covers every club member. A highlighted law student is therefore also a part-time worker.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t294 text Try it:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t295 text  All A are B. All A are C. Must some B be C?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t296 text Worked answer\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t297 text Not yet. The two all rules tell us what is true \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t298 text if\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t299 text  something is A, but neither tells us that any A exists. Add “at least one A exists,” and the overlap follows.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t300 heading Two majorities can also compare group sizes, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t301 text Two majorities can also compare group sizes\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t302 text Here is a different comparison. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t303 text Most debate team members are seniors\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t304 text , but \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t305 text most seniors are not on the debate team\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t306 text . The seniors on the team are more than half of the team and less than half of the seniors. The same overlap takes up a larger share of the team than of the senior class. Therefore, \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t307 text there are more seniors than debate team members\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t308 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t309 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t310 text Visual:  An example in which six of ten debate team members are seniors, while six of twenty seniors are on the team.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t311 text The numbers in the picture are one possible case. The conclusion follows from the two majority claims, not from those particular numbers.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t312 heading Similar chains can leave a gap, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t313 text Similar chains can leave a gap\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t314 text Two some statements need not describe the same person or thing:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t315 text Some volunteers speak Spanish.\nSome Spanish speakers are trained.\n\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t316 text The trained Spanish speakers could all be people who do not volunteer. We cannot conclude that any volunteers are trained.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t317 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t318 text Visual:  Two different Spanish speakers satisfy the two some claims without any volunteer being trained.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t319 text Replacing the second “some” with “most” does not fix the gap. The Spanish-speaking volunteers could sit in the untrained minority. Even two most statements that count different groups do not automatically produce a new majority claim. Before drawing a conclusion, ask: \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t320 text Am I carrying a known group through an all rule? Or do two majorities count the same group?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t321 text  If neither is true, check whether the groups could miss each other.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t322 text Quick check:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t323 text  A club has 13 members. Most are women, and some are dancers. How many female dancers are guaranteed? How many are possible?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t324 text Worked answer\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t325 text Zero are guaranteed; as many as 13 are possible.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t326 text  Seven women and one dancer meet the statements even if that dancer is one of the six men. Both traits could also belong to every member. A most claim and a some claim about the same group do not force the two traits to meet.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t327 heading The moves to keep, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t328 text The moves to keep\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t329 text | What you have | What you may conclude | |---|---| | Some A are B | Some B are A | | Most A are B | Some A are B, and some B are A | | All A are B | A → B, and not B → not A | | Some/most/all A are B; all B are C | The same first quantity of A are C | | Most A are B; most A are C | Some B are C | | Most A are B; all A are C | Some B are C | | Some A are B; all A are C | Some B are C | Two \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t330 text all\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t331 text  claims about A guarantee that every A has both traits. They guarantee \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t332 text some B are C\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t333 text  only when we also know that at least one A exists. Use the sentence behind each arrow to check what it guarantees.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t334 heading Nearby words need a closer look, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t335 text Nearby words need a closer look\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t336 text The words around a quantity statement can look familiar without making the same promise. Sort them by \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t337 text what they guarantee\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t338 text , then check the sentence in front of you: | Word or phrase | What it guarantees | |---|---| | \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t339 text Some\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t340 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t341 text at least one\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t342 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t343 text one or more\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t344 text  | One or more members fit. All may fit too. | | \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t345 text A few\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t346 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t347 text several\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t348 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t349 text many\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t350 text  | A positive number in ordinary use, but no universal cutoff. They imply at least one. | | \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t351 text Most\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t352 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t353 text more than half\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t354 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t355 text a majority of\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t356 text  | Strictly more than half of the named group fit. | | \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t357 text All\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t358 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t359 text every\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t360 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t361 text each\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t362 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t363 text without exception\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t364 text  | Every member of the named group fits. The group may still need a separate existence premise. | | \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t365 text Few\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t366 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t367 text not many\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t368 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t369 text not often\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t370 text  | A small number or low frequency in context. No exact numerical boundary follows. | | \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t371 text No\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t372 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t373 text none\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t374 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t375 text zero\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t376 text  | Not a single member fits. | | \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t377 text Not all\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t378 text  | At least one member does \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t379 text not\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t380 text  fit. |\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t381 text Few\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t382 text  is worth separating from \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t383 text a few\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t384 text . “A few books are hardcover” affirms that at least some are. “Few books are hardcover” stresses how small the number is. It often suggests some in ordinary speech, but it does not set a dependable numerical minimum. “Not many” can include zero. A hundred menu items could make five feel like few; in a menu of six, five would not feel like few. Do not quietly replace any of these phrases with a fixed number.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t385 text Most\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t386 text  is different: it crosses a precise line, \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t387 text more than half\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t388 text . Words such as \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t389 text the majority\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t390 text  plainly express that idea. Words such as \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t391 text usually\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t392 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t393 text typically\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t394 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t395 text generally\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t396 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t397 text commonly\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t398 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t399 text frequently\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t400 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t401 text often\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t402 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t403 text likely\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t404 text , and \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t405 text probably\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t406 text  can suggest prevalence in context, but pay attention to what the sentence actually counts. “Probably” about one event, for example, is a likelihood claim, not a headcount of a group.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t407 text Not all\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t408 text does\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t409 text  give us a precise minimum: at least one exception. “Not all club members are lawyers” means \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t410 text at least one club member is not a lawyer\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t411 text . It does not tell us whether the other members are lawyers.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t412 text Quick check:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t413 text  A menu lists 100 beers. “Many are Belgian,” “few are Belgian,” and “not many are Belgian” are three claims. Can you assign each one an exact minimum and maximum? What does “not all are Belgian” guarantee?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t414 text Worked answer\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t415 text The first three do \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t416 text not\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t417 text  have fixed numerical boundaries. “Many” suggests more than an isolated example, while “few” and “not many” suggest a small number relative to the context. None alone licenses a specific cutoff such as five or ten. “Not all” is exact about one thing: \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t418 text at least one beer is not Belgian\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t419 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t420 heading Pop quiz: decide whether the overlap follows, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t421 text Pop quiz: decide whether the overlap follows\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t422 text For each pair, decide whether it guarantees \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t423 text some A are C\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t424 text . The A that is B must also be C because every B is C.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t452 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t453 AXListMarker 2. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t454 text No.  The A that is B could be outside the majority of A that is C.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t455 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t456 AXListMarker 3. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t457 text No.  The B that is C could be outside A. The all rule runs from A to B, not back from B to A.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t458 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t459 AXListMarker 4. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t460 text No.  The known A that is B could be among the B that are not C.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t461 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t462 AXListMarker 5. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t463 text No.  The B in the first statement could differ from the B in the second.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t464 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t465 AXListMarker 6. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t466 text Yes. Treat each sentence as true.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t486 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t487 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t488 AXListMarker 1. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t489 text Some volunteers speak Spanish.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t490 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t491 AXListMarker 2. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t492 text All Spanish speakers are trained.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t493 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t494 AXListMarker 3. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t495 text Most volunteers work weekends.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t496 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t497 AXListMarker 4. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t498 text Most volunteers are students.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t499 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t500 AXListMarker 5. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t501 text Most weekend workers are trained.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t502 text First, diagram each statement. That volunteer is trained, so \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t520 text some volunteers are trained\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t521 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t522 text 2. Yes.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t529 text  A some statement describes an overlap in either direction: \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t530 text some trained people are volunteers\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t531 text , and \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t532 text some weekend workers are students\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t533 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t98 text Markdown: ## for a heading, - for a bullet, **bold**.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t99 button Cancel\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t100 button Post recap\n\nThe focused UI element is 96 checkbox Back to writing, Value: 1'}]
